How this manual was written

Every chapter was written from the source code and the project documentation. Every reference to a file, function or table was checked in the code. A summary of docs/ or docs/regulatory/ names its source (see How to read this manual). The English chapters are a translation of the Dutch ones, with the same structure and the same references.

1. General architecture & structure

This chapter is the map for the rest of the manual. It describes the three layers of CoGA (frontend, backend and two databases) and follows one request from a click in the browser to the data and back. It points out where the folders, the configuration and the main security measures are. It summarises docs/application-scheme.md and the technical file (docs/regulatory/TF-02-device-description.md).

CoGA in brief

CoGA (Comprehensive Genomic Analysis) is a platform for variant interpretation, genome visualisation and clinical review at family level. It runs as an in-house IVD under IVDR Article 5(5) at CMGG, an ISO 15189-accredited laboratory. IVD stands for in-vitro diagnostics; the IVDR is the European regulation for it. The regulated part (the "device boundary") runs from the annotated VCF file to the closed, frozen analysis in CoGA. A supervisor (or a user with a higher role) closes the analysis with Sign out: the analytical sign-out, which freezes the analysis. The clinical report is drafted and medically signed off in the EPD (the hospital's electronic patient record) and refers 1:1 to that analysis. The EPD is outside the device. The data in the system is synthetic.

The three layers

Layer Technology Role Where in the code
Frontend React and TypeScript (built with Vite, styled with Tailwind) The user interface: login, dashboard, family workspace, filter pages, visualisations frontend/src/
Backend FastAPI (Python) The API server: authentication, access control, clinical logic, database queries backend/app/
Databases Postgres and ClickHouse Metadata and review state (Postgres) alongside the large variant store (ClickHouse) backend/db/schema/ and the ClickHouse services in backend/app/services/

Each layer has one task. This makes it clear where access control, validation and storage happen, which makes auditing and debugging simpler.

Why two databases?

  • Postgres is a relational database and the source of truth for metadata and state: users and project access, families, samples and pedigree, reviews and classifications, panels, reference data and the audit trail. That data is relatively small, highly structured and changes often.
  • ClickHouse is a column-oriented database for very large datasets. It stores the variant rows (small variants and structural variants), the genotypes per sample and the large interval tracks (coverage, CNV segments, APCAD, haplotypes). One family can have millions of rows.

For every request, Postgres first decides who may see what. Then the backend fetches the variants from ClickHouse and attaches the review state from Postgres to them, e.g. a tag or an ACMG class. Chapter 3 describes the tables.

Where in the code: backend/app/core/postgres.py and backend/app/core/clickhouse.py (the connections). The division of tasks is in docs/application-scheme.md, section Storage boundary: "Postgres is authoritative for metadata and state. ClickHouse is authoritative for variant payloads."

From click to data: the path of one request

Example: an analyst opens the small variants of a family.

  1. Click in the browser. The page (e.g. frontend/src/pages/families/FamilySmallVariantsPage.tsx) requests data through the shared API client.
  2. The API client sends the request. Almost all requests go through one axios instance (axios is a JavaScript library for HTTP requests) with the base address /api. An interceptor (code that intercepts every outgoing request) adds the JWT token as Authorization: Bearer <token>, except when logging in, registering and requesting the sign-in method. A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed access credential; chapter 5 explains it. Two parts send the token themselves. The embedded IGV browser fetches its alignments and tracks itself and requests the token for every request, as the interceptor does. The last UI events when leaving a page carry the session's token, which the telemetry refreshes in time (chapter 15).
  3. The request reaches the backend. In development the Vite development server forwards /api to the backend; in the Docker setup the frontend container does this (frontend/server.mjs). All routers are mounted under /api, except GET /metrics for monitoring, which deliberately sits outside it (chapter 7). First the request passes through a series of middleware (intermediate layers that process every request and response): client-IP determination behind proxies (TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS), security headers, trailing-slash normalisation and request logging/audit. Chapter 7 describes the order.
  4. The router checks access. Every protected endpoint requires the dependency get_current_user (a function that FastAPI runs before the endpoint). It checks the token and loads the user fresh from Postgres. Access is project-scoped (RBAC: Role-Based Access Control); chapter 2 explains how.
  5. A service does the actual work. Routers stay thin; the clinical logic is in backend/app/services/, for family variants e.g. in clickhouse_family_variants.py.
  6. The service queries the right database. Metadata comes from Postgres (through SQLAlchemy, asynchronously), variants from ClickHouse (through a direct client). All values are passed as parameters, never as text in the query (chapter 7).
  7. The response goes back. FastAPI converts the result to JSON, the middleware adds the security headers and the browser shows it. If the client gets a 401 (not signed in), it clears the session and returns to /login.

Where in the code: frontend/src/lib/api.ts (API client and interceptors), frontend/vite.config.mts (development proxy), backend/app/main.py (app, middleware and routers), backend/app/dependencies.py (get_current_user). The same flow is described in docs/application-scheme.md, section Runtime flow.

Frontend and backend are separate processes that talk to each other only through HTTP and JSON. That separation is deliberate: all access control happens on the server, not in the browser.

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: which websites may call the API) is configured strictly:

  • An origin pattern must be fully anchored: start with ^ and end with $. Otherwise the configuration refuses it, because a pattern that is too broad, together with credentials sent along, opens a way around.
  • Outside development the backend does not start as long as CORS_ORIGINS or CORS_ORIGIN_REGEX allows a local origin (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1, 0.0.0.0) or any site at all. The development settings allow localhost; in that case a page on the user's own machine could call the API as that signed-in user.
  • A deployment serves the interface from its own origin and needs no cross-origin access. Terraform sets that own origin and an empty pattern.

Where in the code: the CORSMiddleware in backend/app/main.py; in backend/app/core/config.py, validate_cors_origin_regex (the anchoring) and _cross_origin_exposures, which validate_security_defaults calls outside development.

The folders at a glance

The repository holds two application folders (backend/, frontend/), the documentation (docs/), the infrastructure as code for Google Cloud (terraform/) and the Docker Compose files.

Folder or file (backend) Role
backend/app/core/ Connections and runtime: settings (config.py), Postgres, ClickHouse, Azure, logging, a family's folders
backend/app/routers/ The API: one file per domain, bundled in routers/__init__.py
backend/app/services/ The clinical and business logic, including the traceability stack
backend/app/middleware/ Intermediate layers for client IP, security headers and request logging
backend/app/main.py Builds the app: routers, CORS, middleware and the startup routine
backend/app/db_migrate.py Schema migration and first administrator, also runnable as a separate step
backend/db/schema/ The five Postgres baselines (01_access to 05_grants) and the ClickHouse bootstrap
backend/db/migrations/ The Alembic revision 0001, which sets up an empty database from the five baselines; the migration ledger alembic_version records the revision
Folder (frontend) Role
frontend/src/pages/ The screens, grouped by domain
frontend/src/components/ Reusable building blocks, including the route guards and visualizations/
frontend/src/lib/ Non-visual helper code: API client, session, genotypes, ACMG logic
frontend/src/content/docs/ The in-app documentation (user guide and reference docs), shown at /docs

Routing uses react-router. Only the sign-in pages (/login and /login/emergency) and /signup are public. All other screens sit behind the guard RequireAuth. The administration screens (among others /admin/..., with the projects under /admin/access/projects) also sit behind RequireAdmin; the administration dashboard /admin and the workspaces of a superuser (among others /package-import) behind <RequireAdmin superuser />, which also lets a superuser through. Those guards are a convenience, not security (chapter 2).

There is no navigation bar. The main sections (Projects, Variant explorer, Gene explorer, CNV explorer, Panels, Report codes, for a superuser or administrator Admin, and User guide) are in a menu behind a small arrow on the right of the header bar. Below the header bar, a breadcrumb trail follows the route. On a family, the project the workspace works in sits between Families and the family; it leads to the dashboard with that project expanded.

Where in the code: the route tree in frontend/src/index.tsx; the menu in frontend/src/components/HeaderMenu.tsx and the breadcrumb trail in Breadcrumbs.tsx.

Configuration

All settings come in as environment variables and are bundled in one Settings object, which the rest of the code reads. .env.example lists every setting with its default value. The configuration is also a security measure: outside development the backend refuses to start with weak or missing secrets. The full rule is in chapter 2.

Where in the code: backend/app/core/config.py (Settings and validate_security_defaults). The API prefix /api is also there, as API_PATH_PREFIX.

Containers and startup

The stack runs through Docker Compose as five services: postgres, clickhouse, backend, import-worker (the package imports, chapter 4) and frontend. The database images are pinned to an exact digest, for reproducibility. The backend starts only once both databases are healthy; the frontend and the import worker only once the backend is healthy. ClickHouse gets a generous shutdown grace period, because a write that is cut off too early can damage data parts. The development variant docker-compose.dev.yml sets APP_ENV=development, reloads changed code immediately and uses the Vite development server.

What the backend does at startup (schema, first administrator, reference data, background tasks) is in chapter 4.

Where in the code: docker-compose.yml, docker-compose.dev.yml and the lifespan function in backend/app/main.py.

Security and traceability in the architecture

  • Access control on the server. All authorisation happens in the backend (get_current_user, get_current_superuser, get_current_admin_user and the project scoping). The browser decides nothing.
  • Every request leaves a trace. The request-logging middleware writes every HTTP request to the append-only table audit_log_events. The clinical audit trail and the report sign-out records are, in addition, append-only and hash-chained: each row refers cryptographically to the previous one, so that changing or deleting becomes visible (chapter 11).
  • No schema disclosure. Outside development, /docs, /redoc and /openapi.json are switched off.
  • Fail-closed configuration. The app does not start with weak secrets or unsafe production settings (chapter 2).
  • One clear source of truth. Metadata is in Postgres, variants in ClickHouse: for each piece of data, one database is authoritative.

Where in the code: backend/app/dependencies.py, backend/app/middleware/, _docs_kwargs in backend/app/main.py, and the traceability services in backend/app/services/ (among others clinical_audit_service.py, hash_chain.py and integrity_anchor_service.py).

Technology

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, react-router, TanStack Query (server state and caching), axios, D3 (visualisations) and igv (the embedded IGV genome browser); tests with Vitest and Playwright.
  • Backend: FastAPI with Uvicorn, SQLAlchemy (asynchronous) with asyncpg for Postgres, clickhouse-connect for ClickHouse, Pydantic (validation and settings), PyJWT (tokens), bcrypt (passwords) and cryptography (among others the signature of the integrity anchors).

The exact versions are in frontend/package-lock.json and backend/requirements.txt; the SOUP register (docs/regulatory/TF-08-soup-register.md) tracks them for the technical file. The product version is in VERSION.

The field app_version in the backend is the build identity. It is filled in when the image is built and frozen in every signed report (chapter 11). Only the release build gets the version from VERSION itself. Every other build (from main, manual or local) gets that version with dev added (0.1.0-dev, or 0.1.0-rc.1.dev after the release candidate), so that it can never pass for a release (scripts/build-version.sh).

Key files

File Role
docs/application-scheme.md Architecture and storage boundaries
backend/app/main.py Builds the app: routers, CORS, middleware, startup routine
backend/app/routers/__init__.py Bundles all routers
backend/app/dependencies.py get_current_user, get_current_superuser, get_current_admin_user and token issuance
backend/app/core/config.py All settings and the fail-closed checks
frontend/src/index.tsx Frontend entry point and route tree with guards
frontend/src/lib/api.ts The shared API client: /api base, token and 401 handling
docker-compose.yml / docker-compose.dev.yml The five services (Docker setup and development)

2. User roles, permissions & isolation

This chapter is about who may see or do something: the five global roles, isolation per project and the access level per project (analyst or reader). Then comes defence in depth: a restricted database role, security headers and CORS, the refusal of weak secrets and the protection of uploads. The source is docs/security-posture.md; the cybersecurity analysis for the technical file is in docs/regulatory/TF-13-cybersecurity.md.

A few terms first. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is access based on roles. A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed access credential that the browser sends along with every request. In FastAPI (the Python framework of the backend), a dependency is a function that runs before an endpoint and can refuse the request. An endpoint is one API address, e.g. GET /api/families/{family_id}.

Which roles exist

CoGA has five global roles (users.role), listed here from low to high. Each role has all the rights of the roles before it. The database allows no other value. The owner decided this on 2026-11-04.

Role What this role may do
viewer Read, in the projects they are a member of: view and search the families, samples, variants, tracks, reports and signed versions, export CSV and print. They change nothing, whatever access level they have in a project. The only things they save are their own filter presets and the events of their own use of the interface. They do not see the clinical audit trail. Every new account starts as viewer, without a project.
analyst Also analyse, in the projects where their access level is analyst (see Access level per project): review and tag, ACMG and CNV classifications, phenotypes, the workflow fields (status, assigned to, reviewed by) and new families (Family Builder). There they also read the clinical audit trail.
supervisor Also close an analysis with Sign out, the analytical sign-out, in the projects where they are analyst (see Signing out: supervisor or higher). The medical sign-off of the clinical report takes place in the EPD, not in CoGA.
superuser Also every project, member or not: they see and change every record, sign out everywhere, and appear in the Assigned to and Reviewed by drop-down lists of every family. In addition, the configuration the analyses read: gene panels, variant tags, preset filters and the sequencing QC thresholds, and the package import, except overwriting an existing family.
admin The administrator: also all of the administration (see Superuser or administrator below).

In this manual an administrator is someone with the role admin. A superuser never counts as an administrator.

Where in the code: the allowed roles are a CHECK rule on the table users in backend/db/schema/postgres/01_access.sql. In the backend they are in backend/app/services/access_control.py: the order in USER_ROLES, with has_role (this role or a higher one), and for each right the roles that have it: CHANGING_ROLES (analyst and higher), SIGN_OUT_ROLES (supervisor and higher), SUPERUSER_ROLES (superuser and admin) and ADMIN_ROLES (only admin). The functions that query them are role_changes_records, may_sign_out, has_superuser_rights and is_admin_user (only admin). In the frontend: USER_ROLES, hasRole, isAdmin (only admin) and hasSuperuserRights in frontend/src/lib/auth.ts.

Superuser or administrator. Besides every project, a superuser has:

  • the gene panels: create, change and delete them, import a PanelApp panel and rebuild the Mendeliome (chapter 15);
  • the variant tags: create, change and delete the custom tags, on the administration page and on the routes of a family (chapter 10);
  • the overview of everyone's preset filters (chapter 15);
  • the sequencing QC thresholds (chapter 15);
  • the package import: the routes /api/family-imports, with everyone's import jobs (chapter 6). They may not overwrite an existing family (conflict_mode: "overwrite", not a dry run); as a dry run they may, and cancel and update too.

On the administration dashboard they see only those five workspaces: Gene panels, Sequencing QC thresholds, Package import, Variant tags and Preset filters. All the rest of the administration is for an administrator only: accounts and roles (the Users page, PATCH /api/auth/users/{id}) and the account list GET /api/users; projects and their access; the family and sample data and their deletion; the family statuses; organisms and assemblies; HPO, Monarch and the repeat catalogue; ClickHouse maintenance; the audit logs and the integrity checks; the NIPT artefacts; replacing a family's annotation manifest; refreshing the gene reference; rebuilding the clinical CNV knowledge base; a PED upload and the separate per-file uploads; editing the family structure; and overwriting an existing family, with a PED upload, the Family Builder or a package import (REQ-SEC-002).

Assigning a role. An administrator sets an account's role on the Users page (PATCH /api/auth/users/{id} with role), after a confirmation in a dialog. The drop-down list shows the five roles from low to high, each with a tooltip that says what the role may do. Nobody changes their own role or deactivates their own account. The emergency administrator (chapter 5) keeps the role admin and stays active. Every change is in the request's audit row, with the role before and after (request_meta.account_change). Anyone who registers, or signs in for the first time with Microsoft or via CAS, gets an account with the role viewer and without a project. They see no patient data until an administrator adds them to a project, and change nothing until an administrator gives them a higher role (chapter 5).

Who signs out. Only a supervisor or higher can sign out: an administrator gives the role supervisor to whoever the laboratory authorises to do so. An analyst changes the records of the projects in which they are analyst, but does not sign out.

There is no separate permissions table per user. What someone may see follows from their role and their project membership: the link table project_users, which for each member also stores their access level in that project. A family is attached to one or more projects through family_projects. A sample is visible through the projects of its family. sample_projects additionally links a sample directly to projects, among other things for the sample drop-down list of the Variant Explorer. A viewer, analyst or supervisor therefore sees exactly the families of which at least one project is also one of their projects; a superuser and an administrator see them all.

The token carries only the identity: the user's object ID for a Microsoft token, the email address for a local token. The role and the project list are not in it. On every request the backend loads the user, their role, their projects and their access level in each of them fresh from Postgres. Revoking therefore takes effect immediately. Anyone who is deactivated, removed from a project, made a reader there or given a lower role loses the access or the right at the next request, without waiting for the token to expire. An administrator who becomes superuser thus loses the administration; a supervisor who becomes analyst loses signing out.

A job that has not yet run does not run if the account that requested it has since been deactivated or has lost the role the job requires (decision of the owner of 2026-10-28). For an import job (chapter 6) that role is superuser or administrator, and administrator for an import that overwrites an existing family; for a refresh of the gene reference (chapter 13) and a rebuild of the clinical CNV knowledge base (chapter 15) it is administrator. That rebuild also loads nothing if the deactivation or the loss of the role only happened during its build. The job ends failed with the reason, and nothing is written.

Project-scoped access: how every data request is restricted

Every request for a family, sample or variant passes through the same checkpoint. There are two mechanisms: one for lists, one for single objects.

Lists are filtered in the database, not afterwards. When a user requests the families, the project filter is in the SQL query itself: an EXISTS condition on family_projects lets through only families attached to at least one of their projects. Families outside their projects therefore never leave the database; a forgotten filter in the application code cannot let them leak. A user without projects immediately gets an empty list. For a superuser and an administrator the filter is dropped (has_superuser_rights).

Single objects are checked when they are fetched. When someone requests one family by its id, the backend checks whether the projects of that family and those of the user overlap. If not, the backend answers exactly as for a non-existent id: HTTP 404 with Family not found, or for a sample Sample not found. A project outside the user's projects, given in the Family Builder or for a gene profile, likewise gets 404 Project not found. A superuser and an administrator pass. So nobody can open a family by guessing its id (protection against IDOR, Insecure Direct Object Reference). Nor does the answer reveal whether a family or sample of another project exists. The audit log does record the difference (request_meta.record_hidden, chapter 7).

Both checks come together in build_family_metadata_context: the shared checkpoint that almost every family-bound view (variants, tracks, report) goes through first. It loads the family only if the user may see it, and restricts the visible projects to those of the user. build_sample_metadata_context does the same for one sample.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/access_control.py (the access rules, among them user_can_access_metadata_projects), backend/app/services/metadata_service.py (the filtered queries and get_accessible_family_mapping) and backend/app/services/family_metadata_context.py (the checkpoint).

The backend is the real gate

Authorisation is enforced only in the backend, with three dependencies:

  • get_current_user checks the token and loads the user fresh from Postgres. It refuses (HTTP 401) if the token is invalid or the user does not exist or is not active. How the token is checked is described in chapter 5.
  • get_current_superuser builds on it and gives HTTP 403 Superuser access required if the role is not superuser or admin (has_superuser_rights). This is the gate for the configuration the analyses read and for the package import.
  • get_current_admin_user also builds on get_current_user and gives HTTP 403 Admin access required if the role is not admin (is_admin_user). This is the gate for the rest of the administration and for the destructive actions. A superuser does not get through.

A plain endpoint such as GET /api/families/{family_id} asks for get_current_user (authentication) and leaves authorisation to the service layer, through the checkpoint above. An unknown family_id and one from another project therefore get the same answer: 404 Family not found. A family_id with a control character already gets 400 during authentication, the same for everyone (chapter 5). The administration router (/api/admin/...) sits behind get_current_admin_user, except the variant tags, the overview of the preset filters and the sequencing QC thresholds: those ask for get_current_superuser, as do writing the gene panels (/api/panels), the variant tags on the routes of a family and the whole package import (/api/family-imports). Creating, changing and deleting projects is for an administrator. The project list itself shows a viewer, analyst or supervisor only their own projects.

Two nuances for the auditor:

  1. No check outside access_control.py compares a role with a literal role name: every check asks the sets and the functions there (is_admin_user, has_superuser_rights, role_changes_records, may_sign_out). A test refuses any comparison of a role with a literal role name elsewhere (backend/tests/test_admin_role_checks.py). A superuser never counts as an administrator: backend/tests/test_admin_route_gating.py requires every administration route to refuse a superuser, and every superuser route to refuse a viewer, an analyst and a supervisor.
  2. The restricted user list (GET /api/users: name and email address of every active account) is for administrators only (get_current_admin_user). Anyone who is not an administrator, a superuser included, gets 403, as on the other administration routes; a deactivated administrator gets 401. No screen reads that list: the Assigned to and Reviewed by drop-down lists of a family read the family's own list (below), and the Users page reads GET /api/auth/users. The restriction to administrators is a decision of the owner of 2026-10-28.

Where in the code: backend/app/dependencies.py (the three dependencies), backend/app/routers/admin.py, backend/app/routers/panels.py, backend/app/routers/family_imports.py and backend/app/routers/projects.py.

Access level per project: analyst or reader

Besides their role, every project member has an access level in that project (decision of the owner of 2026-10-14). The level only takes rights away, never adds them:

Level May do in the project
analyst (analyst) Read, and change as far as their role allows: analyse with the role analyst, and also sign out with the role supervisor. A viewer with this level changes nothing.
reader (reader), e.g. a student Only read, whatever role they have (below superuser): view and search the families, variants, tracks, reports and signed versions, export CSV, print the report and a signed version, and save their own filter presets. Not: see the clinical audit trail, or change anything clinical: no phenotypes, reviews, tags, ACMG or CNV classifications, Sign out, workflow fields (status, assigned to, reviewed by), new families, uploads, imports, edits or deletions.

The same person can be analyst in one project and reader in another. If a family is attached to several projects, an analyst of any one of them may change it, just as a member of any one of them may see it. A superuser and an administrator have all rights in every project, member or not; their level in a project does not count.

Setting the level. An administrator chooses the level of each member on the Projects & access page, in a drop-down list next to each member of the project. On the Users page they set the same memberships from the account's side: Edit under Project access opens the account's projects, each with its level. The dialog lists what saving will change, and Save project access saves everything in one request. In the API it is the field reader_user_ids of a project: the members who are readers; the other members are analysts. From the account's side it is the fields project_ids and reader_project_ids of PATCH /api/auth/users/{id}: the same rows in project_users. A member without a level is analyst (the column's default value). An update without reader_user_ids (or without reader_project_ids) lets every membership that remains keep its level. A reader who is not a member is refused (400); so is a project that does not exist (404), and then nothing changes, not even a role that was in the same request. Every change from the account's side is in the request's audit row, from and to (request_meta.account_change). Whoever writes the memberships, from the project or from the account, first takes the same lock (_lock_project_memberships): two saves at the same time wait for each other, without deadlock, and the audit row names the memberships the change actually replaced.

Enforced in one place. On every request, get_current_user records whether it changes something: every method except GET, HEAD and OPTIONS, unless the route is marked with changes_only_own_data. Only the routes for the user's own filter presets and for the events of their own use of the interface carry that mark; a viewer and a reader use those too. The checkpoints of family, sample and project (get_accessible_family_mapping, get_accessible_sample_mapping and _resolve_accessible_project_id of the Family Builder) then refuse a change by a viewer or a reader with 403 and the reason (require_change_access). A viewer gets Read-only access: your role is viewer, so you can view and export records but not change them. (VIEWER_READ_ONLY_DETAIL), a reader the sentence that names their level in the project (READ_ONLY_DETAIL). That happens after the visibility check: a family outside their projects therefore still answers 404, like an unknown one. Every route that names a family, sample or project must pass through those checkpoints, so no route can forget the check. The clinical audit trail (GET /api/families/{id}/clinical-audit) also refuses a viewer and a reader (403, with VIEWER_AUDIT_TRAIL_DETAIL or AUDIT_TRAIL_DETAIL). The administration routes stay behind get_current_admin_user or get_current_superuser.

Signing out: supervisor or higher. Closing an analysis with Sign out additionally requires the role supervisor, superuser or admin (TF-06, hazard H15: an analysis signed out by someone without signing authority). sign_out_report calls require_sign_out_authority after the family checkpoint, so that a family outside the user's projects still answers 404 and a viewer or reader is first told that they can only read, and before every gate, so that an analyst does not go through acknowledgements they cannot use. An analyst gets 403 with Signing out needs the supervisor role: ask a supervisor of this family's project to sign out the analysis. (SIGN_OUT_ROLE_DETAIL), and nothing is written. The measure against H15 is thus a check in the software. Who gets the role supervisor remains a decision of the laboratory (chapter 11).

In the screens. The family and the projects the API returns say whether they are read-only for the user (read_only: their role is viewer, or they are reader in every project of the family of which they are a member). The family also says whether they may sign out its analysis (can_sign_out: their role is supervisor or higher, and they may change the family). A family page that is read-only shows Read-only access. The buttons the user may not use are disabled or hidden:

  • the review and ACMG dialogs do not save;
  • the quick tags are off;
  • Sign out report is disabled, also for an analyst without can_sign_out, with the reason Signing out needs the supervisor role …;
  • the audit trail is not requested; the report says on screen and on paper why it is not there;
  • the phenotypes and workflow fields cannot be changed;
  • the Family Builder offers only the projects in which the user is analyst.

That is convenience; the server's refusal is the gate.

Assigned to and Reviewed by. A family's Assigned to and Reviewed by are an active superuser or administrator, or an active analyst of one of its projects whose role is not viewer; never a reader or a viewer. The two drop-down lists on the family page read the family's own list (GET /api/families/{family_id}/assignable-users). Like the family itself, that list answers 404 outside the user's projects. If a save names someone else (a reader, a viewer, someone outside the family's projects or a deactivated account), the server refuses it with 422 and the reason (e.g. their role is viewer), with the hint Choose an analyst of one of the family's projects, a superuser or an administrator., and nothing changes. A value the family already has stays until someone changes it: a person who became reader or viewer stays named, and the drop-down list shows that person with (not eligible). Where in the code: backend/app/services/family_status_service.py (list_family_assignable_users, update_family_metadata_for_user).

The email to the person a family is assigned to. A person whom a save newly names under Assigned to gets an email after the save, through the mail server in SMTP_HOST (chapter 5). The email names the family ID (the pseudonymous lab ID; a decision of the owner), who assigned the family and when, and links to the family if CoGA knows its own address (that of CAS_SERVICE_URL); the subject names no family and the email contains no other patient data. No email goes out if the family keeps the same person, if the field is cleared, for Reviewed by, or if someone assigns a family to themselves. An email that fails to send leaves the save untouched; the log names no address, no family and not the server's text. Where in the code: backend/app/services/family_assignment_mail.py, backend/app/routers/families.py (update_family_metadata).

Tests.

  • backend/tests/test_project_access_levels.py keeps the catalogue of every route that changes something: an administrator's, a superuser's (SUPERUSER_CHANGE_ROUTES), own data, or refused at a checkpoint. A new route fails until it is classified.
  • backend/tests/e2e/test_e2e_project_reader_role.py calls every such route on real Postgres as a reader and requires 403 with the reason. It calls every route that reads a family or sample as a reader and as an analyst, and requires the same answer, except for the audit trail.
  • backend/tests/test_access_rules.py pins down the rules of access_control.py per role and level; backend/tests/test_report_signout.py starts with the role of the person signing out (a viewer and an analyst are refused before every gate; a supervisor, superuser and administrator sign out).
  • backend/tests/e2e/test_e2e_global_roles.py goes through the five roles on real Postgres, with real sign-ins: the viewer reads and is refused a change and the audit trail, the analyst changes and is refused the sign-out, the supervisor signs out, and the superuser, in no project at all, reads the family, opens their workspaces and is refused those of the administrator.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/access_control.py (user_can_change_metadata_projects, user_can_sign_out_metadata_projects, require_change_access, require_sign_out_authority, require_audit_trail_access, changes_only_own_data, request_changes_records), backend/app/dependencies.py (get_current_user), backend/app/services/metadata_service.py (the checkpoints, read_only, can_sign_out and _set_project_user_links), backend/app/services/report_signout_service.py (sign_out_report), the column access_level in backend/db/schema/postgres/01_access.sql; in the frontend frontend/src/lib/familyAccess.ts and frontend/src/pages/families/reportSignOut.tsx.

Guards in the browser: convenience, not a lock

The frontend has its own guards, but they serve only the user experience:

  • RequireAuth sends anyone without a token to /login?next=....
  • RequireAdmin sends users who are not logged in to /login and logged-in non-administrators to /dashboard. With <RequireAdmin superuser /> it also lets a superuser through: that is how it guards the administration dashboard and the five workspaces of a superuser. The menu and the dashboard show Admin to a superuser and an administrator.
  • SessionRedirect chooses a destination depending on "logged in or not".

Why this is not a gate: the role the browser uses is in browser storage, and users can change it themselves. At most, that shows them the administration screens. Every data or action request still goes to the backend, which checks the role and the projects again, authoritatively.

Where in the code: frontend/src/components/RequireAuth.tsx, RequireAdmin.tsx and SessionRedirect.tsx; the session helpers in frontend/src/lib/auth.ts.

Least privilege in the database: the runtime role coga_app

Even a compromised application must not be able to rewrite the append-only evidence tables. "Append-only" means: only add, never change or delete. A separate, restricted database role exists for that purpose.

05_grants.sql creates the role coga_app with SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the ordinary tables. On the append-only tables it revokes UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE again:

  • audit_log_events, clinical_audit_events, report_signouts, integrity_anchors and qc_threshold_changes;
  • family_structure_versions, ui_events and import_delivery_revisions (the pedigree versions, the log of the UI events and the corrections of a delivered package, chapter 6);
  • ancestry_reference_panels, ancestry_results and ancestry_sample_choices, the tables of the exploratory ancestry PCA.

coga_app may only read the migration ledger alembic_version and the baseline digest schema_baselines: only the migration step writes to them, as owner. As a non-owner, coga_app also cannot disable a trigger. The runtime can therefore add rows to those tables, but cannot change or delete any existing row: no audit row, signed report, integrity anchor, QC threshold recorded earlier, pedigree version, UI event or package correction. The only permitted change is made by the database itself, when a user or family is deleted: the reference to it is set to NULL (ON DELETE SET NULL), while a column of the row itself keeps who or which family it was (chapter 11).

The role is shipped without a login: by default the application still runs as the owner of the tables. Switching over is an operational step, not a code change. The schema is then applied separately as owner (backend/app/db_migrate.py, with POSTGRES_RUN_SCHEMA_MIGRATIONS_ON_STARTUP=false for the app), and the app logs in as coga_app. On Google Cloud that is one Terraform variable: db_runtime_role = "coga_app" (default "owner"). A separate Cloud Run job (terraform/migrate.tf) then applies the schema as owner before every rollout and enables the login of coga_app with POSTGRES_APP_PASSWORD. That job has its own service account, so the API cannot read the owner's password.

Every new append-only table must get the same REVOKE in 05_grants.sql, because the broad GRANT automatically gives new tables all rights. The integration test backend/tests/integration/test_app_role_privileges.py guards this: it searches the database for every table with a blocking trigger (*_block_mutation) and fails if coga_app still has UPDATE or DELETE on it.

Where in the code: backend/db/schema/postgres/05_grants.sql; the procedure, verification and rollback are in docs/db-runtime-role-runbook.md.

Other defences

Rate limiting against brute force

Failed logins are counted per email address and per source IP; after a threshold an increasing waiting time follows (HTTP 429). Registration is throttled separately per source IP. Behind a proxy, CoGA takes the client IP from the X-Forwarded-For header, as many steps from the right as TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS indicates. That way a client cannot choose its own IP. The audit rows use that IP too. How this works is described in chapter 5.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/auth_rate_limit_pg.py and backend/app/middleware/client_ip.py.

Security headers and CORS

Every API response gets strict headers, including the 500 for an error that nothing else handles: a Content-Security-Policy that allows nothing (default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'), X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer and cross-origin isolation. HSTS is on only where TLS terminates in front of the app (ENABLE_HSTS). On Google Cloud the load balancer also sets that HSTS header on every response it passes on over HTTPS, including Cloud Run's own error pages. CORS allows only the configured origins, and an origin pattern must be fully anchored (chapter 1).

Where in the code: backend/app/middleware/security_headers.py and the 500 handler in backend/app/main.py; CORS in backend/app/core/config.py; the load balancer's header in terraform/loadbalancer.tf.

Refusal to start with weak secrets

Outside development and test (i.e. if APP_ENV is not dev, development, local or test) the backend refuses to start if:

  • SECRET_KEY is shorter than 32 characters or is secret/change-me;
  • CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD is empty or is admin/change-me;
  • INTEGRITY_ANCHOR_SIGNING_KEY is not the base64 of a 32-byte Ed25519 key, or is equal to SECRET_KEY (then anyone who can create session tokens can also sign integrity anchors);
  • POSTGRES_PASSWORD, ADMIN_PASSWORD or a configured POSTGRES_APP_PASSWORD is admin/change-me;
  • a configured METRICS_TOKEN is shorter than 32 characters, is secret/change-me, or is equal to SECRET_KEY or INTEGRITY_ANCHOR_SIGNING_KEY (whoever reads the metrics must not be able to create session tokens or anchors);
  • AUDIT_LOG_DROP_ALLOWED=true (drop audit rows when the queue is full) or AUDIT_LOG_MODE=off (write no audit rows at all) is set;
  • the CORS settings are open (chapter 1), or the build has no GIT_SHA (chapter 4).

The error message names the fields that do not comply. This is a deliberate fail-closed choice: better not to start than to start unsafely. .env.example contains only placeholders, precisely to force them to be replaced before a real rollout.

Where in the code: validate_security_defaults in backend/app/core/config.py.

Uploads and external HTML

  • Bounded uploads. Uploads (SV, reference, BED, repeats, PED, the NIPT artefact table) and the text files of a family package are read within a size limit and decompressed within a size limit; a small-variant VCF is streamed line by line. That way a small but highly compressed .gz file (a "decompression bomb") cannot exhaust the memory. Too large gives HTTP 413. The many gzip blocks of a BGZF .vcf.gz are read through correctly. HTTP 400 follows for a gzip file that breaks off in the middle of a block, for bytes after the last block that are not themselves a complete block, and for a BGZF file that does not end with the BGZF end-of-file block (chapter 6). Where in the code: backend/app/services/upload_safety.py, which decompresses with gunzip_bounded from bounded_download.py; the limits MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES and MAX_DECOMPRESSED_UPLOAD_BYTES in config.py.
  • HTML sanitisation. The clinical CNV knowledge base contains small HTML fragments that the UI shows as HTML. A strict allowlist restricts them to safe formatting and refuses everything else (script, img, event attributes, javascript: and data: links). This happens both when they are loaded and when they are read back, against stored cross-site scripting. Where in the code: backend/app/core/html_sanitize.py.
  • The pipeline's QC report. That HTML report contains its own scripts and is treated as untrusted. It opens through a short-lived link to the backend, which is issued only after the access check. The link is valid for one report: that of the family, the sample and the analysis it names (a sample sequenced short-read and then long-read has a report of each). The backend looks for the report only in the package folder read by the import of the analysis that recorded it, at the path the import recorded with the sample, and nowhere else: a report gone from that folder gives 404, rather than another analysis's report of the same name. A path that leads out of the folder, or a symbolic link out of it, gives 404. The backend serves the report with Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-scripts allow-popups: the report's scripts run, but in an isolated origin that cannot read the user's session. Where in the code: backend/app/routers/family_qc_reports.py.

Auditing (in brief)

Every HTTP action leaves a trace in the append-only table audit_log_events: who (user and role), what (method, path, status), when and from which IP. Sensitive data are limited. Of a query string, by default only the keys are kept. Password and token fields are masked, in the audit log and in the UI events, according to one list of keys (SENSITIVE_KEY_PREFIXES in core/coga_logging.py). A database trigger makes this table append-only. The hash chain and the signed anchors apply to the clinical audit trail and the signed reports (chapter 11). The middleware itself is described in chapter 7.

Every suppression of a security scan (dependencies, secrets, SAST) is documented and dated in SECURITY-AUDIT-ALLOWLIST.md.

3. Database structures (Postgres & ClickHouse)

CoGA splits its data between two databases: Postgres for metadata, access rights, review state and the clinical paper trails, and ClickHouse for the huge numbers of variant and track rows. The table-by-table reference is docs/database.md; it is the source of truth.

A few terms: DDL (Data Definition Language) are the SQL commands that create or change tables; a foreign key is a reference from a row to a row in another table; an ERD (entity-relationship diagram) draws the tables with their keys and the references between them.

Two databases, one agreement

Postgres is the source of truth for everything that is relational, transactional and safety-critical. It offers foreign keys, CHECK rules and triggers: exactly what access control and an unalterable audit trail need. ClickHouse filters and counts fast over hundreds of millions of rows; that is where the variants and the large interval tracks are kept (chapter 1 explains the choice).

Metadata rows use UUIDs as their key. The variant IDs the API shows are stable strings (e.g. 1-1000-A-T), independent of the storage. For people, family_id and sample_id remain the recognisable names.

Postgres: five baseline files

The Postgres schema is in five SQL files in backend/db/schema/postgres/, grouped by domain. Each table is created there once, in its final form. Revision 0001 applies them to an empty database (see below, How the schemas are applied).

File Domain Main tables
01_access.sql Genome basis and access species, assemblies, chromosomes (with the cytobands), users (with the role rule), projects, project_users, auth_login_attempts
02_reference.sql Reference and knowledge data genes, gene_info, blacklist, clinical_cnvs, dgv_variants, dgv_load_jobs, segmental_duplications, the panels (gene_panels, gene_panel_versions, …), the HPO tables, the Monarch tables, repeat_loci and QA's per-locus count correction repeat_locus_count_units, reference_dataset_imports, and the job tables gene_info_refresh_jobs and clinical_cnv_kb_jobs
03_assay.sql Families, samples and review state family_statuses, families, samples, family_members, family_projects, sample_projects, family_relationships, the append-only history of the pedigree family_structure_versions, individual_hpo, the assay data (repeat_expansions, sample_paraphase_results, nipt_artifact_variants, sample_interval_track_sources), the reviews (small_variant_reviews, structural_variant_reviews, repeat_expansion_reviews, paraphase_reviews), tags and filter presets, the import (family_import_jobs, the deliveries import_deliveries and their append-only corrections import_delivery_revisions), the caches (family_variant_ranking_cache, family_sv_gene_index) and the sequencing QC limits (qc_threshold_profiles, qc_thresholds and their append-only history qc_threshold_changes)
04_traceability.sql Provenance and clinical audit trail raw_import_files, family_annotation_manifest, audit_log_events, clinical_audit_events, report_signouts, integrity_anchors, ui_events, the tables of the exploratory ancestry PCA (ancestry_reference_panels, ancestry_runs, ancestry_results, ancestry_sample_choices; chapter 15), plus the append-only triggers (including those on qc_threshold_changes, family_structure_versions and import_delivery_revisions), the migration ledger alembic_version and the baseline digest schema_baselines
05_grants.sql Separation of privileges The restricted runtime role coga_app, the REVOKE on the append-only tables, the migration ledger and the baseline digest (chapter 2)

Two features stand out. Almost all per-assembly reference data refers to assemblies with ON DELETE CASCADE; the Monarch tables are deliberately assembly-independent (linked on HGNC and MONDO IDs). And the frozen ACMG evidence per classification is in the column small_variant_reviews.acmg_evidence_snapshot, that of a CNV classification in structural_variant_reviews.cnv_evidence_snapshot (chapter 10).

An assembly is its name. assemblies.assembly_name is unique. The variant tables in ClickHouse (below) and every lookup by name read only the name. Two assemblies with one name would therefore share one set of variant tables, while genes, cytobands, panels, DGV and clinical CNVs could each hang on a different row. version and release_date are what the last import from UCSC reported: the GRC patch, e.g. p14. A later import of that assembly keeps the same row and the same ID and updates those two, even if UCSC meanwhile describes a later patch (chapter 4). Add assembly manually refuses a name that already exists (409).

Where in the code: the files in backend/db/schema/postgres/; _store_assembly in backend/app/services/reference_source_service.py and create_assembly_record in backend/app/services/metadata_service.py (the assembly by name); the full column reference in docs/database.md, with an ERD of the core and one per domain of each baseline file (Postgres Tables).

ClickHouse: tables per assembly

The ClickHouse schema file backend/db/schema/clickhouse/001_coga_variant_storage.sql only creates the database. The backend creates the actual tables at runtime, per assembly: their names start with the assembly (e.g. `GRCh38/SNV_INDEL/entries`). First the assembly name is converted to a safe key: characters other than letters, digits, full stop, underscore and hyphen (e.g. a space) become _, so T2T CHM13v2.0 becomes T2T_CHM13v2.0. Import and reading use the same function and so always find the same table.

Tables (per assembly) What they contain
SNV_INDEL/variants/details, …/annotations, …/annotation_index, …/gene_index The variant record, the full annotation per annotation version, and the indexes the filter pages search on (on annotation fields and on gene)
SNV_INDEL/entries The calls per family: per variant the genotypes, depth and quality of each sample. From a single-sample VCF (such as the two files of a NIPT pair) also the FILTER values and the caller metrics of each call (calls.filters, calls.metrics). Per row also transcripts: the values of the row's own annotation that the per-transcript filters test, as …/annotations stores them per transcript, without the transcript and HGVS text. The most-read table
SNV_INDEL/family_variant_summary, …/family_sample_variant_summary, …/family_data_version Summaries per family and per sample, and a version that changes with every change to a family's variant data (the ranking cache uses it, chapter 12)
SNV_INDEL/carriers, …/carrier_generations The carrier summary of the Variant Explorer: per variant the carriers each family contributes, and what each family's contribution was computed from (below)
SV/variants/details, SV/key_lookup, SV/entries, …/family_data_version The same for structural variants, with a version of their own that changes with every change to a family's SVs (the SV index for the second hit uses it, chapter 8)
INTERVAL/entries Interval tracks: coverage, CNV segments, APCAD, PCF segments, haplotype blocks, the genome-wide haplotype lineage (haplotype_lineage) and the coverage per capture target of a NIPT panel (target_coverage), with the source and the file name on each row

An overwrite import of an existing family also creates temporary backup tables <assembly>/SNAPSHOT/<import>/<table>. They hold a copy of that family's rows in SNV_INDEL/entries, SV/entries, SV/variants/details, SV/key_lookup and INTERVAL/entries, to restore the family on failure. The import removes them when it ends. For a stopped import, the worker that ends its job does so, and otherwise the next start (chapter 6).

For a reviewer, five things matter:

  • The entries tables of small variants and SVs have a sign column (CollapsingMergeTree), but CoGA writes every row with sign = 1. Old rows disappear on a new import or a deletion with a synchronous ALTER TABLE … DELETE (mutations_sync = 1), never through a cancelling row (−1). The readers filter on sign = 1, without FINAL. That is only correct as long as no writer writes cancelling rows.
  • The entries tables of small variants and SVs are partitioned per project (PARTITION BY project_guid). That makes the project filter cheap and keeps queries across projects bounded. INTERVAL/entries has no project column and is partitioned per track type.
  • A family has its entries rows once per project it is linked to (without a project, under unassigned), and whoever reads the family reads only the rows of its projects. If an administrator changes its projects, the rows move with them, in two steps under the family's write locks: before the new links are fixed, each new project receives, per callset, a copy from a linked project (rows it already had are replaced); then the rows under the projects the family left disappear. A package import into an existing family also links it to the import's project, and before its snapshot gives each project of the family the callsets that project does not yet have (chapter 6). If a copy fails halfway, it erases what the project received of that callset. A project to which families are still linked is not deleted (409, with the count): the links would disappear and the rows would remain under the deleted project (chapter 15).
  • A row in entries is the call of one callset (source) for one variant, in one family and one project. When ClickHouse merges the parts of a table, it keeps one row per sort key; that is why the sort key of SNV_INDEL/entries ends in key, source, and those of SV/entries and SV/key_lookup also in the callset (docs/database.md, Row identity). So the direct call (named after its caller, such as haplotypecaller) and the imputed call (GLIMPSE2) of one variant remain two rows; the diagnostic lists show the direct one. The calls of two callers (short-read and long-read WGS of the same DNA) also remain two rows. The callset nipt of a monogenic NIPT comes from two VCFs with one sample each, the plasma and the father. Each file fills in, in the same row per variant, only the call of its own sample. A family can hold several pregnancies of one woman, and each pregnancy keeps its data under sources of its own: the callset, the coverage tables and the ccnv output of a pregnancy carry after their name _p and eight hexadecimal characters of the SHA-256 of its pregnancy_id (nipt_p1a2b3c4d, ccnv_p1a2b3c4d). So the import of one pregnancy replaces nothing of another, not even the father's calls; the readers read such a source as the source it is kept for (source_base). For an SV the key itself also holds the source, because the ID of an SV from a per-sample upload does not name the caller: two callers on the same breakpoints remain two rows. The variant ID of a small variant does not depend on the callset. That of an SV usually does not either: only a HiFiCNV call without its own VCF ID and an mtDNA SV carry their source in the ID, and so get a review of their own. Reviews, classification snapshots, the ranking cache and the SV index for the second hit are tied to that ID.
  • The Variant Explorer counts a variant's carriers from the carrier summary SNV_INDEL/carriers, with the project filter (chapter 14). Counting from each family's entries rows does not fit within a page's 110 s at three or four whole genomes. The summary is derived data: every row can be recomputed from entries and the members and projects of the families in Postgres. Every writer of a family's entries rows first takes the family's contribution out, under the family's write lock. The variant carrier worker, which runs where the package imports run, adds every 5 s the contribution of each family whose rows, members or projects differ from what the summary holds. Until that has happened, the explorer calls such a family pending. carrier_generations records what each contribution was computed from. The full rule is in docs/database.md (The variant carrier summary).

Where in the code: the ERDs of the ClickHouse tables and of their link with Postgres in docs/database.md (ClickHouse Tables); ensure_clickhouse_variant_tables(assembly_name) in backend/app/services/clickhouse_variant_storage.py, ensure_clickhouse_interval_table(assembly_name) in backend/app/services/clickhouse_interval_tracks.py, and clickhouse_dataset_key in backend/app/core/clickhouse.py. The keys are built in backend/app/services/clickhouse_variant_ids.py. The carrier summary is in backend/app/services/variant_carrier_summary.py (detach_family_variant_carriers, reconcile_variant_carriers).

How a ClickHouse row is linked to Postgres

The two databases share no physical join; the application links them through shared keys. The ClickHouse column project_guid holds the Postgres project UUID (projects.id) as text, and family_guid the family UUID (families.id).

  1. The backend determines from Postgres which family, samples and projects the user may see.
  2. Those UUIDs go as parameters into the ClickHouse query (family_guid, project_guid IN …), so that only permitted rows come back.
  3. The backend completes the variants with the review state from Postgres. The review tables are unique per family and variant ID: exactly one review belongs to one variant in one family.

So the access decision is always made first in Postgres; ClickHouse only sees the keys that have already been filtered. Anyone who wants to verify that data does not leak between projects checks two things: that the scope is determined correctly in Postgres (chapter 2), and that every ClickHouse query carries the project filter (chapters 8 and 14).

Where in the code: backend/app/services/clickhouse_family_variants.py (family variants) and backend/app/services/variant_explorer_service.py (variants across projects).

How the schemas are applied

The Postgres schema reaches a database through one migration step (backend/app/core/postgres_migrations.py), by default at every start of the backend. If the backend runs as the restricted role coga_app, a separate job runs that step before the rollout. The backend then only checks at start-up that the database is at exactly its own revision and was made from its own baselines (chapter 4). The step runs in one transaction, as owner of the tables: it happens entirely or not at all.

  1. It takes an advisory lock (a lock in the database), so that two instances that start together migrate one after the other.
  2. It refuses to run as coga_app.
  3. It refuses any database this version did not make, before anything happens. It migrates only an empty database (an empty migration ledger and no table in the schema public) or a database whose ledger alembic_version names one of its revisions and whose digest in schema_baselines equals the SHA-256 of its own five baselines. Tables without a ledger, a revision this version does not know (another version made or migrated the database) and a database from other baselines are each refused, with a message that says which case it is.
  4. It runs the Alembic revisions in backend/db/migrations/versions/ that the ledger does not yet list, and records the last one there. Revision 0001 applies the five baselines to the empty database and records their digest in schema_baselines.

Before the release candidate. CoGA holds only test data, and every database is created empty. A schema change is an edit of its baseline, never a migration of an existing database: revision 0001 is the only revision, and a database from the previous baselines is refused at its next start (step 3). Then create it again empty (docker compose down -v, docs/development.md) and import the test data again. The integration test backend/tests/integration/test_postgres_migrations.py shows that an empty database gets exactly the schema of the five files (the same catalogue fingerprint), that a later start changes nothing, and that every refused database stays as it was.

The proposal for QA is that the release candidate freezes the baselines (docs/database.md, Freezing the baselines at the release candidate). A test then records their SHA-256, and from then on every schema change is a revision of its own after 0001, which only runs forward. Anyone who wants to go back to an older version restores the backup from before the upgrade; on Google Cloud the rollout takes that backup itself, before every migration it starts (docs/deployment-gcp.md, 12.1 and 12.3).

The backend creates the ClickHouse tables with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, directly in their final form. Every database is created from scratch; a local database with tables from another version is created again (docker compose down -v).

The depth columns of SNV_INDEL/entries, the read depth (calls.dp) and the per-allele depths (calls.ad), are UInt32, up to 4,294,967,295 reads: a mitochondrial or amplicon call reads far more than the 65,535 of a UInt16. The genotype quality (calls.gq), a phred score, is UInt16.

Every value a loader writes is first bound to its column (clickhouse_column_bounds.py, applied in clickhouse_variant_rows.py and clickhouse_interval_tracks.py). This is because the ClickHouse client refuses a whole insert as soon as one value does not fit its column. A value its column cannot hold, or that is not a finite number, is stored as missing: a GQ above 65,535 or inf, a negative phase set, a QUAL, allele fraction, caller metric or annotation score beyond the largest Float32, an SVLEN outside Int32. An allele fraction that is missing in this way drops out of the call's list. An allele depth that is missing in this way becomes 0, like a missing or unreadable one, so that the other alleles keep their place. A record whose position no column can hold (a negative POS, an END beyond 4,294,967,295, a negative start of a track row) cannot be placed. Its loader skips it as malformed, just like a POS that is not a number, and counts it where it counts those. The full rule per column is in docs/database.md.

Who applies the schema (the app itself as owner, or a separate migration step) and in what order the backend starts up is described in chapter 4.

Where in the code: init_postgres_schema in backend/app/core/postgres.py, init_clickhouse_schema in backend/app/core/clickhouse.py and ensure_clickhouse_variant_tables in backend/app/services/clickhouse_variant_storage.py.

Guarantees in the database layer

Many IVDR guarantees sit in the database itself, so that not even a fault in the application or a misused API request can bypass them.

  • Append-only through triggers. audit_log_events, clinical_audit_events, report_signouts, integrity_anchors, qc_threshold_changes, family_structure_versions, import_delivery_revisions and ui_events each have a trigger that blocks DELETE and refuses UPDATE. The tables of the exploratory ancestry PCA (ancestry_reference_panels, ancestry_results, ancestry_sample_choices) have one too. The only exception is setting a reference to a user or family to NULL when that user or family is deleted; denormalised columns (e.g. user_email, family_identifier) then keep who it was. The triggers are in 04_traceability.sql.
  • Hash chain. clinical_audit_events, report_signouts and family_structure_versions carry row_hash and prev_hash: each row binds its content to the previous row of the same family. Changing, erasing or reordering rows thus becomes visible. report_signouts also carries a hash of the frozen report. The HTTP access log audit_log_events and the log of UI events ui_events are append-only through their trigger, but not hash-chained.
  • Integrity anchors. Each time an administrator or an external scheduler calls POST /api/admin/integrity/anchor, integrity_anchors records the heads of all chains, signed with an Ed25519 key kept outside the database. Outside development an unsigned anchor is refused. CoGA does not schedule this itself: how often it happens is a procedural agreement (chapter 11).
  • Separation of privileges. 05_grants.sql creates the role coga_app without login and revokes UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE on the append-only tables. The migration step enables that login with POSTGRES_APP_PASSWORD (on Google Cloud with db_runtime_role = "coga_app"). By default the app still runs as owner (chapter 2).
  • Access rules in the schema. The CHECK on users.role allows only the five roles, from low to high viewer, analyst, supervisor, superuser and admin (chapter 2). Foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE clean up the associated rows when a family or sample is deleted.
  • Provenance. Three tables record which files and versions produced a result: raw_import_files (the SHA-256 of each source file), family_annotation_manifest (the tool and database versions per analysis of a family) and reference_dataset_imports (each import of reference data). That is the basis for the traceability in chapter 11.
