4. Initial deployment & seeding

This chapter describes how CoGA goes from an empty system to a running platform, in the Docker setup and on Google Cloud with Terraform: how the database structures come into being, how the first administrator and the reference data are seeded (filled for the first time), and in which order the backend does this at startup. The step-by-step guides are docs/development.md (local) and docs/deployment-gcp.md (Google Cloud).

A few terms. A container is an isolated, running software package; Docker Compose starts several containers together from one file. DDL is SQL that creates or changes tables.

From zero to a running stack

CoGA consists of five containers: Postgres (metadata and review state), ClickHouse (the variant storage), the FastAPI backend, the import worker (the same backend image, which runs the package imports) and the React frontend.

The Docker setup

docker-compose.yml describes the five services. Some choices matter for traceability and robustness:

  • Pinned images. The database images are pinned not only by a tag but by a digest (@sha256:…). That way every machine uses exactly the same image.
  • Health and order. The backend starts only when Postgres and ClickHouse are healthy; the frontend and the import worker only when the backend is healthy. The backend gets plenty of time, because at startup it applies the schema and loads reference data. The import worker migrates nothing itself and only checks the schema revision.
  • Graceful shutdown. ClickHouse gets a generous shutdown period: a write that is interrupted in the middle of its work can damage data parts.
  • Restarting. Every service has a restart policy, so that the setup runs again by itself after a restart of the server. Anyone who first stopped the setup with docker compose stop starts it again themselves with docker compose up -d.
  • Build identity. The backend image receives APP_VERSION and GIT_SHA at build time. A local build is not a release: without APP_VERSION the image reports the version from VERSION with dev added (0.1.0-dev). .env.example warns: do not set it in .env, otherwise the runtime overrides the baked-in value and falsifies the version that is frozen in every signed report. Outside development the backend does not start without GIT_SHA (7 to 40 hexadecimal characters), because every signed report states that commit. Of scripts/, the image contains only what the backend itself runs: clinical_cnv_knowledgebase.py (the build of the clinical CNV knowledge base: from Admin, after an assembly import and at startup, below) and import_dgv.py (an import by the administrator). The test seeders stay out; one of them creates a login with a default password.

Where in the code: docker-compose.yml; the warning in .env.example.

The development setup

For development a second file goes on top of the base:

docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up --build -d

docker-compose.dev.yml sets APP_ENV=development and mounts the source code into the containers, so that changes take effect immediately. It starts the backend with automatic reloading and the frontend with the Vite development server. APP_ENV=development also switches off the check for weak secrets, so that you can work locally with the placeholders of .env.example. Outside development the backend would then refuse to start; the full rule is in chapter 2.

Where in the code: docker-compose.dev.yml; the check in validate_security_defaults in backend/app/core/config.py.

Creating the database structures

Postgres

The Postgres schema is in five SQL files (01_access.sql to 05_grants.sql, chapter 3). The backend reads them in name order, splits each file into separate statements and runs everything in one transaction. The splitter takes dollar quotes ($$ … $$) into account, so that a semicolon in a trigger function does not cut a statement off halfway. This happens only on an empty database, by revision 0001, which also records the digest of the baselines in schema_baselines. The migration step refuses a database that this version did not make (tables without a ledger, an unknown revision, other baselines). The log reports the revision the database is at (chapter 3).

Where in the code: init_postgres_schema in backend/app/core/postgres.py; the migration step apply_postgres_schema in backend/app/core/postgres_migrations.py; the revisions in backend/db/migrations/versions/.

ClickHouse

The ClickHouse file only creates the database; the database name comes from the setting CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE. The backend creates the variant and track tables per assembly only when they are first needed (chapter 3).

Where in the code: init_clickhouse_schema in backend/app/core/clickhouse.py.

Two ways to apply the schema

Who may create the schema is deliberately kept separate from who runs the app (the database rights from chapter 2):

Setting Who runs the DDL When
POSTGRES_RUN_SCHEMA_MIGRATIONS_ON_STARTUP=true (default) The app itself, at startup, as owner of the tables The current setup with one database login
POSTGRES_RUN_SCHEMA_MIGRATIONS_ON_STARTUP=false A separate step (backend/app/db_migrate.py) as owner; the app then runs as the restricted role coga_app When the runtime may not run DDL

Both paths use the same functions: there is one source of truth for the schema. The migration step refuses to run as coga_app, before it changes anything. If POSTGRES_APP_PASSWORD is set, the migration step also enables the login of coga_app. The password is not sent to the database in plain text: the step sends a SCRAM-SHA-256 derivative, as \password in psql does, and the password appears in no log line. On Google Cloud this step runs as the Cloud Run job coga-db-migrate (terraform/migrate.tf), as soon as db_runtime_role = "coga_app".

An app that does not migrate itself reads only the migration ledger and the baseline digest at startup. It starts only if the database is at exactly its own schema revision and was made from its own baselines. If the database has no revision in the ledger, the app reports that the migration step must run first. If the database is at a revision the app does not know, or comes from other baselines, then another version made or migrated it (chapter 3). ClickHouse always follows the app's startup path.

Where in the code: backend/app/db_migrate.py; the settings in backend/app/core/config.py; the procedure in docs/db-runtime-role-runbook.md.

Seeding: administrator and reference data

The first administrator

init_postgres_admin_user creates the first administrator from ADMIN_USERNAME, ADMIN_PASSWORD and ADMIN_EMAIL, with the role admin. If that user already exists, the function replaces only the stored hash, and only if it does not match ADMIN_PASSWORD: whoever rotates the secret thus rotates the password (chapter 5). It leaves the user's role as it is; only with the role admin is that user the emergency administrator (chapter 5). An account with that name that is linked to a Microsoft account is left untouched. The password is never stored in plain text: the backend hashes it with bcrypt, which it calls directly (chapter 5). The function also works under the restricted role coga_app, which deliberately keeps INSERT and UPDATE rights on users.

Where in the code: init_postgres_admin_user in backend/app/db_migrate.py.

The reference genome GRCh38

Without an organism and an assembly there is no coordinate system for variants. At startup the backend makes sure that Homo sapiens with assembly GRCh38 exists, with cytobands and genes. If either of the two is missing, it fetches them: cytobands from UCSC, genes from the GENCODE annotation (a GTF file, via REFERENCE_GENCODE_GTF_URL). It reads the cytobands as UCSC publishes them that day, and records the file with its name and SHA-256. If UCSC cannot be reached, it loads the backup copy that CoGA ships (data/ref-data/cytobands/, for hg38 and hg19), only with the pinned SHA-256 (CYTOBAND_BACKUP_FILES); that way the genes still load too, because they come in the same import. If GENCODE fails, it falls back on a UCSC gene table and records that. If the whole download fails, it creates only the organism and the assembly (with version hg38): the platform stays usable, and the genes can be imported later. A following start completes that assembly, and an import from UCSC on the Organisms and assemblies page updates it. Both keep the same row and take over the version (the GRC patch, e.g. p14) and the release date that UCSC gives at that moment. There is never a second GRCh38, not even when UCSC moves to a later patch: an assembly is its name (chapter 3). A strict check on the genome name prevents it from being misused in a download URL (server-side request forgery). REFERENCE_BOOTSTRAP_ENABLED=false switches all this off.

T2T-CHM13v2.0 can optionally be added as a second assembly (REFERENCE_BOOTSTRAP_T2T=true; off by default). Its annotation is poorer: UCSC's RefSeq-derived GTF provides coordinates, but no biotypes, Ensembl ids or MANE labels, and there is no cytoband table. If that import fails, it is never fatal.

The import names the assembly as UCSC's description does: T2T CHM13v2.0, with a space (hs1 if that description gives no name). Its ClickHouse tables are called T2T_CHM13v2.0; NCBI writes T2T-CHM13v2.0. CoGA recognises T2T-CHM13v2.0 under each of those names, with one rule in the backend and one in the frontend, in upper or lower case: T2T-CHM13, T2T CHM13 or T2T_CHM13, with or without v2.0, CHM13v2.0 and hs1 (is_t2t_chm13 in backend/app/services/sex_chromosomes.py, next to grc_build; isT2tChm13 in frontend/src/lib/reference.ts). Another CHM13 release (v1.0, v1.1) or another telomere-to-telomere genome does not count: hs1 is v2.0. That rule chooses the UCSC link (hs1) and the IGV genome, puts T2T after GRCh38 among the loci of a gene and the regions of a panel, and gives the STRchive coordinates at which a repeat call is placed. T2T is outside the validated scope (GRCh38 only).

CoGA also recognises GRCh38 and GRCh37 with one rule, grc_build (grcBuild in the frontend): GRCh38 or hg38, GRCh37 or hg19, in upper or lower case, with or without a patch suffix such as .p14. The UCSC import names an assembly hg38 if UCSC's description gives no name. That rule chooses the gene page's links to UCSC and gnomAD (hg38 and gnomAD v4 for GRCh38, hg19 and gnomAD v2.1 for GRCh37). The UCSC and gnomAD links of the variant list and the hg38 locus of the gene page read the assembly by its name, and otherwise by its version, in each case as a whole. A name the rules do not know, such as GRCh38_no_alt, gets no UCSC link and no gnomAD release, just as IGV opens no genome for it.

Where a project, a family, a gene or the explorers name an assembly, they show its build (GRCh38, GRCh37) or, for another assembly, its name, never its version (assemblyDisplayName in lib/reference.ts). The version is the release of the reference data that CoGA loaded (UCSC's hg38 is GRCh38.p14), not the reference to which a family's data were aligned. A patch adds scaffolds and leaves the coordinates of the chromosomes untouched; the FASTA the pipeline aligned to (an analysis set, with or without ALT contigs, decoys or masked regions) is the family's, and is in its annotation manifest as its reference assembly (chapter 6). A list for choosing an assembly adds the version only where two assemblies would have the same name. The Reference data page shows the version, as the release of the reference data. The assembly of a package file is compared by build with that of the project (same_assembly in services/sex_chromosomes.py).

The loci of a gene, the regions of a panel and the sizes in the panel list are in one order: GRCh38, T2T-CHM13, GRCh37, and then the other assemblies by name (assembly_display_rank; compareAssemblyNames in the frontend). The gene page opens on the first one that has the gene.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/reference_source_service.py (ensure_human_grch38_reference_on_startup, ensure_human_t2t_reference_on_startup); the name rules and the order in backend/app/services/sex_chromosomes.py (grc_build, is_t2t_chm13, assembly_display_rank) and frontend/src/lib/reference.ts.

Built-in tracks and the repeat catalogue

  • Segmental duplications are loaded from a file (REFERENCE_SEGMENTAL_DUPLICATIONS_PATH), only if that dataset is still empty for the assembly. The file must be byte for byte the shipped ClinGen file (release V2.1 for GRCh38; SEGMENTAL_DUPLICATIONS_PINNED_SHA256). The startup does not load any other file: it logs one error with the file, both SHA-256 values and the fix, and continues without that track. The file holds GRCh38 coordinates, so the startup loads it only into the assembly that REFERENCE_BOOTSTRAP_ASSEMBLY_NAME names (GRCh38 by default), if grc_build reads it as GRCh38 (above; the same rule chooses the pseudo-autosomal regions of GRCh38 and GRCh37). If the setting names another assembly, such as T2T-CHM13 or GRCh37, the startup loads nothing and logs one warning with that assembly and the fix: an administrator uploads that assembly's own file through the Reference data page (chapter 15).
  • Clinical CNVs and DGV. If the assembly GRCh37 or GRCh38 does not yet have clinical CNVs or DGV variants, the startup queues the build of the knowledge base and the load of the pinned DGV release (2025-12-01), without an account (queue_startup_reference_loads; REFERENCE_BOOTSTRAP_CLINICAL_CNVS, REFERENCE_BOOTSTRAP_DGV). An assembly import from UCSC does the same, as the administrator who imports it. Those jobs run in the background and never hold up the startup. Without the build script (CLINICAL_CNV_KB_SCRIPT_PATH) the build of the knowledge base does not start. An assembly that already has them gets nothing new: an administrator starts a rebuild or another release on the Reference data page (chapter 15).
  • The repeat catalogue combines a built-in list of loci with the STRchive loci (data/ref-data/STRchive-loci.json). The built-in loci carry the thresholds of their STRchive row, so that the status of a call does not depend on which row finds its TRID. Every start writes both again (updated per locus_id), so a changed threshold applies from the next start. Calls already imported keep their stored status on the genome tracks; the repeat page re-assesses them immediately (chapter 8). The seed never writes QA's count correction per locus (repeat_locus_count_units, chapter 8): a start keeps it.
  • The STRchive release is pinned (decision of the owner, 2026-10-14). The source is the shipped release: the file in the repository, with SHA-256 16301ecb0023… (82 loci). It is STRchive release v2.28.0 (8 October 2026), byte for byte identical to the STRchive-loci-v2.28.0.json that STRchive published with that release: the SHA-256 is the digest the release states for that file (STRCHIVE_PINNED_RELEASE). STRchive's thresholds are CoGA's cut-offs, as the release gives them, without CoGA's own validation per locus (decision of the owner, 2026-11-16). The file itself does not name a release, so the SHA-256 is its identity. STRCHIVE_PINNED_LOCI_SHA256 fixes it completely; no setting can replace it. The startup reads the file from TRGT_STRCHIVE_LOCI_PATH (on Cloud Run the reference data bucket), or the copy in the repository if that file is not there. If the file read is not byte for byte the shipped release, or if there is no file, the backend does not start. It then writes nothing and logs one error with the file, both SHA-256 values and the fix (copy data/ref-data/STRchive-loci.json unchanged). An identical copy is accepted, wherever it is. Every start also removes the STRchive rows of repeat_loci that the release does not know, such as the loci of another release that an earlier start wrote. Moving to another release is a reviewed change: the file, the pin and the thresholds of the built-in loci change together (docs/data-import.md, section The STRchive release).

Where in the code: seed_builtin_reference_tracks in backend/app/services/reference_metadata_service.py, with grc_build in backend/app/services/sex_chromosomes.py (which assembly is GRCh38); seed_builtin_repeat_catalog and read_shipped_strchive_release in backend/app/services/repeat_expansion_pg.py; the pin (STRCHIVE_PINNED_LOCI_SHA256) in backend/app/core/config.py.

The HPO ontology

If there are no HPO terms in the database yet, the backend imports the newest HPO release (decision of the owner, 2026-11-05). It reads from HPO which release appeared last (HPO's latest GitHub release) and downloads it from its own PURL, a URL that does not move along with new releases (https://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/hp/releases/<date>/hp.obo). Every request, every redirect included, goes over HTTPS. The file must be an OBO file that states that release, otherwise the backend refuses it. It stores the release and the SHA-256 of the file with every term. On a database that already has terms, a start changes nothing: an administrator applies a newer release (chapter 12).

The file in the repository (data/ref-data/hpo/hp.obo, release 2026-02-16) is the fallback. The backend uses it if HPO cannot be reached (also if GitHub's limit of 60 requests per hour is reached), if it refuses the downloaded file, or if the download is switched off (HPO_DOWNLOAD_LATEST_ON_STARTUP=false, for an installation without internet). It then logs one warning with what went wrong and the fallback release. It imports the fallback only if its SHA-256 is that of the pinned file:

  • A file that is already in place (HPO_ONTOLOGY_PATH, on Cloud Run the bucket) with a different SHA-256 is refused with one error in the log (the file, both SHA-256 values and the fix). The backend then imports nothing and does not download anything in its place either. The startup continues; the HPO terminology stays empty until a release has been loaded.
  • Only if there is no file and the download is switched on does it download the fallback release from its own PURL. Any other file, e.g. a later release, it refuses before anything is written: it logs an error and imports nothing.

Two installations that start at different times can therefore begin with a different HPO release; the administration page shows which one is loaded. The release and SHA-256 of the fallback are fixed in the code; no setting changes them. A different fallback comes only through a reviewed code change. The release and the date of the ontology are stored along with it, so that it can be seen later which version an analysis used (chapter 12).

Where in the code: ensure_hpo_ontology_on_startup in backend/app/services/hpo_service.py, with fetch_latest_hpo_release and download_hpo_release in backend/app/services/hpo_release_download.py; the release and SHA-256 of the fallback (HPO_PINNED_RELEASE, HPO_PINNED_ONTOLOGY_SHA256) in backend/app/core/config.py.

The gene reference (dbNSFP)

The enriched gene information (aliases, ids, constraint, disease associations) is loaded by a background job, not by the startup. At startup the backend queues a first job if that is switched on (GENE_REFERENCE_BOOTSTRAP_ON_STARTUP), there are GRCh38 genes and the cache gene_info is still empty, also without the local dbNSFP gene file (decision of the owner, 2026-11-05). That file is not in the repository. The other sources (HGNC, ClinGen, GenCC, ClinVar) are always the current export. Without dbNSFP each gene costs one request to NCBI, so the job takes hours, and the dbNSFP fields (constraint, orthologues) stay empty. If the file is there later, while no gene in the cache was synchronised with it, the next start queues another job that adds it. After that, a new synchronisation is an administrator's task. A separate worker runs the job; chapter 13 describes how.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/gene_info_jobs_pg.py.

The startup order

FastAPI has a lifespan: a function that runs once at startup and once at shutdown. In backend/app/main.py it does the following, in this order:

  1. Wait until Postgres can be reached.
  2. Only if POSTGRES_RUN_SCHEMA_MIGRATIONS_ON_STARTUP is switched on: migrate the Postgres schema (an empty database from the baselines, a database this version did not make refused, then the revisions the ledger lacks) and create the first administrator. If it is switched off (the restricted role coga_app), the backend only checks that the ledger names exactly its own schema revision and the digest its own baselines. Otherwise it does not start; the message is also in the log.
  3. Start the background writers for the audit log and the UI events, so that everything after this is already logged.
  4. In one Postgres session: seed the repeat catalogue, ensure GRCh38, optionally import T2T-CHM13, queue the rebuild of the clinical CNV knowledge base and the DGV load for a GRCh37 or GRCh38 assembly that lacks them (above), load the HPO ontology, load the newest Monarch release if there is no Monarch data yet (chapter 12), seed the built-in tracks and, if needed, queue the first gene reference job.
  5. Wait until ClickHouse can be reached and apply the ClickHouse schema: create the database if it is missing. The tables per assembly follow when they are first needed (chapter 3).
  6. Remove the backup tables of overwrite imports that no running import owns, left behind by an import whose process stopped (chapter 6). An error here does not hold up the startup.
  7. Start the ClickHouse integrity monitoring. It checks the variant tables shortly after startup and then at a fixed interval, and logs an error if it finds damage (chapter 11).
  8. Start the gene reference worker and the package import workers (their number via FAMILY_IMPORT_WORKER_COUNT). With 0 the backend starts no import workers and leaves the jobs to import worker processes, as under Docker Compose (below). Only with import workers does it also start the worker of the exploratory ancestry PCA, the variant carrier worker (which keeps the carrier summary of the Variant Explorer up to date, chapter 3) and, if FAMILY_IMPORT_WATCH_ROOTS names a folder, the watcher of the import folders (chapter 6).

At shutdown the backend stops all these workers cleanly and closes the database connections.

Where in the code: the function lifespan in backend/app/main.py; described in docs/application-scheme.md, section Startup and background work.

The import worker in its own process

A Python process uses one processor core for all its work, however many workers it runs. If all import workers ran in the backend, all imports of a large batch of families would share that one core, with the event loop that answers the users' requests. That is why python -m app.import_worker can run the import workers in a process of their own, without an API: it answers no requests and listens on no port. Docker Compose runs it as the service import-worker, from the same image and with the same settings and the same /data folder as the backend. There, the backend itself gets no import worker (FAMILY_IMPORT_WORKER_COUNT=0). Each replica is one process, which runs FAMILY_IMPORT_WORKER_COUNT jobs at a time (1 by default). IMPORT_WORKER_REPLICAS (1 by default) determines how many replicas run, and so how many families are imported at the same time, each on its own core. On Google Cloud the imports run in the backend: terraform/ has no separate worker service.

At startup the process checks what the backend checks before starting its workers, and nothing else:

  • it waits for Postgres and does not start if the database has a different schema revision (it never migrates);
  • it waits for ClickHouse and creates the database if it is missing;
  • it removes the backup tables of overwrite imports that no running import owns;
  • then it starts its workers: the import workers, the worker of the exploratory ancestry PCA, the variant carrier worker and, if FAMILY_IMPORT_WATCH_ROOTS names a folder, the watcher of the import folders (only one watches at a time, in whichever process).

On SIGTERM (docker compose stop) or SIGINT it stops its workers as the backend does at shutdown, closes the database connections and exits with code 0. An import that was running stops where it is; the next worker takes over the job as soon as its heartbeat is ten minutes old (chapter 6). A start that fails, or a worker that stops by itself, ends with code 1, and Compose starts the process again.

What the workers of all processes share goes through Postgres and therefore holds across processes and hosts: claiming a job (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), its heartbeat (which the database's clock sets and judges), ending a job with a stale heartbeat, and the write locks on a family's variants (advisory locks on the import's own connection). A worker logs every job it claims, with its worker id, which begins with the process id: a job's record names its worker only while the job is running. In the development setup the import worker does not reload on a code change, so that an edit does not stop a running import. docker compose restart import-worker picks up a change.

Where in the code: backend/app/import_worker.py; the service import-worker in docker-compose.yml and docker-compose.dev.yml; described in docs/application-scheme.md, section Import-worker processes.

Google Cloud with Terraform

The folder terraform/ builds one CoGA environment in a Google Cloud project. In outline:

  • Network and storage. A private network without public IP addresses for the databases. Cloud SQL (Postgres) and a ClickHouse VM with encrypted disks and daily snapshots. Storage buckets for the import packages and the reference data, both read-only for the app and mounted as a folder in the backend: the imports/ folder of the PHI bucket at /data/imports (FAMILY_IMPORT_ROOTS and FAMILY_IMPORT_WATCH_ROOTS, one folder per project), the reference data at /data/ref-data. No browser reads a bucket: the backend serves the reads, the signal tracks and the QC report itself. Everything is encrypted with a customer-managed key (CMEK). An optional block on outgoing traffic for the ClickHouse VM (clickhouse_restrict_egress, off by default) is in terraform/egress.tf. The ClickHouse VM gets the same per-query memory limits as the Docker setup, from the same file (clickhouse/users.d/memory-guards.xml): at most 4 GB per query, and GROUP BY and ORDER BY write to disk from 2 GB.
  • Application. Backend and frontend run on Cloud Run and can be reached only through the external load balancer. The load balancer handles TLS and sends /api to the backend. Cloud Armor (on by default) adds DDoS protection, rate limiting per IP, an optional list of allowed IP ranges and a web application firewall (OWASP CRS). By default that web application firewall only logs, and it blocks only with cloud_armor_waf_enforce = true. The job coga-db-migrate (terraform/migrate.tf) applies the schema when the app runs as coga_app. Before every schema migration that a new backend image brings (that job, or in owner mode the first start of the new revision), terraform apply takes an on-demand backup of the Cloud SQL database with gcloud and waits until it is complete. That is the restore point if the migration has to be reversed. If the backup fails, the rollout stops before the migration and the running version keeps working. For this the deploy account needs a role of its own from the central infra repo (cogaPreMigrationBackup).
  • What Terraform does not do. This configuration does not itself create the CMEK key or the service accounts, nor does it enable the Google APIs; it only refers to them. At CMGG the central infra repo provides them (template: terraform/main-repo-reference/coga-prerequisites.tf.example). That way the CoGA rollout cannot give itself extra rights. For a standalone project, docs/deployment-gcp.md describes those steps (§5.2 and §5.4).
  • Secrets. Terraform creates only the containers in Secret Manager (coga-secret-key, coga-integrity-anchor-key, coga-admin-password, coga-postgres-password, coga-clickhouse-password, coga-postgres-app-password, and for the monitoring coga-metrics-token). You add the values separately (docs/deployment-gcp.md §5.5), so that they are never in Terraform variables. None of them ends up in the Terraform state or the plan. Terraform does read coga-postgres-password on every plan and apply, to set the owner's password in Cloud SQL. It passes it on through a write-only argument: the state stores only the secret's version number, so that a new version changes the password at the next apply. Still keep the state bucket private: it describes the whole environment. The values must meet the rule from chapter 2: SECRET_KEY has at least 32 characters, and the anchor key is the base64 of exactly 32 random bytes (openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '\n') and differs from SECRET_KEY.
  • TLS for ClickHouse. Terraform creates this itself: its own certificate authority and the server certificate, in coga-clickhouse-tls-key and coga-clickhouse-tls-cert. Every run creates the private keys anew, and neither enters the Terraform state or the plan. The server key goes to coga-clickhouse-tls-key; the certificate authority's key is kept nowhere. Because the certificate authority's key is gone after that run, Terraform always issues the certificate authority and the server certificate anew, together; the ClickHouse VM must then restart (docs/deployment-gcp.md §12.4). Terraform creates a new version of those two secrets before it destroys the old one, so that a VM that starts during the apply always finds a key and a certificate. That requires Terraform 1.11 or later and the google provider 8.x.
  • Monitoring and alerts. terraform/monitoring.tf places a collector next to the backend that reads /metrics every minute, with a token from coga-metrics-token, and sends the figures to Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus. Alert rules report by email to alert_notification_emails, among other things, a damaged variant database, lost audit rows, a stuck import and an unreachable app. An uptime check fetches /api/health every minute through the load balancer. For this the deploy account needs the Monitoring roles from terraform/main-repo-reference/rollout-checklist.md. What each metric and each alert means is described in docs/monitoring.md.
  • The path of a request. A user opens https://coga.cmgg.be → the load balancer (TLS and Cloud Armor) → Cloud Run → the backend. The backend reaches Cloud SQL through the Cloud SQL connector (encrypted, over the private network) and ClickHouse over HTTPS with its own certificate authority. The first login uses the email address of the first administrator (ADMIN_EMAIL, set by Terraform to admin@<app_domain>; signing in always uses an email address) and the password from coga-admin-password. With Microsoft sign-in, that is possible only on /login/emergency, as long as AZURE_ADMIN_OVERRIDE is switched on (chapter 5).

Some IVDR obligations remain a matter of process and fall outside the code, such as change control and an updated DPIA, given that Google hosts the data. Whether Google is a processor or a sub-processor is for the owner to decide (docs/deployment-gcp.md §13).

Where in the code: the .tf files in terraform/; the concise reference in terraform/README.md and the full guide in docs/deployment-gcp.md.

Security and traceability during rollout

  • Secrets. Outside development the backend does not start with placeholder or weak secrets (chapter 2). On Google Cloud they come from Secret Manager and are put into the container only at startup, not into images. The Terraform state holds only a reference to them (above).
  • Encryption in transit. Postgres through the Cloud SQL connector; ClickHouse over HTTPS, with a certificate that the backend verifies (CLICKHOUSE_SECURE, CLICKHOUSE_VERIFY, CLICKHOUSE_CA_CERT). At rest, CMEK encrypts Cloud SQL, the disks and the buckets.
  • Restricted database role. coga_app has no DDL rights and no UPDATE/DELETE on the append-only tables. By default the app still runs as owner, until the switch-over from chapter 2.
  • Reproducibility. The base, database and collector images are pinned by digest. CoGA's own images get a tag with the release or the commit, and are rolled out at the digest their build pushed: the running revision is exactly the built image. A release is built only from a commit on main, and its SBOMs are attached to the release with their SHA-256. APP_VERSION and GIT_SHA are baked in at build time and frozen in every signed report. The dbNSFP file, the ACMG SF list and the GENCODE edition are pinned reference versions. Of HPO only the fallback release is pinned: a new installation loads the newest release and stores which one it is (see The HPO ontology). Every cached gene record notes for each source which edition supplied it (chapter 13).
  • Audit from the start. The audit writer starts before the seeding, and the ClickHouse monitoring runs from startup onwards.

5. Login & authentication

This chapter describes how a user gets access to CoGA. Once CoGA is in service, everyone signs in with their Microsoft account of the hospital or the university (Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure AD; see Signing in with Microsoft), or via the organisation's CAS server, such as login.ugent.be (see Signing in via CAS). Besides these there is local sign-in with an e-mail address and password: in development for everyone, alongside Microsoft only for the emergency administrator. The chapter first follows that local sign-in, from form to token and session, and registration. What a signed-in user may then see is in chapter 2.

Concepts

  • JWT (JSON Web Token): a small, digitally signed proof that the server hands out after a successful login. It contains a few pieces of data (claims), such as who you are and until when it is valid. Because it is signed with a secret key, the client cannot forge it.
  • Hashing: irreversibly converting a password into a string of characters. The server stores only that hash; at login the text entered is hashed again and compared.
  • Rate limiting / lockout: blocking temporarily after too many failed attempts.

The login at a glance

  1. The user enters an e-mail address and password on the login page.
  2. The frontend sends them to the backend's login endpoint.
  3. The backend checks that the address or the IP is not blocked, compares the password with the stored hash and, on success, returns a JWT.
  4. The browser keeps the token and sends it with every following request in the Authorization header.
  5. The backend checks the token at every protected endpoint and derives from it who the user is.

The login endpoints

The endpoints are in backend/app/routers/auth.py, under /api/auth/.... Two entry points lead to the same logic:

Endpoint Input Intended for
POST /auth/login JSON with email and password The login page
POST /auth/token An OAuth2 form with username and password The interactive API documentation, which is reachable only in development; the e-mail address goes in username

Both call _authenticate_and_issue_token. It does, in order:

  1. Check the block. If the e-mail address or the IP is blocked, the answer is 429 ("Too many login attempts") with a Retry-After header.
  2. Look up the user and check the password. An unknown address and a wrong password give the same message: 400 Incorrect email or password.
  3. Check that the account is active. An account that is not yet activated gets 403 User not active. That attempt also counts as failed.
  4. On success: clear the counter of failed attempts and issue a token.

The response contains the token, the type (bearer) and the user's role, so that the frontend knows what to show.

Protection against account enumeration. If the server said "no" straight away for an unknown address, an attacker could tell from the response time which addresses exist: the bcrypt check is deliberately slow. That is why, for an unknown address, the code still runs the check, against a fixed dummy hash. Both cases thus take about as long and give the same message. The hashing runs in a separate thread, so that a slow check does not hold up the server.

Where in the code: _authenticate_and_issue_token in backend/app/routers/auth.py.

Passwords: bcrypt

Passwords are never stored in readable form. The backend hashes them with bcrypt, which it calls directly. Bcrypt is deliberately slow, so that an attacker who steals the database cannot quickly try millions of passwords. The hash is in the hashed_password column of users.

Bcrypt reads only the first 72 bytes of a password. The backend therefore truncates a longer password to 72 bytes itself, both when creating the hash and when checking it, so that both always compare the same part. A stored value that is not a bcrypt hash (e.g. from an account without a local password) simply gives no match.

Where in the code: get_password_hash and verify_password in backend/app/dependencies.py; the tests in backend/tests/test_password_hashing.py.

The token

A successful login yields a JWT:

Property Value
Claim sub The user's e-mail address
Claim exp The expiry time
Lifetime Short: two hours by default (ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES)
Signature HS256 (symmetric), with SECRET_KEY

The short lifetime is a deliberate choice. The token is in browser storage, not in a protected HttpOnly cookie; if it leaks, the damage is limited to that period. Anyone who knows SECRET_KEY can make valid tokens; that is why, outside development, the backend refuses a weak key (chapter 2).

Where in the code: create_access_token in backend/app/dependencies.py; the settings in backend/app/core/config.py.

Checking the token: get_current_user

Every protected endpoint depends on get_current_user, with two exceptions: the download of the QC report, which checks only its own signed five-minute link (chapter 2), and GET /metrics, which asks for its own token (chapter 7). That function:

  1. takes the token from the header Authorization: Bearer …;
  2. checks the signature and the validity; an invalid or expired token gives 401 Could not validate credentials;
  3. reads the e-mail address from the claim sub;
  4. loads the user fresh from Postgres and checks that the user exists and is active; if not, again 401;
  5. attaches the user to the request (request.state.current_user), so that the audit log knows who made the request;
  6. refuses (400) a request with a control character (C0 or DEL, such as a NUL from %00) in a path parameter, in the name of a query parameter or in the value of family_id or sample_id in the query string, and a request with a NUL in any query value. A family or sample ID may not contain such a character, and Postgres cannot compare a NUL. A gene or interval list, typed one per line, keeps its line breaks. The refusal comes after authentication, so that the audit log names the user, and before a route looks anything up, with the same answer for everyone (request_value_problem in backend/app/services/family_identifiers.py).

Two dependencies build on it. get_current_superuser requires the role superuser or admin; otherwise the answer is 403 Superuser access required. get_current_admin_user requires the role admin, that of the administrator; otherwise the answer is 403 Admin access required, for a superuser too. Which routes ask for which dependency is in chapter 2.

Where in the code: get_current_user, get_current_superuser and get_current_admin_user in backend/app/dependencies.py.

The frontend: from form to session

The login page (frontend/src/pages/auth/LoginPage.tsx) sends POST /auth/login, requests the profile with the fresh token (GET /auth/me) and then stores the session: the token, the e-mail address and the role. It then opens the requested page from the next parameter. That parameter is filtered first:

  • Allowed is only a path within the app, in the form the route guards write themselves: the page's path, query string and hash, percent-encoded as the browser keeps them. That is a /, then a letter or digit, and after that only visible ASCII characters without a backslash. A browser always reads such a value as a path on this site.
  • Everything else opens the dashboard, just like a missing next: an external URL, //, a backslash, a space or a control character, and a path that starts with a percent-encoded character, such as /%2F/host. A browser reads a backslash as a slash and drops a tab or line break: next=/%5Chost or next=/%09/host in the address bar is //host to the browser, a different site.

This way an attacker cannot send you to a different site after login (open redirect), and the page after login does not get stuck on "This view could not be displayed" (React Router refuses such an address).

The session is in browser storage (localStorage), which the browser's tabs share. If that storage is not available or refuses a value, the page keeps that value itself, in memory. A value that browser storage did accept is not kept by the page, so that a tab does not read back a session that another tab ended. How the API client sends the token and logs out on a 401 is in chapter 1; the route guards are in chapter 2.

Where in the code: frontend/src/pages/auth/LoginPage.tsx, frontend/src/lib/auth.ts and frontend/src/lib/storage.ts.

Rate limiting and lockout

Failed attempts are tracked in the Postgres table auth_login_attempts. Each row is a scope with a counter:

Column Meaning
scope_type / scope_value The scope: email, remote_ip, signup_ip or cas_ip (below, Signing in via CAS)
failure_count The number of consecutive failed attempts
last_failure_at The time of the last failure
locked_until Until when this scope is blocked

How it works:

  • Every failed login increases the counter for two scopes at once: the e-mail address entered and the source IP. This slows down both hammering one account and trying across many accounts.
  • From a threshold on, a waiting time follows that doubles with each extra attempt, up to a maximum. If the last failure was long enough ago, the count starts again.
  • A successful login clears the counters.
  • Threshold, window and waiting times are configurable (LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT_*, with their defaults in .env.example).

The source IP is the IP that the middleware establishes behind the proxies (TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS, chapter 2), so that a client cannot choose it itself. Registration is throttled separately and only per source IP: someone enumerating accounts tries a different address each time.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/auth_rate_limit_pg.py; the table in backend/db/schema/postgres/01_access.sql.

Registering and approving

Anyone can register via POST /auth/signup (page frontend/src/pages/auth/SignupPage.tsx), but that gives no access:

  • The password must be at least 15 characters long (following NIST SP 800-63B-4, for a password that is the only factor). A shorter password gets 422, before anything is created.
  • Registration is throttled per source IP.
  • A new account gets the role viewer and is not active. A viewer only reads, and changes nothing until an administrator gives them a higher role (chapter 2).
  • The response is always the same ("Registration received …"), whether the address is new or already exists. That too prevents enumerating accounts. Only for a genuinely new address does every active administrator get an e-mail (see The mail to the administrators below).
  • The page shows that confirmation: the account is waiting for activation.

A user can log in only after an administrator activates the account (PATCH /auth/users/{user_id}, for administrators only). The same endpoint also sets the global role (viewer, analyst, supervisor, superuser or admin; any other value gets 422); on the Users page this is done with a drop-down list that shows the five roles from low to high, each with a tooltip. No one changes their own role or deactivates their own account. The emergency administrator's role does not change, and the emergency administrator cannot be deactivated. The endpoint also sets the account's projects and its level in each (project_ids, reader_project_ids; chapter 2), as the project settings do per project. A field it does not know, such as projects from the account list, gets 422. The audit entry of the request records what changed, each field from and to (request_meta.account_change).

Waiting for approval, archiving and deleting. An account that has never been active (a registration, a first sign-in via CAS) is waiting for approval: users.activated_at is empty until an administrator activates it for the first time. The Users page shows for each account the date it was added and its status (Waiting for approval, Active, Inactive, Archived), with the waiting accounts at the top. Each change (activating, deactivating, role, archiving, restoring, deleting) first asks for confirmation in a dialog; ticking a box alone writes nothing.

  • Deleting (DELETE /auth/users/{user_id}) is possible only for an account that was never active. Any other account answers 409 and is archived instead. If a record still names the account (such as a gene panel it created), the database refuses the deletion and the backend also answers 409. The audit entry keeps who it was (id, e-mail address, name, sign-in method). If the same person signs in again later, a new account waits for approval.
  • Archiving (PATCH with archived: true) deactivates the account and removes it from the default list (Show archived accounts shows it). The row stays, so that every record that names the account continues to do so, and a new sign-in by the same person does not create a new request. An archived account is first restored (archived: false, it stays inactive) before it can be activated again (otherwise 409); the database does not allow an active archived account (users_archived_inactive_check).
  • No one archives or deletes their own account or that of the emergency administrator (403).

The mail server. CoGA sends mail via the mail server in SMTP_HOST (port SMTP_PORT, sender SMTP_FROM or otherwise ADMIN_EMAIL; with SMTP_USERNAME and SMTP_PASSWORD CoGA authenticates, after SMTP_STARTTLS, which is mandatory outside development). Without SMTP_HOST no mail goes out. A mail links to a CoGA page if CoGA knows its own address (that of CAS_SERVICE_URL). A mail that fails to send leaves the action that sent it untouched; the log names only the type of the error, never an address or the server's text.

The mail to the administrators. An account waiting for approval is reported by e-mail to every active administrator. The mail gives the name, e-mail address, affiliation, sign-in method and time, and links to Users; it contains no patient data. The Users page shows to whom the mail goes and sends a test mail (GET /api/auth/account-request-mail, POST /api/auth/account-request-mail/test).

The mail to the person being activated. If an administrator makes an inactive account active (the approval of a waiting account, or a new activation after a deactivation), the user gets an e-mail after the response, at that account's address: the account can now log in, who activated it, how it logs in, and a link to the sign-in page. It contains no patient data, and does not mention role and projects: an administrator can still change those afterwards. Any other change (role, projects, deactivating, archiving, restoring) sends no mail. Where in the code: backend/app/services/account_activation_mail.py.

The mail server at UGent. A UGent server sends mail only via ICT's central relay, smtprelay.ugent.be: SMTP_HOST=smtprelay.ugent.be, SMTP_STARTTLS=true and as SMTP_FROM a functional UGent mailbox that ICT accepts as sender. ICT lets the VM send via the relay, or provides a system account for port 587 (SMTP_PORT=587, SMTP_USERNAME, SMTP_PASSWORD), never a personal account. The same mail server also sends the mail to whoever is assigned a family (chapter 2). The steps are in docs/deployment-vm.md (step 1, At Ghent University). Where in the code: backend/app/services/outgoing_mail.py.

With Microsoft sign-in or sign-in via CAS there is no registration: POST /auth/signup answers 403, and the first sign-in creates the account (below).

Where in the code: signup, update_user and delete_user in backend/app/routers/auth.py; creating, changing and deleting the account in backend/app/services/metadata_service.py; the mail in backend/app/services/account_notifications.py; the minimum length in backend/app/schemas/auth.py; the page in frontend/src/pages/admin/UserListPage.tsx.

Signing in with Microsoft (Azure AD / Entra ID)

Once CoGA is in service, everyone signs in with their Microsoft account. Microsoft Entra ID then checks the password and the second factor (MFA); IT handles password resets and closing the accounts of people who leave. The backend turns it on as soon as AZURE_TENANT_ID (the organisation's ID) and AZURE_CLIENT_ID (the ID of CoGA's app registration) are set. It is both or neither: with only one of the two, with a tenant that is not a GUID (such as common) or with the emergency override without Microsoft, the backend does not start. What IT creates for this is in docs/deployment-gcp.md §12.11.

The sign-in at a glance.

  1. The login page asks the backend how users sign in (GET /auth/config: the client ID, the organisation's authority and CoGA's API scope; none of it is secret). With Microsoft it shows only the button Sign in with Microsoft, without a password form and without registration.
  2. The browser goes to Microsoft with MSAL (@azure/msal-browser), using the authorization code flow with PKCE, and requests an access token for CoGA's scope (api://<client-id>/access_as_user). Microsoft always asks which account continues, so that on a shared PC no one gets in as their predecessor without being asked. The page the user requested does not go along to Microsoft: only a random key does, under which the path waits in the tab's session storage.
  3. Microsoft sends the browser back to /login. The page completes the sign-in, requests the profile with the token (GET /auth/me), stores the session and opens the requested page, if it belongs to this site.
  4. Every following request carries the Microsoft token. It lives for about an hour. For each request the API client asks MSAL for the token, and MSAL renews it silently before it expires. The IGV browser, which fetches its files itself, requests the token in the same way for each request (sessionAccessToken in lib/api.ts). MSAL keeps its tokens in the tab's session storage; they disappear when the tab closes.

Checking the token. get_current_user chooses the check by the algorithm in the token's header: RS256 is a Microsoft token, HS256 a local token. A Microsoft token is accepted if it:

  • is signed with one of the organisation's published keys (fetched from its OpenID configuration, kept for a day, and for an unknown key fetched again at most once every five minutes);
  • is a version 2.0 token of the organisation itself (iss, tid);
  • is meant for CoGA's API and was requested by CoGA itself (aud and azp: the client ID);
  • carries CoGA's scope (scp; an application's own token has none);
  • has not expired (with one minute's leeway).

A refused token gets 401. The reason (never the token) goes to the log, except for an expired token.

The account. The backend looks up the account by the user's object ID in Entra ID (oid, column users.azure_object_id), never by the e-mail address. At the first sign-in it creates the account: role viewer, active, member of no project, and therefore without access to patient data until an administrator adds it to a project. It can make changes only once an administrator gives it a higher role (chapter 2). The account has no password (hashed_password holds a marker that no password matches). E-mail address and name come from the token (email, otherwise preferred_username; given_name and family_name) and follow the token when they change. What a user stores as their own is therefore tied to the account (its id), never to the e-mail address or the username. The requester of an import job (chapter 6) and their filter presets (chapter 10) remain theirs when those change. An account that later signs in with the address or name that someone else left behind gets none of it. If another account already has that e-mail address or that username, the backend refuses the first sign-in (403) and links nothing: an existing account is never taken over via an e-mail address. A deactivated account gets 401 with the message that it is not active. The audit entry of the request that created the account says so (request_meta.account_change).

The emergency administrator. Besides Microsoft there is one local account: the emergency administrator (break-glass). That is the account that ADMIN_USERNAME names (coga-admin on Google Cloud), with the role admin: an account with that name and a different role, superuser included, is not an emergency administrator. CoGA does not let its role be changed and does not let it be deactivated, so that the emergency sign-in works as soon as the override is on. Its password is ADMIN_PASSWORD: the seed replaces the stored hash as soon as it no longer matches, so whoever rotates the secret rotates the password. The emergency administrator signs in on /login/emergency, a page the login page does not link to, and only while AZURE_ADMIN_OVERRIDE is on (off by default). Any other account, another administrator included, gets 403 there; a local token that is not the emergency administrator's gets 401. Every emergency sign-in and every request made with it writes a warning (azure_admin_override) to the log and is marked in the audit entry (request_meta.emergency_sign_in, Emergency sign-in on the Audit logs page). Turn the override on only for an emergency, and off again afterwards.

Logging out. Logout clears CoGA's session and MSAL's tokens in the tab. UI events that the API did not accept at logout (the token had already expired, or the last request did not arrive) are not lost: they wait in the browser under the account until it signs in again (chapter 15). The sign-in with Microsoft in the browser remains; the login page then offers Sign out of Microsoft, which ends that too (advisable on a shared PC).

Logging out also ends the session on the server, on every device. The browser sends POST /api/auth/logout (endServerSession in lib/api.ts) as soon as the API has answered the last UI events, or after two seconds, and immediately if the page closes in the meantime. The server records when the account logged out (users.sessions_ended_at) and from then on refuses every token the account received before that moment, CoGA's own tokens and Microsoft's (_refuse_if_signed_out in dependencies.py). A copied token therefore stops working when the user logs out, instead of when it expires. CoGA's own tokens state to the microsecond when they were issued (iat), so that a sign-in just after logging out works normally; a token without that time is refused, because no logout could refuse it. Entra ID dates its tokens about five minutes too early: a Microsoft token therefore counts as issued at its iat plus five minutes, the latest possible moment (TOKEN_DATED_EARLY_SECONDS in core/azure.py). Logging out ends the sessions at least just after the issue time of the token used to log out, so that this token too is refused, however early it is dated. If the request does not arrive (offline, or the token had already expired), the tokens stay valid until they expire.

Logging out in one tab ends the session in every tab of the browser. The tabs share the session, and the browser notifies every other tab that the token is gone. That tab then clears its cached data and MSAL's tokens, and shows the login page (Layout.tsx).

If a different account signs in in another tab (on a login page that was still open there), the session ends in the same way. The other tabs see the username, the account's address, change. The session of that other account is cleared too, so that no tab carries on as an account it does not show; that account signs in again. A renewed token, and a new sign-in by the same account, leave the username unchanged, and the session continues.

Where in the code: backend/app/core/azure.py (checking the token), backend/app/services/user_accounts.py (the account and the emergency administrator), the Microsoft branch in get_current_user (backend/app/dependencies.py), GET /auth/config in backend/app/routers/auth.py, and in the browser frontend/src/lib/microsoftSignIn.ts and frontend/src/pages/auth/LoginPage.tsx.

Signing in via CAS (login.ugent.be)

If the organisation offers not an app registration in Entra ID but a CAS server, everyone signs in there. At UGent that is login.ugent.be, which itself signs in via Microsoft Entra ID. The backend turns it on with CAS_SERVER_URL (the CAS server, https://login.ugent.be) and CAS_SERVICE_URL (CoGA's own login page, https://<host>/login). It is both or neither; alongside Microsoft sign-in, with an address that is not HTTPS (outside development) or with a service other than /login, the backend does not start. CAS_DISPLAY_NAME (default UGent) is the name on the button.

The CAS server gives CoGA the attributes chosen when the application was registered. CoGA needs four: azureObjectId (the user's object ID in Entra ID), mail, givenName and surname (the names are configurable with CAS_*_ATTRIBUTE). Without an object ID CoGA refuses the sign-in. If mail, givenName or surname is missing, the backend writes a warning to the log (cas sign-in) with the names of the attributes the response does carry, never their values. Without givenName CoGA shows only the surname; if the CAS server releases the attribute later, the next sign-in fills in the first name.

  1. The login page asks the backend how users sign in (GET /auth/config: the CAS server's login page for CoGA's service, and its logout page). With CAS it shows only the button Sign in with UGent, without a password form and without registration.
  2. The browser goes to the CAS server. The page the user requested waits in the tab's session storage: the CAS server sends the browser back to exactly /login.
  3. The CAS server sends the browser back to /login with a service ticket, which can be used once. The page takes it from the address bar and gives it to the API (POST /auth/cas/session).
  4. The backend validates the ticket with the CAS server (/serviceValidate, over HTTPS, for CoGA's service). A value that is not a service ticket does not go to the CAS server. The backend reads the response only if it is a CAS response of at most 64 KiB, without a document type, so that no entity is expanded.
  5. The account belongs to the object ID, never to an e-mail address: it is the same account that a later Microsoft sign-in finds. If there is none yet, the first sign-in creates it as a viewer without a project, inactive and waiting for approval, and every active administrator gets a mail. CAS lets in every account of the organisation, students included: that is why the new account waits for an administrator, who activates it on the Users page. Until then the sign-in answers 403 with that message.
  6. If the account is active, the browser gets CoGA's own token (HS256), as with a password. With CAS such a token signs in only an account that is bound to an object ID, or the emergency administrator while AZURE_ADMIN_OVERRIDE is on.

A refused ticket answers 401 and counts towards the source IP (auth_login_attempts, scope cas_ip); after too many refusals the sign-in answers 429. A successful sign-in does not count, so that colleagues behind the same address do not hold each other up. The ticket and the CAS server's response do not go into the log. Logging out clears CoGA's session; the login page then offers Sign out of UGent, which ends the session on the CAS server.

Where in the code: backend/app/core/cas.py (the ticket and the response), cas_session in backend/app/routers/auth.py, _cas_session_user in backend/app/dependencies.py, backend/app/services/user_accounts.py (the account), and in the browser frontend/src/lib/casSignIn.ts and frontend/src/pages/auth/LoginPage.tsx.

Security and traceability

  • Every request is logged, including every login attempt, with status code, time, source IP and user agent (chapter 7). A failed login can be recognised by 400, 403 or 429.
  • Passwords and tokens do not go into the logs. The audit log masks sensitive fields, also in the form of /auth/token.
  • The table auth_login_attempts shows the failures and blocks per e-mail address and IP: useful for recognising an attack.
  • The emergency sign-in always leaves a trace in the log and in the audit entry of every request (request_meta.emergency_sign_in).
  • An account created by a first Microsoft or CAS sign-in, and every change of role, activation or project access, are in the audit entry of the request, each field from and to (request_meta.account_change).
  • Short tokens and logging out on 401 limit the consequences of a leaked token.

Key files

File Role
backend/app/routers/auth.py Login, token, registration, profile and user management
backend/app/dependencies.py Passwords (bcrypt), making and checking tokens, Microsoft branch and emergency administrator
backend/app/core/azure.py Checking Microsoft tokens
backend/app/core/cas.py Validating a CAS ticket with the CAS server
backend/app/services/user_accounts.py The account of a Microsoft sign-in; the emergency administrator
backend/app/services/auth_rate_limit_pg.py Rate limiting and lockout
backend/app/schemas/auth.py Login and registration input (minimum password length)
backend/db/schema/postgres/01_access.sql The tables users and auth_login_attempts
frontend/src/pages/auth/LoginPage.tsx · SignupPage.tsx Logging in (also with Microsoft and on /login/emergency) and registering
frontend/src/lib/microsoftSignIn.ts Signing in with Microsoft in the browser (MSAL)
frontend/src/lib/casSignIn.ts Signing in via CAS in the browser
frontend/src/lib/auth.ts · frontend/src/lib/storage.ts The session in the browser

6. Package import — manifest, checks and traceability

CoGA reads in a complete family package of genome data in one controlled operation. The package comes from a folder on disk, passes a manifest and a series of checks, and ends up in Postgres and ClickHouse. The common thread: an auditor must be able to trace afterwards which file, made with which tools, ended up in which table. The reference for administrators and developers is docs/data-import.md (folder layout, manifest format, settings); the provenance of versions is in docs/annotation-provenance.md.

A few terms:

  • Manifest: a YAML or JSON file (manifest.yaml) that lists which datasets a family contains and where each file is, like a packing list.
  • PED: the classic pedigree file (six columns) with the family members and their parents.
  • VCF: the standard format for variants. The ## lines at the top (the header) name the tools used and their versions.
  • Dry-run: a trial run that checks everything but writes nothing.

The pipeline at a glance

Only a superuser or an administrator can import: every endpoint of the router /api/family-imports requires get_current_superuser (chapter 2). Overwriting an existing family is for an administrator only, like every replacement and deletion of a family's data (REQ-SEC-002). POST /api/family-imports/deliveries/{id}/approve with conflict_mode: "overwrite" and without a dry run refuses anyone else with 403 and Only an administrator can overwrite an existing family: import with update to add the missing datasets, or ask an administrator. (OVERWRITE_ADMIN_ONLY_DETAIL). A superuser may run such an overwrite as a dry run, and may import with cancel and update.

Endpoint Purpose
GET /family-imports/packages The family folders that can be added by hand, each with the families that were loaded from it
GET /family-imports/deliveries The deliveries, with their state
POST /family-imports/deliveries Add a folder to the deliveries by hand (a project_id without a project gets 404)
GET /family-imports/deliveries/{id}/package and POST …/revisions Read and correct the package of a delivery
POST /family-imports/deliveries/{id}/approve and /refuse Approve a delivery (also as a dry run; the import is then queued) or refuse it
POST /family-imports/deliveries/{id}/archive Confirm the vanished package folder of an imported delivery as deliberately archived, with a reason
GET /family-imports and GET /family-imports/{job_id} Follow the status

The import does not run in the web request but in a background worker, so that a large package does not block the server. The worker takes the next job, validates the package, registers the family and then imports dataset by dataset. Under Docker Compose the workers run in a process of their own, the service import-worker, not in the backend. That way every import gets its own processor core and does not hold up users' requests (chapter 4). A job stays queued as long as no worker is running.

Where in the code: backend/app/routers/family_imports.py; the orchestration and the worker in backend/app/services/family_package_import.py.

Where the package comes from

A package reaches an import only as a delivery: delivered into an import watch folder, or added to the deliveries by hand (below). Both read only local folders under FAMILY_IMPORT_ROOTS; you mount a bucket as a local folder (on Google Cloud the folder imports/ of the PHI bucket, read-only at /data/imports). A folder with a scheme (gs://, s3://) in that list stops the backend at start-up. CoGA writes nothing into a package folder, so a share or bucket that is mounted read-only works as it is.

The manifest CoGA keeps. Every import reads the manifest that CoGA keeps: the manifest that the package of an approved delivery makes (coga_package_manifest.package_manifest), with the members under family.add_members, never a file in the package folder.

  • The job stores it in family_import_jobs.manifest_text, with its SHA-256 in manifest_sha256. A worker that picks up the job, including a worker that picks it up again after the job's worker stopped, reads the stored text.
  • The paths are relative to the package folder and the same guards apply: a path out of the folder is refused. A manifest file in the folder, even a symbolic link, is just a file: no import opens it.
  • The validation report names the manifest it read: manifest_source (coga) and manifest_sha256. The family's package record for the package's analysis (families.metadata.package_imports) keeps both. The family's files (raw_import_files) hold a managed copy of it, as dataset manifest, to download and verify.

Loaded folders are marked. A package folder stays on the share after the import: CoGA never moves it, and shows the alignments and the QC report from it. The list of folders that can be added by hand therefore gives, for each folder, the families one of whose package records names that folder as the folder they were loaded from (folder_path of a record in families.metadata.package_imports, with or without a trailing /); a family loaded for two analyses from two folders is listed under both. It also gives when their last import from that folder registered them, and whether that import is unfinished or still running (the family carries the flag import incomplete, or the marker of a running import). The form marks such a folder as imported: add it again only to add or replace data, with update or overwrite. The list reads the families' records, not the folders; a folder whose family was deleted is not marked. A folder whose last import was undone because the package changed while it was being read is flagged (changed_during_import). Where in the code: backend/app/services/imported_package_folders.py.

A package that changes after it was checked. A package folder is the output of a pipeline on a share that other machines also write to, and an import is validated, queued and run at different moments. To see that the folder changed in the meantime without reading the content of the files, CoGA takes a fingerprint of the package: a SHA-256 over every item of the folder, at every depth (for a file the path, the size and the modification time in nanoseconds; for a symbolic link the path and the target, without following the link), and over the manifest that CoGA keeps for the import, if there is one. Files that a file manager writes and that no import reads (.DS_Store, Thumbs.db, desktop.ini, ._*) do not count, and an empty folder adds nothing. Where in the code: backend/app/services/family_package_fingerprint.py.

  • The check takes the fingerprint before it reads the folder, and reports it (package_fingerprint). A folder with more than 100,000 items (package_folder_too_large, probably an import folder chosen by mistake) or a folder that cannot be read (package_folder_unreadable) is refused before anything in it is read.
  • A delivery keeps the fingerprint with which its check read the folder. If the folder's fingerprint differs when the delivery is approved, the approval gets 409 and no job is created.
  • The job stores the fingerprint of the folder as it enters the queue (family_import_jobs.package_fingerprint).
  • When the job starts, the check takes the fingerprint again. If it differs from the one taken at queueing, the job ends failed with package_changed_since_queued, and nothing has been written. The job log names the fingerprint with which the import read the folder.
  • After every dataset, and once more after the last one, the import takes the fingerprint again. If it differs from that of the check, or the folder cannot be read any more, what the import read may be partly the old and partly the new package: the import stops and is undone (owner's decision, 2026-11-05). Every dataset it wrote or still had to do counts as failed; a dataset that an update skipped wrote nothing and stays skipped. A family that the import created is deleted with everything on it, including the managed copy of a stored manifest. For an existing family the datasets are restored from the snapshot taken before the datasets (with an update just as with an overwrite, as soon as the package has a fingerprint), and so is what the registration wrote (put_back_family_package_record): the package record of the package's analysis, the family's analyses, what it wrote of each sample (its assays, its capture panels, its manifest entry and its package records, as the record keeps them in previous_samples), and the rows of the raw files from the package folder when no record names that folder any more, with the copy of the manifest CoGA kept for the job. The records of its other analyses stay as they are. The pedigree that the registration changed stays, as with every failed overwrite; every change is on the clinical audit trail. If the restore fails, the family gets the flag import incomplete. The job ends failed with package_changed_during_import, and the list of folders offers the folder again, with the label changed during import. Import the package again when it is finished, first with a dry run.
  • The package record of the package's analysis keeps the fingerprint with which it was loaded (package_fingerprint in families.metadata.package_imports).

Import watch folders. A pipeline, or the step that copies its output to the share, can deliver a package without anyone typing the path: it writes the package folder into its project's folder in an import watch folder (<watch folder>/<project>/<package>), with its package file coga-package.json. The watch folder holds one folder per project, with exactly the name of the project in CoGA (owner's decision of 2026-11-10). A delivery in the folder of a project other than the one its package file names needs attention (package_project_folder_differs), as does a package folder placed directly in the watch folder (package_not_in_project_folder): correct the project in Deliveries, or move the folder to its project's folder. That one file describes the package in place of a PED, a manifest and a ready marker, and its status says when the package is complete (docs/coga-package.md). The watcher finds the delivery, checks it once and stores its state. It imports nothing: on the page Package import a person approves every delivery that is ready. Where in the code: backend/app/services/import_watcher.py, backend/app/services/coga_package.py and backend/app/services/coga_package_manifest.py.

  • Settings. FAMILY_IMPORT_WATCH_ROOTS names the watch folders: local folders under FAMILY_IMPORT_ROOTS (a folder outside the import folders is not watched; a mounted bucket is, through its folder). Empty, the default, means that no folder is watched; the rounds run all the same, for what they do beyond the watch folders (recording the end of an approved delivery's import, offering a failed one again, following the folders of imported deliveries), which a folder added by hand needs too. FAMILY_IMPORT_WATCH_INTERVAL_SECONDS (default 300) is the time between two rounds. The watcher runs where the import workers run: in every import worker process, and in the API if it runs imports itself. Only one watches at a time: it holds a Postgres advisory lock on a connection of its own.
  • The package file (format coga-package/1): a JSON object of at most 20 MB, always written in full, first under a temporary name and then renamed. Every file contains schema, status, written_at and pipeline (name, version, run_id); a complete file (status: complete) also project (the unique project name), assembly (that of the project, compared on build: GRCh38.p14 and hg38 belong to a GRCh38 project), analysis_type, family (with family_id, and optionally roi and the PGT details) and files: per file the path in the folder, the size and a sha256 or md5. members is the pedigree (the import reads no PED), datasets the dataset block of a manifest; if a file leaves them out, CoGA proposes them from the folder, as Discover does, and the delivery warns about it. The optional reference is the FASTA the pipeline aligned to: the import sets it as the reference assembly in the family's annotation manifest. A field the format does not know is refused. The full description is in docs/coga-package.md.
  • A run in progress. If the package file says running or failed, the folder is not a delivery: the pipeline is still writing it, or stopped. An earlier open delivery of that folder becomes superseded, with the run noted, until the file says complete again.
  • A round. In every watch folder, every package folder with a complete package file is one delivery per fingerprint: a folder that changes is a new delivery. A new delivery is checked once: the package file; the size of every file (otherwise incomplete: the copy is still running); the checksum of every file for which the package file gives one (a checksum is optional: without one CoGA computes the SHA-256 itself and the delivery warns that the copy was not checked against the pipeline's output, package_files_without_checksum; the import takes over that SHA-256 instead of reading every file again); the pipeline's QC, the project and its assembly; the manifest that CoGA makes from the package file and that the delivery keeps; a PED in the folder that says something other than the members (a warning: the pipeline's tools may have read it); the validation as a dry run does it; that every file the import reads is in the package file (a file that is not in it, such as a CRAM put into the folder later, CoGA adds to the package itself, with its size and the SHA-256 it reads, and the delivery warns, package_files_proposed: the approver checks it; the owner's decision, 2026-11-23); and a family or samples that already exist (an existing family calls for a choice of update or overwrite, never a new family). If anything fails, the delivery is needs_attention, with every error as a reason; otherwise ready. An open delivery (ready or needs_attention) that the watcher sees again is checked again as soon as what CoGA holds has changed since its check: the project the package file names (added, deleted or of a different assembly), or a family or samples of the package (loaded or deleted). If you add the missing project, the delivery is ready at the next round, without the folder changing. What the check read of the family (the members' values, their links, the region, the package records) it also keeps as a digest (family_state): if you change a member in the members editor, or the region on the family page, as a reason asks, a new check follows. It stays the same delivery; the event import_delivery_checked_again records the state and the reasons before and after. A delivery whose package file could not be read, or whose check could not run, is checked again only when its folder changes.
  • States. incomplete, ready, needs_attention, superseded (a newer delivery of the same folder arrived before anyone decided, or the pipeline is running again in the folder) and gone (the folder or its package file is missing for two rounds while the watch folder was readable; a project folder that cannot be read does not count), each reopened (import_delivery_reopened) when the folder is again as it was checked, for example when a lock file of a document that was open on the share disappears again; after a decision queued, imported, failed (until the next round offers it again) or refused; changed_after_import, the reference delivery of a family whose package folder changed or disappeared after the import, and archived, one whose vanished folder a superuser confirmed as deliberately archived (below). A watch folder that cannot be read, or that shows nothing but hidden items while it had open deliveries (a share that is not mounted looks like an empty folder), is skipped that round: nothing is decided. A watch folder that shows anything else, even only folders without a package file, is mounted: the watcher looks into it, so a delivery whose folder was removed is gone after two rounds. A watch folder that was emptied completely keeps its open deliveries until a delivery or another folder is in it again.
  • Correcting. What the pipeline does not know (the clinical status, HPO terms, the inheritance model) or filled in wrongly, a superuser corrects before the approval: POST /family-imports/deliveries/{id}/revisions with the revision they saw, a reason and the changes; GET /family-imports/deliveries/{id}/package shows the package as the import would read it now, the pipeline's file and every correction. The pipeline's file never changes: every correction is a revision in the append-only table import_delivery_revisions (what changed, the value before and after, the reason, who and when, and the whole package afterwards) and an event on the chain system:import-inbox. The laboratory's fields change freely, with a reason; sex, parents and couples, which the pipeline used, do too, but as long as a dataset that the pipeline computed with them (pipeline_used_pedigree) is in the import, the delivery needs attention (package_pedigree_changed). The pipeline's own fields (run, assembly, family ID, sample IDs, files, QC) are refused. A sample that the package's files name but that is not a member, a column of the phased family VCF (dataset_vcf_sample_unknown, one reason per column, with the name), is added as a member, with a reason (owner's decision of 2026-11-11): an affected relative for the segregation, or a PGT index that the PED lacks. The sample ID is that of the file; no other member is added to a pipeline's package (400). A member that was added in CoGA can be removed again; a member that the package delivered cannot.
