If the account is deactivated, is not a superuser or administrator any more, or is gone when a worker picks up the job, the worker does not run the import. That also applies to a job that was still validating and is picked up again after its worker stopped. The job ends failed with the reason, nothing of the family is written, and the log names neither the account nor its address. An active superuser or administrator puts the import back in the queue. A job that overwrites an existing family moreover runs only as long as that account is an administrator. If it is superuser or lower by then, the job ends failed with the reason (REQUESTER_CANNOT_OVERWRITE_ERROR), and nothing of the family is written; an update, or an active administrator who puts the overwrite back in the queue, brings the package in. An import that was already running when the account was deactivated or given a lower role runs to the end: the account is checked when the import starts.

A job goes to running only once it has recorded the family it imports (family_id), before the import writes anything of that family. That is how a sign-out recognises a running import (chapter 11, gate 0b). If that fails, the import stops without writing and the job ends failed, with the reason. The job's later updates (log lines, per-dataset summary, heartbeat) are informational: if one fails, the import carries on, because the status and the family stay in place. If an update does not find the job as its worker's any more (another worker ended it), it changes nothing; the backend log mentions that, with the job's id.

Progress and time left. Every dataset gets a progress in its summary: when it started and ended. Some importers also count how many bytes of their files they have read (for a gzip file the compressed bytes): the small variants (the SNV VCF, the SNV files of a long-read couple, the two files of a NIPT pair and the imputed genotypes) and APCAD. From that follow the part read and the time left: the rest of the files at the pace since the first report. The time before that does not count, because the importer is not reading anything yet then (reading in a VEP table, wiping the rows of an overwrite). An estimate appears only after half a minute of reading. It applies to the dataset that is running; the datasets after it are not estimated, and the page says how many follow.

A worker takes a job atomically (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), so that several workers do not get in each other's way, not even from different processes. A running job writes a sign of life (heartbeat) every minute. The database's clock sets the timestamp and judges the age, so that workers on hosts with a different clock agree. If the sign of life is ten minutes old, the process that ran the job counts as stopped (a restart, a crash, out of memory), and the next worker takes over the job:

  • If the import had not yet started writing the family (the job was still at validating), the worker runs it again from the start. The earlier attempt's log lines stay.
  • If it had (running), the job ends failed, interrupted, and does not run again: a new run does not undo what it already wrote. The log and the per-dataset summary stay as the import left them.

The process may also still be alive and merely have been unable to write its sign of life (no database connection for it, or an event loop kept busy by other work). In that case, too, the import is stopped: as soon as its heartbeat reaches the database again and sees that the job is not its worker's any more, the import stops where it is, as with a stopped process. The error handling below then does not run, and the import writes nothing more. The family keeps the import's item in import_unfinished, as the job's Interrupted record says, and the write locks on its variants are released with their connection. Until then the import may have run on: an update of the job that does not find a row any more (the progress, or how the import ended) changes nothing, and the backend log mentions it with the job's id. That does not last long. An import whose sign of life has not reached the database for five minutes (half of those ten) stops itself this way, even before a worker can consider the job stopped. The job ends as interrupted as soon as a worker finds its sign of life stale.

One import per family at a time. An import holds its family's import lock, on the family ID, from before the registration until it ends, whichever worker or process runs it. The imports of two analyses of one family so run one after the other: the second waits until the first is done, and its log says Another import of the family is running: this import waits for it to end. Without that lock one import could register the family (its pedigree, its samples' metadata, its package record) while the other wrote, restored or deleted it.

The connection of the write locks. An import holds its import lock and the write locks on the family's variants each on a database connection of its own, and Postgres releases them if that connection drops. That is why a running import checks those connections every ten seconds (SELECT 1 in the locks' transaction; without an answer after thirty seconds a connection counts as lost). If one is gone, another import or write may already have started. The import then stops where it is and restores nothing: its job ends failed with the reason, the backups it made of the family are deleted, and the family keeps the import's item in import_unfinished until it has been imported again with overwrite.

The error handling is built so that a half-imported family is never left behind unnoticed ("fail-clean"):

  • Every dataset is imported separately. If one fails, its Postgres work is rolled back and the import carries on with the rest. What the dataset already wrote to ClickHouse is cleaned up only by the small variants and the haplotypes themselves. Part of another dataset may remain; then what follows below applies (deleting, restoring or the flag import_incomplete).
  • If the family is new and nothing succeeded, the empty family is deleted again, with its ClickHouse rows.
  • If an overwrite of an existing family fails, the family is restored to its state from before the import.
  • Taking turns: every write on a family's variants (an upload, a deletion, an import) first takes that family's write lock and holds it until the write is committed. An import holds it from before its snapshot until it is done or has restored the family.
    • A separate upload of a sample's TRGT calls or of an interval track (BED) also takes the lock, because the restore also rewrites those rows; likewise an administrator's deletion of a sample's track or TRGT calls.
    • The demo script scripts/load_demo_quartet.py loads through the same uploads, and like them keeps track of what it brings in.
    • A track upload with overwrite that fails after its wipe also removes the track's Postgres record. A package dataset that replaces a caller's track also wipes that caller's rows for which Postgres has no record.
    • Two writes on the same family therefore run one after the other, even from different workers. The restore cannot undo an upload that came in during the import: that upload waits until the import is done.
    • As long as a family's import job is running or queued, or a writer holds the lock, its report cannot be signed out. A sign-out shares the lock as long as it reads the family (chapter 11, gate 0b).
  • In every other case the successful datasets stay and the family gets the flag import_incomplete: the failed and the successful datasets, the timestamp and the import job's id. The error per dataset is in that job; the flag does not copy the error text. The partial state is thus visible, not silently "complete": the family is on Import incomplete (see What goes into which table).
    • When the flag disappears: only when an import has imported every failed dataset again, or a separate upload brought it in again, for the same samples and (for the small variants) the same callset (see below). An import that succeeds without that dataset leaves the flag in place and says so in its log.
    • An update is enough: the failed dataset's rows were rolled back or cleaned up, so the update finds none and imports the dataset in full. A dataset whose rows remained, it skips, and that does not count; nor does a skipped sample. A dataset that it imported for some samples and skipped for others therefore counts only for the imported samples. An update reads what is already there from the stored rows (the variants and tracks in ClickHouse, the repeats and the Paraphase results in Postgres), not from what Postgres keeps of a track (sample_interval_track_sources). A dataset that it skips for every sample ends as skipped, not as imported.
    • What counts as imported again: a dataset that the import ends imported, also with warnings (warning: the phenotype rows it refused, it leaves out and names in the job). registered also counts, if the package contains nothing for it that CoGA imports (phenotypes without an HPO row, per-sample GLIMPSE2 BCFs, an APCAD BED for the whole family, a pipeline record without versions or parameters): nothing of those can be missing, and that registration completes nothing of data that another import brought in. A dataset that was only registered because the family is not linked to a single assembly, or because a file could not be found or read, does not count: data may be missing there.
    • Repeated failures: if a later import fails, the previous import's failed datasets stay in the flag. If the same dataset fails again for another callset or other samples, both stay. The flag keeps per dataset every callset and every set of samples for which it failed, each with the job in which its error is (failed_scopes); a dataset leaves the flag only when each of them has been brought in again. failed_jobs names per dataset the job of its last failure; the family pages and the sign-out show that job. Each failure also names the analysis of the import it failed in (analysis_type: the key of its package record; none for a single-file upload), and failed_analysis_types names per dataset the analyses of its failures: a short-read and a long-read package both have an snv, a qc and alignments. The same scope failing in the imports of two analyses is two failures; only an import of the same analysis, or an upload, brings a failure of an analysis in again, and the sign-out of an analysis is held only by its own failures and those of no analysis.
    • Without a job: a dataset that failed in a separate upload (or in an import outside a job) has no job there. The family pages and the sign-out then say that no import job keeps track of its error, and never name the job of another failure.
    • Other shapes: the flag, the entries in import_unfinished and the datasets' scopes each have one shape, and CoGA reads them only in that shape. A value in another shape (e.g. true, text or a list) is never read as something it does not say: the read fails (ImportMarkShapeError). A sign-out that meets one therefore fails, and the gate stays closed. An import, separate upload or deletion that meets one leaves it as it is; an upload or deletion fails on it.
  • An import that stops halfway, because its process is gone, carries out none of the above. That is why an import puts a marker on the family before it writes anything of it: an item in import_unfinished in the family metadata, with the job, the start, the analysis of its package and the datasets (a new family is created with it straight away). It records there every dataset it finishes, and removes the item when it ends, unless its restore failed halfway (see below). If the item stays, it names a stopped import and the datasets it did not finish: those may be half-written or missing. The family is then on Import incomplete. Only an import that succeeds with overwrite and imports those datasets again, for the same samples and (for the small variants) the same callset, wipes the item: an overwrite replaces no more than that. An update cannot do it, because it skips a dataset for which data already exist, even half-written data. If an import fails after the marker but before its first dataset (e.g. during registration), it wrote none of its datasets: its item then becomes the flag import_incomplete, with all its datasets as failed.
  • The backup of a stopped overwrite: an overwrite of an existing family first copies its variant and track rows to backup tables in ClickHouse (<assembly>/SNAPSHOT/<import-job>/…), to restore the family on an error, and deletes them when it ends.
    • Process stopped: the worker that ends the job deletes those tables, and at every start every backup that no running import owns disappears. The family is not restored with it: the Postgres part of the backup was in the stopped process, and the family may have been written to in the meantime.
    • Backup already gone: an import that was still alive when its job was ended can reach its restore before its heartbeat stops it, with the backup already gone. That is why a restore first checks that every backup table is there, and wipes nothing if one is missing. The family then keeps what the import left behind and gets the flag import_incomplete, with the failed and the successful datasets.
    • Restore failed: a restore that fails in another way (e.g. halfway) may have wiped rows of every dataset of the family: table by table, it wipes the family's rows before it restores them from the backup. The flag then names every dataset of the import as failed, also the successful ones and those it only registered, and none as imported. The family stays marked until an import has imported each of them again. The job's record says the same: the table of datasets shows each as failed, with how its loader ended, and the error message names them all.
    • Postgres after ClickHouse: Postgres is restored only after ClickHouse, so after such a restore Postgres may still keep track of a track whose rows the restore wiped. An update therefore reads the rows: a dataset whose rows the restore wiped, it imports again, and that dataset leaves the flag; a dataset whose rows are still there, it skips, and that dataset stays in the flag.
    • Data from outside the import: such a restore also wipes rows of datasets that the import did not bring (e.g. another source of small variants, the SV calls of another package, or data from a separate upload). The flag cannot name those, so the import's item in import_unfinished stays as well. As soon as the restore begins, that item names every dataset the family holds in ClickHouse, as its imports and separate uploads keep track of what they brought in (imported_scopes in the family metadata), and every dataset of the import, each with its samples and (for the small variants) its callset. A dataset of another import or upload that is only in Postgres (repeats, Paraphase, QC, phenotypes) it does not name: Postgres is restored in one transaction and an error rolls that back entirely, so the restore cannot leave such a dataset half-written.
    • Recovery: the family stays Import incomplete until each of them has been brought in again with overwrite. An administrator does that recovery: an overwrite and a separate upload are reserved for an administrator (chapter 2). So import the whole family again, every package of it, not only the failed datasets, and upload again with overwrite what a separate upload brought in. Every import that succeeds with overwrite, and every separate upload with overwrite, removes from the item what it brought in again; with the last one the item disappears. A dataset of the import that contained nothing CoGA imports also counts by registering it; data that the family holds count only by bringing them in again. An update removes nothing from it, because it skips a dataset whose rows are still there; neither does an upload without overwrite. The job's log says so and names the datasets, as does the log of every import that still leaves some in place.
    • An import whose process stops during the restore leaves the same item behind. A restore that puts the family back or refuses to begin removes the item.
    • What a separate upload keeps track of: what it brought in, in the same transaction as its data. That is recorded under the dataset of the package that brings in the same data (snv with its callset, haplotypes for imputed genotypes, repeats_trgt per sample), or under a name of its own where no package does so (sv_sniffles, sv_spectre or sv_manual, and bed_<type>, per sample; docs/data-import.md).

  • The small-variant callset: an import keeps track of the small variants as the callset in which it stores them: in the flag, in its item and in imported_scopes. That is the source_format that the SNV dataset states. With auto (the default) it is the callset that its family VCF contains, read from the file before the import writes anything of the family, as the small-variant loader reads it: the caller that its header names, otherwise glimpse2 for imputed genotypes (genotype posteriors in the first record, or phased genotypes in a file whose header or name says it is phased). A file whose caller neither the dataset nor the header names is refused. The files of a NIPT pair are nipt, those of a long-read couple the callset of the caller that their dataset names.

    • Two imports that both leave auto in place therefore complete each other's failed dataset or item only if their files contain the same callset. An import of direct calls does not bring in a family's imputed genotypes again, and vice versa; one caller's calls do not bring in another caller's again. A separate upload and an import bring in each other's callset again if they stored the same one.
    • The import stores the file as that callset. If the file reads as another callset when its dataset's turn comes, it changed while the import was running; it is refused before anything of it is written.
    • A registration whose callset reads auto names no callset, and no import or upload completes it, whatever callset that import or upload stores. Such a registration comes from an import that could not read its family VCF when it began (that import then fails on the file, or only registers it). A family that is marked like that stays marked, and its sign-out requires the acknowledgement.

    Where in the code: family_package_datasets.py (snv_dataset_callset, and the SNV importer) and family_package_registration.py (dataset_scopes, _scope_covers).

  • On every error the job ends failed, never a silent completed.

  • A failed SNV import cleans up only the rows of the callset it stores, the callset that the flag then names: with auto the one from its family VCF (see above). A failed import of imputed genotypes leaves the direct calls in place, and vice versa.
    • An update of the SNV dataset also looks at that callset's rows. It skips imputed genotypes if the family already has them, or the haplotype blocks made from them (the loader writes both; the dataset haplotypes does the same, and reads the blocks in ClickHouse, not what Postgres keeps of them). Next to direct calls it does import them. Likewise it imports one caller's calls next to another's: a long-read package imported with update into a family that holds the short-read callset imports its own callset.
    • If the import could not read the family VCF when it began, it reads it when the dataset's turn comes. If that still fails, it refuses the file as the loader does, before it counts, writes or wipes anything.
    • The clean-up of snv and haplotypes (for the latter the imputed genotypes and their haplotype blocks) runs only once the loader has started writing in ClickHouse: wiping the callset it replaces, or, without a stored callset, its first insert. A file that the loader refuses earlier, such as a VEP table without a header line, replaces nothing: the family's callset stays, the dataset fails and the flag names it.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/family_package_jobs.py (the job life cycle, and taking over a job or ending it as interrupted), family_package_import.py (the fail-clean rules, and the heartbeat that stops an import whose job was ended), clickhouse_family_snapshot.py (the backup of an overwrite and the restore) and family_package_registration.py (the flag and the marker import_unfinished).

Provenance: the annotation manifest

Besides the hash per file, CoGA keeps an annotation manifest per analysis of a family (family_annotation_manifest): per tool or database the version, with a detail and, where needed, the version per modality. That way every result can later be traced back to the versions that made it. The rules:

  • Per analysis: a family sequenced short-read and then long-read, or a family with the NIPT of several pregnancies, keeps a row per analysis (analysis_type, the key of its package record). An import writes the row of its own analysis and leaves another's; a single-file upload writes the row of no analysis (unspecified), which is every analysis's. An analysis's manifest is its own row over those of no analysis; a sign-out of the analysis freezes that, never another analysis's versions.

  • Refreshed on a new import: new versions overwrite the old ones per tool; what the new input does not name stays (a new SV import therefore does not wipe the SNV versions).

  • Manual work wins: an analysis's manifest that was replaced by hand is always recorded as manual and is never overwritten by an import. There is no screen for it: only an administrator can replace it, through the API (PUT /api/families/{family_id}/annotation-manifest, with the analysis in analysis_type). The manifest itself is not an append-only table, but every replacement goes into the clinical audit trail, with the analysis and the manifest before and after (chapter 11).
  • Taking turns: an import and a replacement of the same family take the same lock before they read the manifest, and an import holds it until it is committed. A replacement therefore cannot fall between an import's read and write; it waits until a running import of that family is done.
  • Together with the data: the write belongs to the same transaction as the import. The provenance is therefore stored if, and only if, the data it describes are stored as well; an error in the provenance does not break the import.
  • Per modality: SNV, SV and repeats are annotated by different pipelines and can name different releases of the same database (e.g. two GENCODE versions). That is why the version per modality is stored as well.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/annotation_manifest_service.py.

The register of source files

The traceability register par excellence is raw_import_files: one row per physical source file, with file name, kind, family or sample, storage path, size, SHA-256 and source. A new import of the same file updates the row instead of making a duplicate. Package files are registered in place: CoGA does not move or delete them.

The storage path is read back as given, and a changed database row can name any path. That is why the administration page reads a file only where an import of its family puts it. The real path, with symbolic links followed, must lie in a package folder that a package record of the family names (the folder_path of each record in families.metadata.package_imports, one per analysis, if that lies under a folder of FAMILY_IMPORT_ROOTS, as for the files that IGV reads), or in the upload folder data/raw_imports, where every copy of CoGA's own is kept; the file is read through that real path. So the package of another family in the same import folder is not read.

  • A row with another path is listed as unavailable, without the path being looked up; downloading and Verify give HTTP 403.
  • The list marks such a row as not read (outside_read_folders), and the page says why Verify refuses.
  • If the family has no usable package folder, or the list is empty (the development mode in which the import accepts any local folder), the page reads only in the upload folder.
  • The package folder is that of the family's last import. A file that an earlier import recorded from another folder is shown as not read, just as IGV does not read that folder either.

Whoever deletes a sample or family wipes only CoGA's own copies of uploads in the upload folder. A row that names another path is skipped and logged, and nothing is wiped for it. The copies go only once the deletion is committed: a deletion that fails leaves every file its rows name in place. A copy that cannot be wiped after the commit stays and is logged with its row, its path and the kind of error: a file without a row, never a row without a file. A package folder need not be named after its family, nor an upload folder after the family's current ID.

An auditor can thus trace per family: which files were read in, with which hash or which storage record (to be checked again), in which dataset; with which tool and database versions per analysis (family_annotation_manifest); and how the job went, with status, timestamps, log lines and validation findings (family_import_jobs). That closes the chain annotated VCF → stored data → provenance → report.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/raw_import_files_pg.py and family_package_registration.py.

The administration page

The page Package import (/package-import) shows the deliveries and the import jobs.

  1. Deliveries: every delivery with its state, its problems and warnings. Add a folder by hand adds a folder that no pipeline delivered: choose it (or type the path), the project and the analysis. Folders of which every family was loaded completely appear in the list only if you tick Show imported folders; a folder whose import was not complete is marked (import incomplete, or import undone if its last import was undone).
  2. Correcting: Correct… opens the package as a form, with the reason and the earlier corrections. A sample that the package's files name but that is not a member (an affected relative in the phased family VCF) you add under Add a member; for a folder that was added by hand, any other member too, and there you also edit the package as JSON. What the discovery step proposed and whoever imports must check (the NIPT pair and a NIPT file whose column is not named after its sample, the couple from a long-read package, the linking of a PGT index) is listed with the delivery's warnings.
  3. Dry run and approval: Dry run checks the delivery as an import would, without writing anything; Approve… puts the import in the queue. If the family already exists, you choose a policy for existing data (update or overwrite); only an administrator overwrites an existing family. If the package's members differ from the family's in more than new members, only overwrite is possible.
  4. Following: under Recent family imports are the last 10 jobs; Show all shows up to 100 (the maximum of the job history) in a list that scrolls. As long as a job is running, the page refreshes the status and shows per dataset the part of its files read and roughly how long it will still take, at the pace so far (see above). View shows the report: counters, errors, warnings, the result per dataset, the log lines, the SHA-256 of the stored manifest and the package's fingerprint.

docs/data-import.md describes this way of working with the dry-run first: whoever imports sees the outcome of the checks before anything goes to the database.

Where in the code: frontend/src/pages/dashboard/ImportDeliveriesPanel.tsx, AddDeliveryForm.tsx, DeliveryCorrectionDialog.tsx and ImportJobsPanel.tsx.

7. Backend: routers & services in detail

CoGA's API layer follows a fixed pattern: router → service → storage. FastAPI gives each endpoint the database session and the logged-in user. A few security rules apply everywhere: every database query is parameterised, every ORDER BY comes from a fixed list, and every LIMIT/OFFSET becomes an integer. Further on: the overview of all routers, and the request logging, which records every request in the audit log.

A few terms:

  • Router: a group of HTTP endpoints (e.g. GET /api/families/...), in FastAPI an APIRouter.
  • Service: a Python module with the actual logic (database queries, clinical calculations). Routers deliberately do not contain that logic.
  • Dependency injection: in an endpoint's parameter list you say "I need X" (e.g. a database session), and FastAPI creates X and passes it in.
  • Pydantic model (schema): a Python class that describes and checks the shape of incoming and outgoing JSON.
  • Parameterised query: a database query in which values are passed separately instead of pasted into the text; the standard defence against SQL injection.

Thin routers, thick services

CoGA keeps three layers strictly separate:

  1. Router (thin): reads the path and the parameters, has them validated, enforces access and returns the response as JSON.
  2. Service (thick): the clinical and business logic, such as filters, prioritisation, ACMG rules and hash chains. Only services talk to the storage, apart from a few small, parameterised lookups in routers (in cram.py, signal_tracks.py, family_qc_reports.py, repeat_expansions.py, families.py and health.py).
  3. Storage: Postgres through SQLAlchemy (asynchronous) and ClickHouse through a direct client.

An example: GET /api/families/{family_id}/small-variants.

  • The router (backend/app/routers/families_small_variants.py) receives the page size as an integer with a lower and an upper bound. A value that is too large is refused with 422 before anything runs. A separate dependency reads in the many filter parameters, so that the ordinary endpoint and the CSV export use exactly the same filters.
  • The access checkpoint build_family_metadata_context loads the family only if the user may see it, and restricts the projects to those of the user (chapter 2). That happens before any variant query goes to ClickHouse.
  • The service (backend/app/services/clickhouse_family_variants.py) builds the ClickHouse query, with the scoping in it (e.family_guid = %(family_guid)s, e.project_guid IN %(project_ids)s) and the values as parameters.
  • The response is checked against a Pydantic model and returned as JSON.

The router touches no SQL here, the service no HTTP or tokens. That way a reviewer sees at once where the access control, the validation and the query construction sit.

Dependencies: session, user, scoping

Two dependencies recur in almost every protected endpoint:

  • get_postgres_session gives a fresh database session per request and closes it afterwards.
  • get_current_user checks the token and loads the user (chapter 5); get_current_superuser additionally requires the role superuser or admin, get_current_admin_user the role admin (chapter 2).

A router can also put a dependency on all its endpoints at once. That is how the routers for DGV, CNVs, chromosomes, blacklist and segmental duplications require a valid token for every endpoint, including a future one.

Where in the code: backend/app/dependencies.py and backend/app/core/postgres.py.

Schemas: validation and documentation

All shapes of requests and responses are in backend/app/schemas/, one module per domain. They do three things:

  • they check input: invalid JSON gives 422 before the router runs;
  • they fix the shape of the response (response_model=), so that unintended fields drop out;
  • they provide the OpenAPI description of the API.

Every route that answers with JSON names its model, never a bare dict. The frontend reads the response through the type generated from it (frontend/src/lib/apiSchema.generated.ts), and test_api_response_models.py fails on a route without a model. Only the BED read routes return the JSON their service builds. Their model describes it without validating the up to a million rows again; tests compare each track type with the model. Outside development /docs, /redoc and /openapi.json are disabled. Because all schemas are in one place, a reviewer can check there which data go into and out of the system.

Security rules that apply everywhere

These rules sit in a few shared helpers, not separately in each function.

1. All queries are parameterised

Values never go into a query as text, always as a separate parameter.

  • Postgres: SQLAlchemy with named parameters (:naam). For a list of UUIDs (e.g. IN :project_ids) a helper function makes a safe list of variable length, without pasting text.
  • ClickHouse: parameters in the form %(naam)s, which CoGA passes to the client (clickhouse-connect) separately from the query text. The client puts each value, escaped, into the query that goes to the server (client-side binding). The query text that CoGA builds itself never contains the value.

  • A UUID from the request (in the path, the query string or the body: a file, an import job, an HPO annotation, a panel, a project, the assembly of a NIPT artefact, …):

    • is read once, where the record is looked up, so after the access checks;
    • gets, if the value is not a UUID, the same response as a UUID without a record (the route's 404, or the 400 the route gives for an invalid ID), and then never reaches a query;
    • is bound in its canonical form (lower case, with hyphens), so that {…} or urn:uuid:… finds the same record.

    A write action that refers to a record looks that record up first. A NIPT artefact for a non-existent assembly or an import job for a non-existent project gets a 404 before anything is written, and the audit trail of the artefact list gets no event for it.

Only table names do appear in the text. They are derived from the assembly name through one function that allows only safe characters (chapter 3).

Where in the code: backend/app/core/sql.py (uuid_list_bindparam, canonical_uuid, require_uuid) and execute_clickhouse in backend/app/core/clickhouse.py.

2. ORDER BY comes from a fixed list

A column name cannot be a parameter in SQL. That is why CoGA never puts text from the user into an ORDER BY, but translates a sort key through a fixed table. In the Variant Explorer an unknown key falls back to the default (total_samples). In the integrity check of the hash chains the sort columns come from a fixed list per table.

Where in the code: _SORT_EXPR in backend/app/services/variant_explorer_service.py and _CHAIN_ORDER_COLS in backend/app/services/integrity_anchor_service.py.

3. LIMIT and OFFSET become integers

Page limits always go through int(...), become at least 0 and are themselves parameters in the query. A high page number cannot provoke an unbounded scan: the page is clamped.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/clickhouse_variant_queries.py.

4. Extra protection around ClickHouse

  • Limits per query: a maximum execution time, query size and memory limits, so that one broad filter does not occupy the server without limit. A query that is too heavy gives a 422 asking the user to refine the search, not an unclear 500.
  • Transient errors: on a broken connection the client recovers and tries once more, without changing the query.

Where in the code: backend/app/core/clickhouse.py (limits and recovery); the translation of a query that is too heavy into 422 in backend/app/services/clickhouse_family_variants.py.

All routers

All routers are listed in backend/app/routers/__init__.py and hang under /api. Only metrics.py is deliberately mounted by main.py outside /api (see Metrics for monitoring). The router families.py includes six sub-routers under the same path /families; they therefore have no prefix of their own. Only health.py, lookups.py and ancestry.py have no prefix at all; ancestry.py writes /families/… in each path.

Metrics for monitoring

GET /metrics gives the backend's operational figures in the Prometheus format:

  • requests, errors and duration per route;
  • the last scheduled integrity check of ClickHouse per assembly;
  • the queue and the unsaved events of the audit pipelines;
  • the active import jobs, and how long they have given no sign of life;
  • the running build.

It holds no clinical data. A request gets the template of its route as its label (/families/{family_id}, as the audit log also stores it), never the path with its identifiers.

The endpoint is off as long as METRICS_TOKEN is not set. If it is set, it answers only a request that carries that token as a bearer token. It lies outside /api, and the load balancer and the frontend server forward only /api to the backend: the internet therefore never reaches it. In the deployment a collector (the Google-Built OpenTelemetry Collector) reads it every minute with the token. That collector runs as a second container in the same Cloud Run service and writes the figures to Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus. Alert rules in Cloud Monitoring read them there and mail the addresses from alert_notification_emails (terraform/monitoring.tf). docs/monitoring.md describes the metrics and proposed alert rules.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/operational_metrics.py and backend/app/routers/metrics.py; the counting of each request in the request-logging middleware.

Request logging: every request leaves a trace

Two components make sure that every HTTP request is logged and audited.

Structured logging. The backend writes its own log lines as JSON lines on stderr. uvicorn's own lines (the start-up, the access log on stdout, the traceback of an unhandled error) keep uvicorn's text format. Control characters (including line breaks) in values are replaced before they reach a log line, so that nobody can insert false log lines (log forging).

The request-logging middleware records every request in the append-only table audit_log_events:

  • Who: user, email address and role, from the user that get_current_user attached to the request.
  • What: method, route, status, duration, IP and user agent. Of a query string, by default only the keys are kept (AUDIT_LOG_QUERY_STRING_MODE): this shows which filters a search used, without their values.
  • The content of a change: for POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE the body is kept, with sensitive fields (password, token, secret, …) masked, also in the form of /auth/token. A body that cannot be read is not kept raw. The middleware also derives which entity and which fields were changed (db_update): the fields are the keys of the body that the route's model reads. A key that the model ignores changes nothing and is not listed; the body does keep it.
  • Requests for records of other projects: a family, sample or project outside the user's projects gets the same response as an ID that does not exist (404, chapter 2). Only the audit row keeps track of the difference: request_meta.record_hidden names the kind of record (family, sample or project). That way it stays visible who requested records of other projects; the Audit logs administration page shows it in the column Flags (chapter 15).

  • Separation of clinical data and application log: the body (possibly clinical data) goes only into the protected audit database, never into the ordinary application log. That also holds for the text of an error: with a failed query, that text quotes the SQL and the parameters, with values from the request or values that were read for it.

    • The 500 line of an unhandled error names the kind of error (the type with SQLSTATE, or ClickHouse's error code), the route and the frames of each exception in the chain, without their messages.
    • uvicorn logs the same error once more, because Starlette passes it on to the server after the 500 response. A filter (RedactServerErrorFilter) writes that traceback in the same way.
    • Every other log line with an exception (logger.exception(), exc_info=True) is also written that way by the JSON formatter (JsonLogFormatter), from every logger (including a library's) and at every level: the kind of error in error, the frames of the chain in traceback, never the message.
    • The full text is only in the audit row (audit_log_events.error).

    The only exception is an audit row that the database cannot store. That row is logged with its content, body and error text included, so that it can be recovered (see below).

  • What Postgres cannot store: a NUL character (a %00 in the path or the query string, \u0000 in a JSON body), half of a UTF-16 surrogate pair and the numbers NaN and Infinity. Such a value is kept as a visible escape: a NUL as the four characters \x00, a half pair as \udXXX, a number as the text "NaN", "Infinity" or "-Infinity". request_meta._escaped names the columns in which that happened (core/pg_storable.py). The UI event log does the same, with _escaped in detail. The Audit logs administration page shows both in the column Flags, with the columns listed (chapter 15).

The audit lines go through a queue that in production never silently drops anything:

  • With a full queue the backend writes synchronously.
  • Without a queue (AUDIT_LOG_MODE=sync, or as long as no worker is running, such as during start-up and shutdown) each request writes its own line.
  • The worker writes a batch in one INSERT. If that also fails at the last attempt, it writes the lines one by one, each once and without waiting. A line that the database refuses on its own account (a constraint, or a value the driver cannot encode, such as a timestamp before the year 1 in UTC) thus costs only itself, not the whole batch (up to AUDIT_LOG_BATCH_SIZE lines from any user).
  • A line of a user whose account was deleted while the line was waiting (only possible with SQL by an administrator) is stored on its own at write time, without the link to users: the user's ID is in request_meta._deleted_user_id (for a UI event in detail._deleted_user_id), and user_email and user_role stay as they were. The log reports it with the kind of error, without values.
  • Each event gets its own ID (event_id) as soon as it is made, before it goes into the queue. The INSERT does nothing for an ID that the table already has (ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING). If the response to a successful commit was lost, the worker writes the batch again, and each line is still there once.
  • If the database cannot be reached, the one-by-one writing stops after the first line: the remaining lines are logged and counted without a new attempt.
  • A line that truly cannot be stored is logged with its content and counted, in every mode. The alert on coga_audit_events_not_persisted_total fires, and the line can be recovered from the log. Of the error when writing, only the kind is logged (type and SQLSTATE), not its text, which quotes the query and the row. The user's request does not fail because of it, and a batch of UI events still gets 202.
  • Only in development may a full queue drop lines (AUDIT_LOG_DROP_ALLOWED) or may the audit log be switched off entirely (AUDIT_LOG_MODE=off). Outside development the backend refuses to start with those values. The default is async.

Where in the code: backend/app/core/coga_logging.py (JSON logging, naming errors without their text), backend/app/middleware/request_logging.py (the middleware), backend/app/services/audit_log_pg.py and event_pipeline.py (writing without loss), backend/app/core/pg_storable.py (the escapes).

The order of the middleware

In Starlette (on which FastAPI runs) the last registered middleware is the outermost. From inside (close to the route) to outside (close to the client):

  1. CORSMiddleware — only allowed origins may call the API with credentials.
  2. log_request_response — the request logging above.
  3. normalize_api_collection_root_paths — accepts collection paths both with and without a trailing slash.
  4. security_headers_middleware — sets the security headers on every response (chapter 2).
  5. TrustedProxyClientMiddleware — registered last, so the outermost: determines the real client IP (TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS) before logging, rate limiting and audit read it.

Outside that chain there is also Starlette's ServerErrorMiddleware. It answers an error that nothing else handles with a 500, through the handler _answer_server_error from main.py: the same text as Starlette's own response, but with the same security headers, HSTS included. It then raises the error again, so that uvicorn still logs it; by then the request logging has already logged the request and put it in the audit log.

Where in the code: the end of backend/app/main.py; backend/app/middleware/.

backend/app/main.py Mounts the routers under /api and sets up the middleware chain
backend/app/routers/__init__.py The list of all routers
backend/app/dependencies.py get_current_user, get_current_superuser and get_current_admin_user
backend/app/schemas/ All request and response models
backend/app/core/sql.py · backend/app/core/clickhouse.py Parameterised queries in Postgres and ClickHouse, limits per query
backend/app/services/clickhouse_variant_queries.py The construction of the variant queries, with integer LIMIT/OFFSET
backend/app/services/family_metadata_context.py The access checkpoint for family data

8. Filter pages ↔ API

After a correct import (chapter 6), CoGA filters and shows a family's variants. Part A follows that chain for the two largest data types: the small variants (SNVs and indels: point mutations and small insertions or deletions) and the structural variants (SVs: large deletions, duplications, …). Part B summarises it for the specialised analyses: mitochondrial DNA and sample QC, Paraphase, repeat expansions, monogenic NIPT, conventional NIPT and PGT. The clinical rules for the laboratory are in the app, under Docs; this chapter points to where they sit in the code.

An endpoint is a URL the backend listens on; a query parameter is a ?key=value pair in that URL, through which the frontend passes on the filter choices. A parameterised query passes user values separately instead of pasting them into the SQL text (chapter 7).

The fixed pattern

For every variant data type, searching runs the same way:

  1. Filter in the UI: the analyst fills in a filter form (frequency, effect, genes, genotype per sample, tags, …).
  2. Query parameters: the frontend converts the choices into a query string and requests the endpoint.
  3. Endpoint: the router checks access and builds the family's context (chapter 2).
  4. Filter service: a service turns them into a parameterised ClickHouse query, with pagination and a bounded count.
  5. Link with Postgres: the variant rows are supplemented with review state, tags, gene metadata and the frequency in the in-house cohort.
  6. Display: the browser shows the result as a table or as cards.

Where in the code: the routers in backend/app/routers/, the filter services in backend/app/services/clickhouse_family_variants.py and clickhouse_variant_queries.py, the pages in frontend/src/pages/families/.

Part A — Small variants

The filter form

The page FamilySmallVariantsPage.tsx loads the family and the gene panels; the search state is in smallVariantSearch.ts, the form in SmallVariantFilterForm.tsx, the filter categories in smallVariantFilterSections.tsx. The categories are under Advanced filters, closed when the page opens, one per row, as in seqr; when closed, the button says how many categories hold a filter. A row with a filter is red on the left; Expand all and Collapse all open or close all rows. The SV and NIPT pages share that layout (VariantFilterAccordion.tsx).

Category What it sets
Phenotype the phenotype prioritisation, and with Rank by the order: the combined score or the variant score (chapter 12)
Structural second hit "only genes that are also hit by an SV"
Inheritance inheritance model (de novo/dominant, recessive, X-linked, compound heterozygous), genotype per family member, expanded carrier screening
Pathogenicity the ClinVar status
Annotations impact (HIGH, MODERATE, …), consequence terms, the SpliceAI minimum, transcript, rsID, HGVS, only canonical or MANE transcripts, only loss-of-function
In silico CADD, REVEL, SIFT, PolyPhen; the SpliceAI minimum also counts as a predictor
Frequency maximum frequency in gnomAD (exomes, genomes), popmax (gnomAD's own popmax, otherwise VEP's MAX_AF, the highest frequency across the populations of 1000 Genomes and gnomAD) and TOPMed; homozygote and hemizygote counts (gnomAD's total: the combined count, otherwise exomes plus genomes); "a (likely) pathogenic ClinVar variant passes the frequency filter"
Call quality genotype quality, read depth, allele fraction, alt depth, and Pass variants only (the caller's FILTER)
Locations a gene panel (by default the Mendeliome), genes, a list of intervals. A locus (chromosome, start, end) comes in only through a link, e.g. from the genome browser
Exclude ClinVar statuses, review tags, genes and intervals to exclude
Review and curation ACMG class, tags, "has notes"

Without a gnomAD count. A maximum on a gnomAD count keeps a variant that has no such count, as absent from gnomAD. One line above the list counts, per filter, the shown variants that stayed in unchecked in this way and may still be in gnomAD: those with a gnomAD frequency, or from a callset that was not annotated with gnomAD (gnomadCountNotes.ts). A hemizygote count counts only on chrX and chrY outside the pseudo-autosomal regions.

Annotations, Frequency and Call quality follow seqr's layout:

  • Annotations groups the VEP consequences as seqr does (nonsense, essential splice site, frameshift, missense, in frame, synonymous, extended splice site, other, motif and regulatory features), with a box per group for all its terms. A term from a saved search that has no box of its own is shown ticked under Other selected terms, so that it stays visible and can be unticked.
  • Frequency has a slider per population, with seqr's steps (0 to 1). AF in the header sets all populations at once; next to it are AC (the allele count in gnomAD) and H/H (homozygotes and hemizygotes in gnomAD).
  • Call quality sets the minimum genotype quality, allele balance (the call's allele fraction), depth and alt reads, for all members or per member. With Affected only, which is on as long as no unaffected member has a minimum, they apply only to the affected members: a parent's reference call need not meet an allele balance it cannot have.

Pass variants only (under Filter value, parameter pass_only) keeps a variant if every call with the ALT allele passed its caller's FILTER (PASS, . or no filter), independently of Affected only (the owner's decision of 2026-11-03). Only the calls of the shown members count: a sample that left the family or is not in it yet holds nothing back and does not decide which FILTER counts. The same goes for the phase set (ps): only that of a shown member counts (the owner's decision of 2026-11-06). Which FILTER counts depends on the callset:

  • One file per sample: every call has its own FILTER (calls.filters), and only that of the calls with the ALT allele counts. A parent's RefCall or NoCall record, which the import stores as their 0/0 or ./. call, therefore does not hold back a de novo variant.
  • Multi-sample VCF: it stores no FILTER per call; there the site's FILTER (filters) applies.

As soon as one call of a row has its own FILTER, the row is read the first way. The condition is _small_pass_only_condition in clickhouse_variant_queries.py. The quick choices High quality and Passing turn the filter on, as in seqr; All variants turns it off; the built-in presets do not set it. The NIPT list and the Variant Explorer do not apply it.

If the page opens without a search in the URL, it applies the built-in preset Phenotype priority (Exomiser-style) within the Mendeliome panel:

  • phenotype prioritisation;
  • impact HIGH or MODERATE;
  • in gnomAD (exomes, genomes, popmax) at most 1% and at most 10 homozygotes and hemizygotes;
  • a (likely) pathogenic ClinVar variant as an exception to the frequency limit;
  • ClinVar (likely) benign excluded;
  • in the affected members Hom or Het, with a genotype quality of at least 20, a depth of at least 10, an allele fraction of at least 0.2 and at least 4 alt reads.

The annotation filters apply per transcript. Impact and consequence, transcript, HGVS, Canonical only, MANE only and LoF only, the ClinVar status, the frequencies and the predictors must hold together for one transcript of the variant (one row of the table annotations). With MANE only and impact HIGH, a variant whose HIGH transcript is not the MANE transcript therefore drops out. Of the predictors, one is enough, and a SpliceAI score at or above the cut-off also counts as a hit for impact and consequence. The gene, the panel, the rsID and the ClinVar statuses to exclude apply to the variant as a whole.

Each row with its own annotation. A row of entries is read with the annotation it was imported with: its variant key and its annotation set (annotationSetHash, the hash of its annotation), under whichever version (the source, e.g. vcf_info or vep_tsv). Rows with one key and one set carry the same annotation.

  • The family search reads the transcripts of that annotation together with the row (entries.transcripts; see The endpoint and the filter service).
  • When a search reads the shared annotation tables (the Variant Explorer; the family search for a gene, panel, rsID or text), it compares key and set, not the version: the version makes the set ClickHouse builds per filter two to three times slower. In a measurement in the Variant Explorer, a search with a frequency, impact or CADD filter on 4 million rows took 0.6 to 1.0 s with the version and 0.23 to 0.47 s without (_OWN_ANNOTATION in clickhouse_variant_queries.py).
  • The rsID from the VCF sits beside the annotation: a row also finds the rsID that another import of the same variant with the same annotation wrote, under whichever version.

Per kind of filter:

  • Gene. A gene term is a symbol or an Ensembl gene ID. In every view, the gene filter keeps every variant that carries the gene in its annotation, including one that VEP assigns to it from just outside (upstream or downstream). An excluded gene leaves out every variant that carries it in its annotation, and every variant in its loci.
  • Panel. A panel keeps a variant that lies in one of its regions (PanelApp's regions for the family's assembly, and the locus of each gene in the gene reference) or carries one of its genes, however large the panel is: CoGA compares even the Mendeliome, with more than 1000 regions, by position (the owner's decision of 14 October 2026). A gene that the panel names by its Ensembl gene ID counts with that ID and its symbol in the annotation, and with the ID's loci (chapter 15). The regions go to ClickHouse merged (_small_region_bounds): regions of one chromosome that share a base become one region. In this way the roughly 42,000 loci of the Mendeliome (one per transcript) become about one region per gene, with the same variants. The Variant Explorer builds its annotation and panel condition with the same function (chapter 14).
  • Precision. Frequencies, in silico scores and a call's allele fraction are stored in ClickHouse as a 32-bit number (Float32), and a filter compares them with its limit at that precision (toFloat32). In this way a value exactly on the limit does not round past it: CADD 25.3 meets a minimum of 25.3, a gnomAD frequency of 0.001 a maximum of 0.001.
  • MANE. MANE only keeps a variant with a MANE Select or MANE Plus Clinical transcript. VEP sets those flags only on GRCh38, so MANE only keeps nothing on GRCh37 and T2T.

SIFT and PolyPhen: the prediction, not the score. VEP writes the prediction with its score, e.g. deleterious(0.01) or probably_damaging(0.998); the import stores them like that, in lower case. A choice under SIFT or PolyPhen keeps a transcript whose prediction is exactly that choice, with or without a score: deleterious keeps deleterious(0.01) and deleterious, not deleterious_low_confidence(0.03) (a choice of its own). Case does not matter and a space counts as an underscore. The SQL applies the pattern in_silico_prediction_pattern (family_variant_filters.py) with match on the columns sift and polyphen.

The transcript the filters apply to. A variant's fields (consequence, impact, HGVS, LoF, frequencies, CADD, REVEL, SpliceAI, SIFT, PolyPhen) come from its primary transcript: MANE Select, otherwise canonical, otherwise the most severe impact (_select_primary_annotation). The ranking and its cache, the ACMG suggestions, the report and the signed record read that primary transcript. The annotation filters may apply to another transcript: SIFT deleterious, for example, keeps a variant for which SIFT calls the primary transcript tolerated and a second one deleterious; the card and the CSV then read tolerated. Therefore:

  • If the primary transcript does not pass the annotation filters, the variant names in filter_transcript (SmallVariantFilterTranscriptOut) the transcript that does pass them, with its gene, transcript, impact, consequence, HGVS, LoF, CADD, REVEL, SpliceAI, SIFT and PolyPhen. Without annotation filters, or if the primary transcript passes them, the field is empty.
  • Which transcripts pass the filters is decided by the SQL: the same per-row condition on annotations that the search applies, for the variants of the page in one query (_filter_transcript_matches), each transcript recognised by the hash of its stored row (annotationHash). The transcript named is the first of those transcripts in the order used to pick the primary one. If no transcript of the variant is recognised in those rows, the field stays empty, never a wrong transcript.
  • Every page of the search gives the field (the ClickHouse page, the candidates with their pairs, the track, the prioritisation computed, from the cache and from a broader panel ranking), as do the CSV export and the NIPT list; the ranking itself computes without it (filter_annotation_hashes=None).

The display:

  • the card says it under its transcript, a table row under its effect (Filters met on, FilterTranscriptNote.tsx), with the values of that transcript that differ from those of the row (describeFilterTranscript): consequence, LoF, CADD, REVEL, SpliceAI, SIFT and PolyPhen;
  • the card's transcript list marks the transcript Filters met;
  • the CSV gives it in its last columns, Filter-matched transcript to Filter-matched PolyPhen, after all the other columns.

Where in the code: frontend/src/pages/families/SmallVariantFilterForm.tsx, smallVariantFilterSections.tsx and smallVariantSearch.ts; the transcript the filters apply to in _filter_transcript_matches and _small_variant_outs (clickhouse_family_variants.py), _filter_transcript_annotation (clickhouse_variant_queries.py) and describeFilterTranscript (smallVariantResultUtils.ts).

From form to request

buildSmallVariantQueryParams converts the choices into a query string. Three details matter for traceability:

  • Default values are sent explicitly. The phenotype prioritisation and the ClinVar exception to the frequency filter are on by default. They are always sent as true or false, so that a choice that was turned off is kept in the URL.
  • A filter per sample is sent as one parameter: sample_filter=<sample>:<genotypes>:<quality>:<depth>:<allele-fraction>:<alt-depth>, for example child:0/1|1/1:20:10:0.2:5.

  • What the list does not apply is not sent. The small-variant page shares the saved searches (of every user, in every family) with the NIPT page. A search from the NIPT page can carry filters that only the NIPT list knows: an inheritance view (de_novo, paternal_dominant, maternal_dominant, recessive_at_risk), the categories, the minimum confidence, include_not_inherited, de_novo_priority and the recurrence filter max_unexplained_recurrence.

    • The list's request and that of the CSV export are built without those filters (smallVariantListFilters). The page shows no chip for them, does not count them under Active filters and names them once under the active filters. The URL and Save current do keep them.
    • Another spelling of an inheritance model that the backend reads as that model (_SMALL_INHERITANCE_ALIASES, e.g. dominant) is sent by the page as that model. The backend refuses de_novo (400), like the other NIPT views: NIPT's de novo view reads the fetus in the cfDNA, the de novo/dominant pattern reads the genotypes of the affected and unaffected members.
    • test_small_variant_page_sends_what_the_list_reads.py keeps the page's lists (SMALL_VARIANT_INHERITANCE_MODES, SMALL_VARIANT_INHERITANCE_ALIASES, SMALL_VARIANT_UNSUPPORTED_FILTERS) in line with those of the backend and with the endpoint's query parameters.
    • Conversely, the NIPT page sends nothing from a small-variant search that its list does not apply.

The backend reads genotypes as classes, not as literal text: hom_alt (all alleles the same ALT, including a haploid 1), het (at least one ALT, including 1/2 or ./1), hom_ref (all alleles 0) and no_call. A filter on "Hom" therefore also finds a hemizygous 1 on chrX in a male or on chrM. One definition serves all filters, counts and tracks.

De novo in a son on X and Y. Outside the pseudo-autosomal regions a male has one X and one Y. A de novo variant there is usually written as 1 or 1/1 in the VCF; a 0/1 (e.g. with mosaicism) also counts as a call with the alternative allele. The de novo/dominant pattern counts such a call in an affected male as one copy. The strict de novo check follows the transmission: a son gets his X from his mother and his Y from his father. Only that parent therefore has to be reliably reference; the other parent must not carry the variant (that points to an artefact). The boundaries of the pseudo-autosomal regions are fixed per assembly (GRCh38, GRCh37 and T2T-CHM13v2.0); on an assembly without known boundaries the diploid rules apply. Those of T2T-CHM13v2.0 come from the T2T consortium's PAR file (chm13v2.0_PAR.bed) and NCBI's region report for GCF_009914755.1, which agree: there, PAR1 runs from the first base and PAR2 to the last.

Where in the code: frontend/src/pages/families/smallVariantSearch.ts; the genotype classes in backend/app/services/genotypes.py (mirrored in frontend/src/lib/genotypes.ts); the PAR boundaries in backend/app/services/sex_chromosomes.py.

The endpoint and the filter service

GET /api/families/{family_id}/small-variants bounds the page size, reads all filters through one shared dependency (the same one as the CSV export) and builds the family's access checkpoint. The service then chooses a path:

  • a presence check (count_only) for the dashboard: "does this family have small variants?";
  • first the scoping: panel, review selections, intervals and excluded regions. If the question cannot return anything (e.g. a panel without genes), an empty page follows straight away. An unreadable interval line (e.g. a BED line or an end before the start) gets 422, naming the line; the form already reports such lines before searching;
  • the phenotype prioritisation (on by default), with a cache (chapter 12). It changes the order of a search, never what the search finds: for compound het, recessive or carrier screening it applies the same rules as without prioritisation (the pairs, the couple's gene rule, below) and only ranks the variants and pairs that remain;
  • the track mode for the genome browser: above a limit it returns only the count, so that the track can say there are too many variants;
  • otherwise ClickHouse filters and paginates itself, or the service fetches a bounded candidate set and applies in Python what ClickHouse cannot (carrier screening, inheritance across variants such as compound het).

The filters live in one place: in the SQL. Every view of the search (the list, the list on one page, the track and its sampled subset, the prioritisation computed or from the cache, the pairs and the carrier screening) reads the rows the SQL keeps (_small_query_filter_parts in clickhouse_variant_queries.py). Python then only compares rows with each other: the pairs and their phase, the couple's gene rule, the ranking. The inheritance models for a single variant (de novo/dominant, homozygous recessive, X-linked) are SQL too: whatever needs them (the recessive union, the ranking's segregation) asks for them as a flag per row (segregation_*). Every view keeps what the list keeps (the owner's decision of 2026-11-06; the roadmap: One filter definition). That every view reads every filter in this way is tested on ClickHouse by integration/test_small_variant_filter_parity_clickhouse.py.

The query itself always starts with the family and sign = 1, adds the project filter and then each filter, each time as a parameter.

One analysis at a time. A family can hold several analyses, on the same DNA or on different samples of one person (short-read and then long-read WGS). They stay apart: no two analyses share a storage source, and a family two or more of whose analyses have a small-variant callset of their own is read one analysis at a time (analysis_scope.py). The request names the analysis (analysis), also when it names one callset (source); without it, it gets 422. The query leaves out the other analyses' callsets, so another analysis's callset reads nothing, and an inheritance filter reads the members the analysis's package lists: only a member that only another analysis's package lists is left out. The SV list, its count, export and reviews are read the same way among the analyses with an SV caller of their own (the conventional NIPT of each pregnancy). The pages offer the analysis beside the family name, the variant summary too, and the links between the family's pages keep it; a review belongs to the analysis it was made in. So the monogenic NIPT of each pregnancy, too, reads only its own calls (see Monogenic NIPT).

Members without calls. A member the analysis's package lists can still have no calls in it: long-read WGS of the proband alone, with a PED that lists the parents. An inheritance filter reads a call it does not find as no ALT allele: the de novo/dominant, homozygous recessive, X-linked and compound-het filters read an unaffected member without calls as reference, and keep no variant when an affected member has none. The filter stays as it is, and the list says so (the owner's decision of 2026-11-20): the response names those members (members_without_calls, with each one's role and how an inheritance filter reads it), the page warns while an inheritance filter that reads them is applied and mentions them otherwise, and the export names them in its last column (Members without calls). CoGA finds them in a fixed sample of the rows the list reads, the 2,000 with the smallest storage keys (family_members_without_calls): a member holds calls when it has a called genotype in one of them (0/0, 0/1, 1/1, a haploid call); a no-call (./.) does not count.

  • The per-transcript filters (impact, consequence, ClinVar, frequencies, scores, Canonical, MANE, LoF), the ClinVar statuses to exclude and the salient variants of the broad track are tested on the transcripts that each of the family's rows carries itself (transcripts, with arrayExists; _small_own_transcripts_condition). That column stores the filtered values of the row's annotation set as its rows in annotations store them, without transcript and HGVS text (ENTRY_TRANSCRIPT_FIELDS in clickhouse_variant_rows.py). In this way the search reads only the family's rows, however large the cohort is.
  • A gene or a panel is looked up in the gene index, an rsID and a transcript or HGVS text in the other annotation tables (_small_annotation_row_membership_condition). Those tables are shared by all families; for a panel, an rsID and a text the query reads only the family's variants from them (_small_family_key_condition).

The rows are deduplicated per variant, each variant from one stored row (that of the callset whose name comes first, with all its columns), and sorted by genomic position; the user does not control that order (the sort buttons in the table work in the browser). The full annotation per variant comes separately for each page, by the sort key of variants/details, only for the variants of that page. The count is bounded: above a limit the UI shows a "+" counter instead of an expensive full count. A query that is too heavy gives 422, asking for the search to be refined.

Where in the code: backend/app/routers/families_small_variants.py; get_family_small_variants_page in backend/app/services/clickhouse_family_variants.py; the WHERE builders in clickhouse_variant_queries.py; the filter set in family_variant_filters.py.

Supplementing with Postgres

For each page the rows are supplemented with:

  • the review: class, ACMG criteria, tags and note from Postgres (chapter 10);
  • the frequency in the in-house cohort across the accessible projects, so that recurring artefacts stand out;
  • gene constraint from the table gene_info;
  • a mark if a structural variant hits the same gene (the "second hit", below).

The display

SmallVariantResults.tsx shows the counter, the choice between table and cards ("Auto" picks cards for a small number, otherwise a table), the CSV export with the same query string, a warning if the search read only part of the callset, and a notice if the ranking comes from the cache. That warning (CandidateCapNotice.tsx) comes from two flags in the response:

  • candidates_capped: compound het, recessive or carrier screening read a bounded candidate window, between 1,000 and 5,000 rows depending on the requested page, and always 5,000 with prioritisation;
  • ranking_truncated: the prioritisation ranked only its window. For a ranked search with pairs or carrier screening, both flags are then on.

candidate_limit says after how many candidates the search stopped. The counter is then a lower bound, and the warning asks for the filters to be refined with a region, a gene panel or a gene. Compound heterozygous pairs are at the top as pair cards, also with prioritisation: a pair then takes the place of its best-ranked variant, and each variant shows its own rank. The table (SmallVariantTable.tsx) sorts in the browser by position, gene, impact and, with prioritisation, the score.

A card, also on the NIPT page, names in a line under its header the gene's diseases with their source, and the gene's inheritance, ClinGen dosage curation and ACMG SF status (VariantGeneDiseases.tsx; chapter 13). HGVS.g is VEP's HGVSg; if the annotation has none, the card derives the change from the VCF record, not HGVS-normalised, and says so in the tooltip. The predictors get coloured dots at seqr's cut-offs (chapter 10). The card's background follows ClinVar as clinvarClass reads it: light red for (likely) pathogenic, light green for (likely) benign; a conflicting, uncertain or other status leaves the card white (getClinvarHighlightTone, .small-variant-card in variant-tables.css).

Compound heterozygous, second hit and carrier screening

In a recessive disorder, one heterozygous variant is usually not causal. Two different heterozygous variants in the same gene can be, if they lie in trans (one on each allele). CoGA therefore shows such candidates as a pair, with their phase: in trans or unknown.

  • A pair arises when both variants are heterozygous in all affected members and no unaffected member carries both.
  • The phase comes from the reads (a shared phase set), otherwise from the parents in the pedigree: if each variant goes back to a different parent, they lie in trans. A half call with one missing allele (e.g. .|1) does not say on which haplotype the variant lies; the phase then comes from the parents. A family member who carries neither variant and is not a parent says nothing about the phase.
  • A pair in cis drops out: the reads place both variants on the same haplotype, or both go back to the same parent while both parents are genotyped for both variants.

The same phase rule applies to the second hit, which does show a phase in cis: a heterozygous small variant together with a structural variant (e.g. a deletion) in the same gene, where the deletion removes the second copy. If several SVs hit the gene, each SV gets its own phase relative to the small variant. The mark summarises them:

  • a deletion in trans makes the gene effectively bi-allelic, whatever the other SVs are;
  • otherwise it says trans if one SV that the affected members carry lies in trans;
  • and cis only if every such SV lies in cis.

The explanation with the mark lists the SVs, each with its phase. A deletion is a DEL (also DEL:ME), a LOSS or CNV_LOSS, or a CNV, unless the stored copy number of its carriers shows no loss; the ranking of the SVs reads a deletion the same way (chapter 12). For each family CoGA keeps an index of the genes an SV hits; the SNV page uses it as a mark and as a filter. Every change to a family's SVs (an import, an upload for one sample, a deletion) changes a version in ClickHouse (SV/family_data_version), and the next time the page opens CoGA rebuilds the index. The rules for trans and cis are in the app (Docs → SNV + SV compound heterozygosity, frontend/src/content/docs/sv-second-hit.md) and in docs/snv-sv-compound-het.md.

Expanded carrier screening is a reproductive question: are two partners together at risk of having an affected child? The difference with compound het: there, two hits sit in one person; here, one hit in each of two partners. The choice appears only when the frontend recognises a couple in the family: the two partners of a couple link, else the mother and the father, else the family's two people. Two samples of one person (same_individual) are never a couple. CoGA then shows:

  • the genes in which both partners carry a qualifying variant;
  • every variant that either partner carries on chrX outside the pseudo-autosomal regions, each on its own, whatever the other partner carries: in an X-linked disorder a woman's carrier status alone puts a son at risk, and a man passes his X to every daughter. This rule does not read the partners' recorded sex. On an assembly without known boundaries of the pseudo-autosomal regions, only the rule of both partners applies, as it does on chrY (_filter_expanded_carrier_screening, with hemizygous_chromosome from sex_chromosomes.py).

A mitochondrial variant (chrM) does not count: mtDNA is inherited only through the mother, so a variant of both partners in one chrM gene says nothing about a child's risk.

The built-in preset Expanded carrier screening turns the choice on, together with rare (below 1%, popmax included), impact HIGH or MODERATE, and ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic as an exception to the frequency limit. In this way a frequent founder variant (CFTR p.Phe508del) stays in. The preset leaves out ClinVar benign and likely benign: such a variant never makes a gene one in which both partners carry a variant. Without an impact filter, a long-read genome contains hundreds of thousands of rare variants: the search then stops at its candidate limit long before chrX, and the X-linked rule never sees the partners' variants.

Where in the code: the pairs in clickhouse_variant_queries.py and SmallVariantPairCards.tsx; the phase rule via the parents in backend/app/services/compound_het_phase.py; the SV index in backend/app/services/sv_gene_index_service.py; the carrier screening in clickhouse_variant_queries.py and smallVariantSearch.ts.

Part A — Structural variants

The SV page follows the same pattern, with its own files (FamilyStructuralVariantsPage.tsx, structuralVariantSearch.ts, StructuralVariantFilterForm.tsx). The filters cover type (DEL, DUP, …), length, source, region flags, frequency in controls and population, gene constraint, phenotype fields, gene or panel, inheritance and genotype per sample. Besides the filtered request, the page makes one request without filters, for the total "All variants". The length rule and the panel rule below apply in every view: the list, ranked or not, the CSV export, the genome track and the track availability.

The length. The two length filters, a minimum (min_length) and an exact length (length), measure an SV the way the list shows its length, without the minus sign of a deletion. They take the call's SVLEN (column svLen of SV/variants/details), and END − POS only if the call has no SVLEN. Most callers (Sniffles2, pbsv) write an insertion with END equal to POS and its length in SVLEN; measured as END − POS, such an insertion would be 0 bp long, so that a minimum would leave it out and an exact length would never find it.

  • Sequence allele without SVLEN. Such a call is stored with the length its alleles give, len(ALT) − len(REF) (VCF 4.4 prescribes SVLEN only for a symbolic allele, and . for a sequence allele): for an insertion the inserted bases, for a deletion the removed bases as a negative number, the way Sniffles2 and pbsv write the SVLEN of a deletion (the owner's decision, 2026-10-14). Every SV reader does this (record_sv_len in structural_variant_ingest.py): the uploads, including a TSV row with REF and ALT as sequence, and the NeedlR, HiFiCNV and chrM files of a package. A written SVLEN stays as written, and END and the SV's id do not change.
  • Translocation. A translocation (type BND or TRA) has no length and is never a small event: it meets every minimum and no exact length, whatever SVLEN or END its caller wrote (the owner's decision, 2026-10-13).
  • Other call without SVLEN. With END equal to POS it measures 0 bp, e.g. a symbolic insertion <INS> from a TSV upload, which has no SVLEN.

That one rule is in structural_variant_length_filters_match (family_variant_filters.py). No SQL applies a length filter: a search with a length never goes through the native page, but reads the candidates (up to 50,000 SVs) and filters them in Python.

The gene panel. A gene panel keeps an SV whose annotation names one of its genes (the SV's gene symbols, in upper or lower case; a gene that the panel names by its Ensembl gene ID counts with its symbol, because an SV's annotation names genes only by symbol), or that overlaps one of its regions. Those regions are PanelApp's regions for the family's assembly and the loci of its genes in the gene reference. Overlapping means: on the same chromosome, with the SV's start at or before the region's end and its end at or after the region's start. The partner of a breakend does not count here. This holds for every panel, however large, the Mendeliome included, as with small variants (the owner's decision of 20 October 2026).

The rule is in SQL (_structural_panel_filter_condition in clickhouse_variant_queries.py) and in Python (_StructuralPanelMatch).

  • In SQL, a join on windows of 64 kb finds the regions for the family's own SV rows (_structural_family_region_condition), as on the small-variant page. A search on one chromosome, such as that of a track, binds only that chromosome's regions.
  • The regions go to ClickHouse without the regions that lie within another one (_structural_region_bounds). Unlike with small variants, regions that share a base are not merged: an SV stored with its END before its POS overlaps, by the rule, a region that contains both, and a chain of merged regions can contain both where none of those regions does.
  • Because the panel scopes the candidates in SQL, the limit of 50,000 SVs applies to the panel's SVs. A panel and a gene filter apply together. The costs are in docs/variant-ranking-cache.md (Structural variants).

The classification filter. The filter Classification under Review keeps an SV by the class that its review shows on the SV page, as with small variants (the owner's decision of 10 November 2026).
