9. Visualisations (chromosome, genome, circos, IGV)

CoGA shows genomic data in four views: the genome overview, the chromosome view, the Circos plot and the embedded IGV browser. They rely on tracks, the ideogram and the pedigree. For each view this chapter gives the endpoint that supplies the data, how it is drawn and how the region shown is determined. The explanation for users is in the user guide in the app (frontend/src/content/docs/user-guide/visualization.md).

A few concepts:

  • Track: one horizontal strip that shows one kind of data over a genomic range.
  • SVG is a vector format (sharp shapes); canvas is a pixel surface (faster with very many points); D3 is a JavaScript library that draws data on SVG or canvas.
  • Downsampling: choosing a representative smaller selection from a large dataset, so that drawing stays fast.

The two main pages

Genome overview (GenomeOverviewPage.tsx with GenomeOverviewWorkspace.tsx). For each selected family member it shows genome-wide tracks for coverage, APCAD, structural variants, haplotypes and repeat expansions, with an ideogram per chromosome at the bottom. Chromosomes 1–22, X and Y lie one after the other on one axis. A dragged selection opens that region in the chromosome view.

The mitochondrion is missing from the overview, as it is from the Circos plot: 16.6 kb of a 3.1 Gb genome is about 0.006 pixel wide on a 1200-pixel track. It is therefore not on the axis, in the chromosome strip or in the sidebar's Chromosomes list, and the overview does not request a track for it. The chromosome view's drop-down list and the mtDNA page do show it (the owner's decision, 2026-10-28).

Chromosome view (ChromosomeViewPage.tsx with ChromosomeViewWorkspace.tsx). At the top is the full ideogram, with the window shown in red. Below it come the sample tracks of each member (coverage, APCAD, SVs, small variants, haplotypes, repeats). At the bottom are the reference tracks (genes, clinical CNVs, DGV, blacklist, segmental duplications) and a zoomed ideogram of the window. Buttons zoom and pan; a field jumps to a gene or locus.

If the family has a region of interest (ROI), it lies across the tracks in both views as a light red band with edges (RoiMarkerOverlay.tsx).

Which tracks a member gets. The frontend first asks which tracks a sample has (GET /api/families/{family_id}/track-availability), so that no empty strip appears for data the family does not have. With a gene panel, availability follows the lists of chapter 8:

  • SVs. If the view is opened from the SV page with a panel, a member gets an SV track if the panel keeps one of their SVs, by the rule of the SV list: the annotation names a gene of the panel, or the SV overlaps a panel region.

  • Small variants. A member gets a track if the small-variant list with that panel shows a variant of theirs in the window: a gene of the panel in the annotation (the row's gene symbols or the gene index) or a position in a panel region, however large the panel. Availability builds that condition with the list's own function: _small_variant_present_sample_names in clickhouse_family_variants.py calls _small_query_filter_parts. The regions go to ClickHouse once, as a parameter; a join on 64 kb windows matches them to the family's own rows. A panel without genes and without regions for the family's assembly keeps nothing in the list and therefore offers no track.

    The query is one SELECT over the family's rows, which for each row takes the members with an ALT allele from the calls. With the Mendeliome it takes 0.04 s over a 10 Mb window (measured on ClickHouse 26.8; measurements in docs/variant-ranking-cache.md, A panel of any size).

Where in the code: frontend/src/pages/genome/; availability in backend/app/routers/families_tracks.py.

The ideogram

The ideogram is the striped chromosome drawing. The cytobands come from Postgres (GET /api/chromosomes/{assembly}/{chrom}) and are drawn in SVG, with a colour per stain code (e.g. gpos100, acen for the centromere). On the full ideogram the user selects a range; the zoomed ideogram shows only the window shown. On the genome overview a chromosome is only a few pixels wide; there the bands are merged per pixel group into the predominant stain.

Where in the code: frontend/src/components/visualizations/Ideogram.tsx and ZoomedIdeogram.tsx; the helper functions in frontend/src/lib/ideogram.ts and stainColors.ts.

The sample tracks

  • Coverage and segments. A canvas shows the log ratio of the coverage as dots per bin, with the CNV segments as lines over them. The colour thresholds (gain, loss) are configurable per browser. The legend always shows them and marks values that differ from the defaults, because another workstation may colour the same data differently.

    The data come from the interval table in ClickHouse: the overview requests all chromosomes at once (GET /api/bed/{sample_id}/coverage/batch and …/segments/batch), the chromosome view one chromosome (GET /api/bed/{sample_id}/coverage and …/segments). Each CNV caller gets its own track; with coverage and segments the views name the caller (source). If the sample has coverage from several callers in the requested area, a coverage request without a caller is refused (400). The read routes answer in JSON, also without format; a request for the text format gets 422.

    GET /api/families/{family_id}/track-availability names the callers, with for each coverage track the conversion (coverage_normalizations) and the content (coverage_contents: read_depth, log2_ratio or unknown, by the rule of the depth readers, chapter 6). Each track goes on the axis of its content (coverageScale in frontend/src/lib/coverageSources.ts, the prop scale of CoverageSegmentsChart):

    • a log2 ratio on the log2-ratio axis, with the colours for gain and loss and the caller's segments;
    • the maternal plasma of a conventional NIPT (ccnv, under its pregnancy's own source, ccnv_p…, which the views read as ccnv: sourceBase in frontend/src/lib/pregnancySources.ts), a log2 ratio too, on a NIPT axis of its own (±0.3): a fetal trisomy raises the plasma by only log2(1 + FF/2), some +0.08 at a 12 % fetal fraction, which the colour thresholds (±0.35) would never colour. Each segment and its bins take the colour of ccnv's call (gain, loss, or purple for a call ccnv calls discordant with the fetal fraction), and dashed lines show where a fetal trisomy and monosomy lie at ccnv's effective fetal fraction, on chromosomes 1–22 and X (frontend/src/lib/ccnvTracks.ts). The track's header shows that fetal fraction, the fetal sex and the sex-chromosome call (ccnv in the track availability), and every estimate on hover;
    • read depth (a coverage BED declared as read depth, or HiFiCNV's depth, stored as read because the file gave no usable autosomal median) on a depth axis from 0 to a round number above the 99th percentile of the values shown, without those colours or segments, which are log2 ratios;
    • values of an unknown kind (a coverage BED without a declaration, a conversion the viewer does not know) on their own range, without an axis.

    The track's header says why: in a neutral style for HiFiCNV's depth, in the warning colour for unknown values (coverageScaleNote). A segments read delivers each segment with the values its caller gives beside it (details: for ccnv the call, z-score, bins, expected ratio, implied fetal fraction, discordance and origin, for WisecondorX the z-score); the views show them over the segment under the pointer.

  • APCAD. A scatter plot of the B-allele frequency, with two homozygous bands and a heterozygous middle band: the signal that distinguishes parental haplotypes. Data: GET /api/bed/{sample_id}/apcad and …/apcad_pcf, on the overview their …/batch variant.

    A sample has millions of markers, so the server chooses a selection: only informative markers that passed the quality filter, spread over the chromosomes according to the number of stored sites, so that each chromosome keeps its own density per Mb. Within a chromosome the best come first, spread so that all bands stay visible. A ranking on quality over the whole genome would draw a chromosome denser than its sites are: joint variant calling scores a chromosome's markers higher where one sample of the family has extra reads there (e.g. an embryo with a trisomy), and does so for all embryos.

    If a track has not a single marker with a parental origin (HiFiCNV's minor-allele fraction, from a bigWig), it shows its unphased markers, on an axis from 0 to 0.5. An embryo from the PGT pipeline with its APCAD table shows the sites that that run read (parents homozygous for opposite alleles): for a euploid embryo a middle band around 0.5 per parent, without the homozygous bands of a trio VCF.

  • Parental origin (ParentalOriginChart.tsx). For an embryo with the PGT pipeline's segregation table, in both views; off by default, turned on with the tick box Parental origin (aneuploidy). Data: GET /api/bed/{sample_id}/apcad_segregation and …/batch, read-only.

    Drawn like the pipeline's own figures, in two panels: Mother heterozygous (group 2: mother heterozygous, father homozygous) and Father heterozygous (group 3). Each site sits at the embryo's allele fraction (0 to 1), coloured by the other parent's homozygous allele: amber for the reference allele (2B, 3B), the heterozygous parent's colour for the alternative allele (2A, 3A). The server stores each site at the fraction of the allele that the homozygous parent lacks, with its group (group); the chart calculates the allele fraction back from that. In the genome overview all chromosomes are side by side, so that an aneuploid chromosome stands out among the others.

    How to read a panel:

    • bands at 0, ½ and 1: one homologue from that parent (disomy);
    • only ⅓ and ⅔, nothing at 0 or 1: both homologues (heterodisomy);
    • 0, ⅓, ⅔ and 1: two copies of one homologue (isodisomy), or in a trisomy the panel of the parent who gave one copy of the three.

    Read against the centromere, heterodisomy at the centromere points to meiosis I; isodisomy at the centromere that becomes heterodisomic beyond a crossover, to meiosis II; isodisomy over the whole chromosome, to a mitotic error. CoGA draws the sites and makes no classification from them.

  • Small variants. One mark per variant of the sample (GET /api/families/{familyId}/small-variants in track mode, with an upper limit). The marks (frontend/src/lib/smallVariantMarks.ts):

    • a variant that ClinVar calls (likely) pathogenic: a larger red diamond, whatever its impact;
    • every other variant: a dot 6 px wide, whose colour gives the class: green for ClinVar (likely) benign, then by impact orange for HIGH, yellow for MODERATE and grey for LOW, MODIFIER or none;
    • a review tag: a ring in the tag's colour around the mark.

    The dots differ only by their colour; the tooltip names the impact and the ClinVar class, and the track's accessible name counts the diamonds and the HIGH variants. The most salient mark lies on top: grey first, then green, yellow, orange and finally the diamonds.

    If the sample is not a father or mother and the family has at least one parent, the track splits into rows by parental origin (paternal, undetermined, maternal): with both parents by their genotypes, otherwise by the child's phase.

    Up to a window of 250 kb the track draws every variant. In a wider window it uses salient_only to request only the variants it draws as salient: ClinVar (likely) pathogenic, or HIGH or MODERATE impact on a transcript and not ClinVar (likely) benign (_small_salient_condition in clickhouse_variant_queries.py, a filter of SmallVariantQueryFilters like the others, with its case in the parity test). A WGS trio has about 1.5 variants per kb per member: a 2 Mb window would otherwise read thousands of variants per member with their full annotation, only to draw them as grey dots. The track's header says so (SMALL_VARIANT_ALL_MARKS_MAX_SPAN and smallVariantTrackScope in frontend/src/lib/trackSampling.ts).

  • Structural variants. The overview uses SvTrack (canvas, with a computed hover), the chromosome view VariantTrack (SVG shapes with their own mouse handling). Both fetch GET /api/families/{familyId}/structural-variants, in track mode for the track's sample. Every SV that the SV list shows is drawn, in one of six rows: DEL, DUP, INV, INS, BND and, at the bottom, Other.

    • An SV that removes a copy goes under DEL; one that adds a copy, under DUP. The backend says for each SV which of the two it is (copy_change), with the rule of the SV ranking and the second hit (sv_copy_change.py), from the call of the track's sample. So a DEL:ME goes under DEL and a DUP:TANDEM under DUP.
    • A CNV goes under DEL or DUP by its copy number; a male has one copy on chrX and chrY outside the PARs. A CNV without a stored copy number counts as a loss, as in the ranking.
    • Every other SV goes under its type without subtype (an INS:ME under INS), a TRA under BND. A type that names no row (e.g. CPX) and a CNV that changes no copy go in the grey Other row.

    DEL, DUP and Other are bars, INV an outlined bar, INS a vertical stroke and BND a triangle. The tooltip names the type as stored, for a CNV with the copy change with which it was drawn, and for each call the copy number (CN) if the call has one. It writes the chromosome as the header names it (chr1), however it is stored.

    The overview places an SV on its chromosome as the axis names it (normalizeChrom in frontend/src/lib/chromosomes.ts), however the VCF wrote it (chrX or X). The chromosome view of chrM shows an SV on the mitochondrion, such as the mitochondrial SVs (callset mito_sv, stored as M); the overview leaves out the mitochondrion and therefore does not draw or count such an SV.

  • Haplotypes. On the overview GenomeHaplotypeTrack, per chromosome HaplotypePhasedTrack, with data from GET /api/families/{family_id}/haplotypes and …/phased-markers; the overview requests the haplotypes of all chromosomes with …/haplotypes/batch. The import stores a block's name without chr; the overview places a block, like an SV, on its chromosome as the axis names it.

    • The raw phased markers are coloured per marker, without grouping; the haplotype track is the cleaned-up version (docs/haplotype-segregation-analysis.md). The marker overlay appears only if both parents are present, the user turns it on and the window is 5 Mb or smaller (PHASED_MARKER_MAX_SPAN); in a wider window the track's header says that the markers appear on zooming in.
    • A child's header names, next to the track name, its informative sites in the window, or, above a Mendelian error ratio of 2 %, those errors in red (HaplotypeMarkerNote.tsx). The header and the track read the same markers, from one request (usePhasedMarkers).
    • The risk haplotype is derived in the region of interest. Its lane gets an edge in the risk colour at the top and bottom, solid for affected and dashed for carrier, and in the chromosome view a light tint of that colour behind the band, which keeps its homologue colour (drawHaplotypeRiskLane in frontend/src/lib/haplotypeCanvas.ts). On the overview it is drawn only on the chromosome of that region, because the labels of the homologues apply per chromosome. Without a region of interest the overview draws no risk and shows the status "not assessed".
    • A corrected phase. A continuous line with a small triangle (in the warning colour) marks where CoGA corrected a parent's phase. There (almost) all the couple's children switched haplotype at the same time on that parent's side: more likely a phase switch in the parent than crossovers. From that point on, the haplotype blocks, the lineage colouring and the raw markers read that parent's phase swapped; the genotypes themselves stay as they were called. If such a correction lies in or just next to the ROI, each embryo shows the warning phase corrected.

  • Repeat expansions. One mark per locus in the colour of the status, from GET /api/families/{familyId}/repeat-expansions/sample/{sampleId}. The statuses are normal, review, not assessed, intermediate, premutation and pathogenic; any other status is coloured as unknown. Not assessed is a count at a locus without thresholds, outside the benign range that the catalogue gives for it. The status is that of the repeat page: the call re-assessed against the catalogue row that currently classifies it, with the remark for two different chrX alleles in a male. On the overview a locus, like an SV, lies on its chromosome as the axis names it. The chromosome view of chrM shows a locus on the mitochondrion, however it is stored (chrM or M); the overview leaves out the mitochondrion.

    • A corrected repeat count. If QA has recorded a count correction for a locus (chapter 8), the track draws the status of the corrected count. The tooltip names the corrected counts with TRGT's counts in brackets, and the correction (allele_repeat_counts, allele_trgt_repeat_counts, count_offset).
    • A count close to a boundary. The tooltip names every count within 3 repeats of a boundary, with the boundary, why, and what is known about TRGT's count for the gene (count_unit_warnings in the same response; chapter 8). The track's accessible name counts such loci (1 near a boundary).

Aneuploidy and large SVs in PGT: the analyst assesses. On each embryo's segment, copy-number (coverage) and APCAD tracks the analyst assesses aneuploidy and structural variants larger than 10 Mb themselves. CoGA shows those tracks, but has no automatic aneuploidy detection (TF-09a, REQ-PGT-008). The limits of that assessment (mosaicism above 35 %, SVs above 10 Mb) are still to be established by the clinical validation (TF-10 §3.2).

Where in the code: frontend/src/components/visualizations/ (CoverageSegmentsChart.tsx, ApcadChart.tsx, SmallVariantTrack.tsx, SvTrack.tsx, VariantTrack.tsx, the haplotype and repeat tracks); the small-variant marks in frontend/src/lib/smallVariantMarks.ts; the APCAD selection in fetch_apcad_downsampled (backend/app/services/clickhouse_interval_tracks.py).

The reference tracks

These tracks are not tied to a sample and show reference annotation over the window shown:

Track Endpoint Shows
GeneTrack GET /api/genes/{assembly}/{chrom} Genes with exons and introns (D3), one transcript per gene: the MANE Select transcript (GENCODE, or HGNC's MANE accessions for a RefSeq reference), otherwise Ensembl's canonical transcript (GENCODE's tag Ensembl_canonical), otherwise the longest. Chevrons along the introns point in the direction of transcription (› on the + strand, ‹ on the − strand). The tooltip names the strand, the transcript, above an exon or intron its number counted from the start of the transcript (Exon 3 / 12), and the panels the gene is in
CnvTrack GET /api/cnvs/{assembly}/{chrom} Clinical CNVs; a click opens the detail page
DgvTrack GET /api/dgv/{assembly}/{chrom} DGV variants; with too much overlap the server shows a density profile instead of individual variants
BlacklistTrack · SegmentalDuplicationTrack GET /api/blacklist/{assembly}/{chrom} · GET /api/segmental-duplications/{assembly}/{chrom} Unreliable regions and segmental duplications

Where in the code: the components in frontend/src/components/visualizations/; the routers in backend/app/routers/.

Large and still correct: downsampling

How many points or segments a track shows at most depends on its width in pixels (frontend/src/lib/trackSampling.ts). That does not affect correctness: CoGA summarises only at overview level, where several positions fall on the same pixel anyway. Zooming in gives more detail, and all records of the window as soon as their number falls within the track's limit. For APCAD, quality and signal drive the selection, not chance. The exact assessment never happens on these tracks, but on the filtered variant lists (chapter 8) and in IGV.

Circos

The Circos plot lays the chromosomes out in a circle and draws structural variants as arcs between them, with D3 on SVG. Each SV is drawn as in the SV tracks, with the calls of the whole family: a copy loss as a deletion, a copy gain as a duplication, a TRA as a breakend. An SV that names no row of the tracks is thin and grey (Other in the legend).

The page takes the assembly of the family's project (useFamilyReference, like the other views). It fetches the chromosomes of that assembly, with their lengths and bands (GET /api/chromosomes/{assembly}/details), and, as soon as the assembly is known, also all the family's SVs. It draws the chromosomes 1–22, X and Y that the assembly has, each at its own length; it leaves out contigs and the mitochondrion. An SV lies on its chromosome however the name is stored (chrX, X or x, via normalizeChrom). An SV's tooltip writes the chromosomes as the chromosome view names them (chr1:10 → chr2:30).

If the page cannot draw the assembly, it says why and draws nothing. That happens with:

  • a family without a linked project;
  • a family or project list that did not load (with a button to try again);
  • an assembly without chromosome lengths;
  • an assembly that has none of the chromosomes 1–22, X and Y;
  • an assembly with chromosomes that the plot cannot place (chr23 and higher, W, Z). The page names those chromosomes: without them the plot would pass for the whole genome.

A click on a chromosome opens the chromosome view; a click on a translocation (BND or TRA) opens the genome overview with both chromosomes.

Where in the code: frontend/src/pages/genome/CircosPlotPage.tsx and frontend/src/components/visualizations/CircosPlot.tsx.

IGV: reads at base level

For the finest check, the individual reads, CoGA embeds the IGV browser. IgvViewer.tsx requests two lists: the alignment files of all family members, the proband first (GET /api/cram/{familyId}/manifest), and separately the CNV caller's signal files (depth, allele fraction and copy number: GET /api/signal-tracks/{familyId}/manifest). If that second request fails, the reads still load and the page reports that the signal tracks are missing. A sample with an alignment of more than one analysis, such as short-read and then long-read WGS of the same DNA, gets a track of each: the manifest gives each alignment with its analysis (analysis_type, also as ?analysis= in the addresses), and the track carries the sample's name with that analysis (alignmentTrackName in lib/alignmentTracks.ts). In a family of several analyses every track names its analysis, also when only one alignment of the sample can be shown; one that no import recorded is named analysis not recorded.

The backend serves the files with the same access control as the rest: every endpoint of cram.py and signal_tracks.py checks that the sample belongs to a family the user may see, and otherwise gives 404. With range requests IGV requests only the bytes it needs. IGV never gets the address of a bucket or share: every byte comes via the backend.

Every request carries the token the session has at that moment: each track's oauthToken function asks sessionAccessToken from lib/api.ts for it, like the API client. A Microsoft token lives about an hour; a token that IGV read only once, on opening, would leave a long session without tracks.

Where the backend looks for a file:

  • The package folder. At the path that the import recorded for the sample, in the package folder read by the import of the analysis that recorded it. A package is read where it lies, so also on a share or bucket mounted as an import folder (/data/share, /data/imports), and in a folder named differently from the family. That package folder counts only if, with symbolic links followed, it lies under a FAMILY_IMPORT_ROOTS folder and is not that folder itself (local_family_package_folder in services/family_package_source.py). The file must lie in the package folder, and a recorded CRAM/BAM or index must have that file type's extension. A changed database row can thus at most point to another file of that kind in the family's package, never to another family's package. A recorded signal file is looked for there alone: one whose analysis has no package folder, or that is gone from it, is missing.
  • The family's own folders. A CRAM is combined only with its own index. A recorded alignment whose file is gone is missing: the backend does not look for it elsewhere, where it could find another analysis's reads. Only for a sample whose alignment no import recorded does the backend look in data/<family>/ and data/families/<family>/: the reads at their fixed places (<sample>.cram with <sample>.cram.crai). A path that leads out of such a folder is not looked up: a sample ID such as ../F2/S2. A file that, via a symbolic link, lies in another family's folder or outside the data folder is not listed and not served.

IGV draws the reads and variants on the genome of the assembly from the family's project (mapAssemblyToIgvGenome in frontend/src/lib/reference.ts):

  • hg38 for GRCh38 or hg38;
  • hg19 for GRCh37 or hg19 (in upper or lower case, with or without a patch suffix: the rule of grc_build in the backend);
  • hs1 for T2T-CHM13v2.0 under any of its names (isT2tChm13, chapter 4);
  • a few others (mm39, mm10, equCab3).

If CoGA knows no IGV genome for the assembly, the page opens none and says so ("No IGV genome for …"): on the genome of another assembly the reads would be in the wrong place.

Where in the code: frontend/src/components/IgvViewer.tsx and frontend/src/pages/families/FamilyIgvPage.tsx, with the genome in frontend/src/lib/reference.ts; backend/app/routers/cram.py and signal_tracks.py, with the family's own folders in backend/app/core/family_folders.py.

The pedigree

The pedigree is not fetched separately, but computed in the browser from the members and relationships that come with the family. The drawing follows the parent IDs and the relationships, not the flat role field (which also says mother/father for grandparents).

  • Males are squares, females circles, unknown sex a diamond; affected members are filled, carriers half filled; consanguineous partners get a double line.
  • A member related to another member in an unknown degree (a relationship relative, such as a PGT index of whom only the side is known) stands next to that member in that member's generation, connected by a dotted arc with a question mark.
  • Two samples of one person (a relationship same_individual, such as the plasmas of a monogenic and a conventional NIPT of one pregnancy under two sample IDs, or the plasmas of two pregnancies of one woman) are one symbol, drawn under the sample with the most links in the pedigree (on a tie the first member) and labelled with all IDs (PLASMA1 / PLASMA2). Every other link to either sample runs to that symbol. The symbol draws what either sample records (sex, affected and carrier status, parents): one sample's unknown value never hides the other's known one. Its QC ring is the worst of the samples, the HPO badge shows when any of them has HPO terms, and the accessible name says how many members are drawn with several samples. The members table keeps a row per sample.
  • A fetus (role fetus) carries a P in its symbol, as the pedigree nomenclature draws a pregnancy; its label is, like an embryo's, a size smaller.
  • The QC verdict per sample is a ring that differs not only by colour: a thin ring with ✓ for pass, a dashed one with ! for warn and a thick one with ✕ for fail.

Where in the code: frontend/src/components/visualizations/Pedigree.tsx.

Errors and limits

A track, a page or IGV always shows a failed request as an error, never as empty data.

  • If the request for the available tracks or for the chromosome lengths fails, the workspace reports "Could not load … — this is not an empty result", with a button to try again.
  • While panning, the previous image stays only while the new window loads. If the request fails, the track shows the error above an empty window, never the data of the previous window.
  • A window without width requests nothing and is called "no region in view".
  • If a window has more variants or SVs than a track can draw, the track says so ("Too many … Zoom in or apply filters.") instead of drawing part of them; on the overview and in Circos this also happens above the backend's limit.

Chromosome names. In the track names, the chromosome lists and the header the mitochondrion is called chrM, however the data write it. The chromosome view's Chromosome drop-down list names each chromosome like the header (chr1, chrX, chrM); the genome overview's chromosome strip writes them without chr (1, X). The ideograms follow the same rule; their accessible name writes the chromosome without chr (Chromosome M ideogram). A band of the mitochondrion, which has no cytobands, is called chrM in the tooltip and in the zoomed ideogram's accessible name, just like a band without a name of its own. The repeat tracks read a locus's chromosome as the API reads it (MT, M, chrM and chrMT are one chromosome). The ROI marker review page also writes the ROI's chromosome this way (chr1, chrX): in the explanation at the top, the window shown, the title of each site and the tooltip. It requests the markers and the blocks with the name as the family stores it.

An interrupted drag. Sometimes a drag cannot end with the release of the mouse button: the track on which it started disappears during the drag, the pointer is cancelled (pointercancel), or the window loses focus and with it the release. The gesture then breaks off without moving the window, and removes its offset or selection band from the tracks.

Security and traceability

  • Everything behind a login. The reference routers (chromosomes, cnvs, dgv, blacklist, segmental-duplications) require login on all their endpoints; the other routers require it per endpoint.
  • Project-scoped access. Family and sample tracks go through the access checkpoint (chapter 2). Someone who knows a family_id but has no access to it does not get the tracks.
  • Uploads for administrators only. Uploading a BED track (POST /api/bed/upload/{sample_id}/{bed_type}) requires get_current_admin_user, and the source file is registered.
  • Provenance of the tracks. Each row in the interval table carries its source and file name. sample_interval_track_sources keeps, per sample, kind, source and file, the number of rows and the upload time, and also the conversion if the import converts a track's values (normalization): for HiFiCNV the copy number and the depth become a log2 ratio. If a depth file gives no usable autosomal median, the depth stays as read and the import records that as none. A coverage BED records what it declared to contain (content: read_depth, log2_ratio, or unknown without a declaration; chapter 6).

Key files

File Role

frontend/src/pages/genome/ChromosomeViewPage.tsx · ChromosomeViewWorkspace.tsx Chromosome view
frontend/src/pages/genome/CircosPlotPage.tsx · frontend/src/components/visualizations/CircosPlot.tsx Circos
frontend/src/components/visualizations/ All tracks, the ideogram, the ROI band and the pedigree

10. Variant tagging & semi-automatic ACMG classification

This chapter describes how an analyst labels (tags) and classifies variants, with the help of a semi-automatic ACMG/AMP classifier. CoGA does not classify on its own. The software pre-assesses each criterion from the variant, family and gene data and places it on a points scale; the reviewer can adjust any criterion. The server always recalculates the class and the points total, and the evidence used is frozen. If that evidence changes later, CoGA reports drift, and that blocks the sign-out (chapter 11). The rules per criterion are in the app: Docs → Semi-automatic ACMG classification (frontend/src/content/docs/acmg-classification.md).

A few terms:

  • ACMG/AMP criteria: a standardised set of evidence rules (Richards et al., 2015) with codes such as PVS1, PM2 or BA1. A P points to pathogenic evidence, a B to benign evidence.
  • Tag: a label on a variant (e.g. "Report" or "Send for validation").
  • Snapshot: a frozen copy of the data as they were at a given moment.

Two separate properties: phenotype and carrier status

CoGA keeps two separate properties for each family member:

  • Clinical status (clinical_status): unknown, unaffected or affected: does the person have the disorder?
  • Carrier status (carrier_status): unknown, not_carrier or carrier: does the person carry the risk allele, affected or not?

This separation matters clinically: in a recessive disorder a parent is often a carrier but not affected. The segregation rules of the ACMG evaluator read only the clinical status and the genotypes. The carrier status serves the haplotype segregation of PGT (chapter 8).

Part 1 — Tagging

What is recorded

A review records, per variant and per family: the class (e.g. "VUS - class 3"), a list of tags and a note. For each tag CoGA also keeps who set it and when.

A review per analysis. When a family holds several analyses (short-read and then long-read WGS of the same DNA, or the monogenic NIPT of several pregnancies), a review belongs to one analysis (the owner's decision of 2026-11-20): a variant reviewed in the short-read analysis is not in the long-read analysis's record unless it is reviewed there too. Each row names its analysis (analysis, empty for a review of a family without an analysis). A reading for analysis X reads, per variant, X's own review, else the shared one (stored under no analysis the family holds), never another analysis's. A save in X always writes X's own review, made from the review it read and the save's values; the shared review stays as it is. A save that empties X's review keeps it, empty, while a shared review of the variant holds something, so X reads the variant as not reviewed. A family with several analyses with small variants of their own names the analysis on every save (analysis), otherwise 422. Each audit event of a review names the analysis (metadata.analysis). The Variant Explorer shows, per family, the tags and classes of every analysis's review.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/analysis_reviews.py; upsert_small_variant_review in small_variant_review_pg.py.

Class labels in sentence case. The class tags and the VUS levels are in sentence case: "Likely pathogenic - class 4", "VUS — hot" (the owner's decision). A tag is stored on a review as a key. The class text of a review is free text: a save stores it as sent, without leading or trailing whitespace (_stored_classification in review_pg_utils.py). The filters and the Variant Explorer read a class label regardless of case.

Which class a review shows. One rule determines the class a review shows (review_class_label in review_pg_utils.py; in the frontend normalizeReviewClassification):

  1. a bare class word in the text ("VUS") gives the label of that class;
  2. otherwise the most severe class tag (acmg_class_5 … acmg_class_1);
  3. otherwise the text as stored.

Both sides read the cases from the shared table review-class-cases.json. Every place that shows a class or filters on it follows this rule (the owner's decisions of 10 November 2026):

  • Display. The table, the cards, the compound-het pairs, the mtDNA cards and the light review dialog of the family page, and the table and the cards of the SV page; the tables and cards via reviewClassChips in smallVariantResultUtils.ts. A review shows one class: a class tag of another class does not appear next to it. The VUS levels and Secondary finding remain tags, never the class.
  • Filters. The classification filter of the family page, of the SV search and of the Variant Explorer keeps a variant by the class its review shows, or for a small variant the review of its compound-het pair, regardless of case. So Likely pathogenic - class 4 also finds a review with only the class tag acmg_class_4, and not a review with the text "VUS - class 3" next to the class tag acmg_class_5: that one shows class 5. A filter value is read like the text of a review: "VUS" asks for class 3, free text for the reviews that show that text (so without a class tag). The family page and the SV search filter in Python (review_shows_class), the Explorer in SQL (review_class_label_sql, which binds the class words, the class tags and the labels from the Python tables). An integration test on Postgres sets the SQL beside the Python rule for every case of review-class-cases.json.
  • Exports. The CSV exports of small variants, of SVs and of the Variant Explorer write in the column Classification the class the review shows (review_class_label), and in Classification text next to it the classification as the reviewer wrote it and as it is stored. So "VUS - class 3" next to the tag acmg_class_4 stays in the file, even though the review shows class 4. A review with only a class tag has an empty Classification text. The Explorer writes the text of the review whose class it shows: its own review or that of the compound-het pair, in the family that gives the most severe class (chapter 14).
  • CNVs. A CNV classification counts through the class label that the CNV dialog stores as text; in doing so the dialog removes every ACMG class tag from the review. The page does not show its class in cnv_class alone, and so the filter does not read it.

A quick tag does not change the classification. Review, Exclude and Report send the classification text back as it is stored (quickTagTogglePayload in smallVariantReview.ts, also on the SV page). Such a save writes only the tag to the audit trail. The light review dialog opens on the class shown. If the class is left alone, the dialog keeps the text and the class tags as they were. If the user picks a different class, or none, it replaces the text and every class tag; otherwise a more severe class tag next to it would keep hiding the chosen class. The report and a signed version show the same class as the family page: the report reads it with this rule, a signed version from the frozen record (class_shown, chapter 11), with the ACMG or CNV score next to it when that gives a different class.

Where in the code: the labels in acmg_points.py, cnv_acmg_points.py and small_variant_review_tags.py; the filters in small_variant_review_pg.py, structural_variant_review_pg.py and variant_explorer_service.py.

Concurrent editing. If a review (of a small variant or a structural variant) was changed by someone else in the meantime, the server refuses the save (409) and sends the current version along. That way nobody overwrites someone else's work unnoticed.

Whoever saves a compound heterozygous pair also writes the review of the partner variant. If a pair falls apart in the process, CoGA rewrites the review of each of its variants. CoGA first locks all those reviews, in one fixed order, as with an ordinary save, and only then reads them. A partner review that was saved in the meantime (e.g. as class 5 with a new note) is therefore kept and is never reset to a copy read earlier. The server checks the partner's version just like that of the variant itself (compound_het.partner_expected_updated_at). If the partner was changed in the meantime, the same 409 follows, naming the partner. updated_at never goes back in time.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/small_variant_review_pg.py (the pair in _lock_pair_save_reviews); the check for concurrent changes in _raise_on_stale_review (backend/app/services/review_pg_utils.py).

Which tags exist

  • System tags are built in and cannot be changed: collaboration tags (e.g. review, send_for_validation, validated, report, excluded) and the class tags (acmg_class_1 to acmg_class_5, the VUS levels acmg_vus_hot, acmg_vus_warm and acmg_vus_cold, and secondary_finding).
  • Custom tags are created by a superuser or an administrator. They apply everywhere (global) or to one project (project); a project tag can be shared with additional projects.

On save, the backend checks that every tag the review adds exists and may be used in this family; an unknown tag gives 400. A tag the review already carries stays, even if it has been deleted in the meantime. After all, the quick buttons and the review dialog send the stored tags back; otherwise every following save of that variant would fail, including the one that removes the tag.

Reviews, saved filter presets and the audit trail refer to a tag by its key (key). The key is derived from the label when the tag is created and is then fixed. Renaming changes only the label; the tag therefore stays on every review and in every filter. A label that reads like that of another active tag or of a system tag is refused (409). If a new tag gets the label of a renamed or deleted tag, it gets a numbered key (e.g. probe_x_2). It takes over no reviews of the old tag.

Only a superuser or an administrator (get_current_superuser, chapter 2) creates, changes or deletes custom tags, on the administration page and on the routes of a family; anyone else gets 403 Superuser access required. Deleting does not erase a tag but sets it to inactive. Reviews that carry it still show it with its label, marked as (deleted). It can be removed from them, but no longer added to any review. The management screen is under Administration (frontend/src/pages/admin/AdminVariantTagsPage.tsx).

If a project is deleted, its tags go the same way. delete_project_record first sets them to inactive and deletes the project in the same transaction; the tags continue to exist, without a project (project_id becomes NULL). They remain project tags, so no list shows them as a global tag, and they keep their key: a new tag with the same label gets a numbered key and takes over no reviews, signed records or audit rows. In addition, a family's tag list shows, as inactive, every tag that its own reviews carry but that its projects do not (or no longer) know, such as a tag of a deleted project or of a project the family left. A tag of another project that none of its reviews carries stays invisible.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/small_variant_review_tags.py; the tables small_variant_tag_definitions and small_variant_tag_definition_project_links in 03_assay.sql.

Filter presets and the light review dialog

An analyst can save their filter settings as a preset; a viewer or a reader can do so too, because these are their own data (chapter 2). Only the person who saved the preset is offered it and can delete it; a superuser or administrator sees everyone's small-variant presets (chapter 15). The owner is the account (owner_id), not the username: if the username changes on a sign-in with Microsoft, the preset stays theirs. The preset shows the username under which it was last saved (owner). A small-variant preset applies in every family the owner can open. A structural-variant preset applies to one family, or, as a reusable preset, to all their families.

Next to the full ACMG classifier there is a light review dialog: pick a class, switch tags on or off and write a note, with the priority score (chapter 12) as an aid.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/small_variant_review_presets.py and, for the SV presets, structural_variant_review_pg.py; frontend/src/pages/families/SmallVariantReviewDialog.tsx.

Repeat loci and Paraphase regions

A repeat locus and a Paraphase region get a review of their own, per family and assembly. It uses the same tag catalogue, but classifies on the type's own scale instead of with an ACMG class (REQ-DIAG-009; docs/repeat-paraphase-review-design.md).

  • The card on the repeat page and on the Paraphase page has the buttons of every variant card. Review, Exclude and Report switch their tag on or off; Tags & notes opens the dialog (FindingReviewDialog.tsx).
  • The dialog does not offer the class tags with key acmg_* (the ACMG classes and the VUS levels). If a review carries one anyway, the dialog shows it marked, so that it can be removed (decision B14). Secondary finding remains available.
  • The card shows the classification (Review: …), the tags and the note. Differs from CoGA's status appears when the classification fits none of the members' calls. Changed since review reports drift; the tooltip says what changed. Exclude collapses the card to its header.
  • A save writes the review straight into the loaded table. The server's response, with the drift, replaces it; a failed save puts the card back (useFindingReviewSave in findingReview.ts).
  • The family page counts the reviews per type (GET /families/{id}/finding-review-summary).

Part 2 — The ACMG classifier for small variants

Decision support, not an automaton

From a variant, ACMG classify opens a dialog that:

  1. pre-assesses the criteria from the data CoGA already holds, and shows those data next to the criteria: one card per kind (consequence and transcript, population frequencies, in-silico scores, the gene, ClinVar, the proband's phenotype and the family's genotypes), each with the criteria it supports; a value the annotation does not have is shown as — (AcmgEvidencePanel.tsx);
  2. puts each criterion in one of four states;
  3. lets the analyst confirm, adjust or reject each criterion;
  4. places the accepted criteria on a points scale;
  5. recalculates everything on the server on save.

The four states

State Display Meaning
Applies ticked, green (pathogenic) or grey-blue (benign) The data clearly support the criterion; it counts
Consider orange dot, not ticked Relevant signal, not decisive
Argues against red cross, not ticked The data point the other way (e.g. a benign prediction for PP3)
Not applicable grey, struck through Cannot apply to this variant type, but remains clickable

All four can be adjusted: a click on a criterion always switches it on or off. An unticked criterion that never applies together with a ticked criterion gets ⊘ and a dotted border; ticking it swaps the two (see Criteria that never apply together).

Reopening a classified variant. The dialog shows each stored criterion with its state, strength and evidence. The evaluator only fills in missing evidence, and gives criteria that were never stored their own state. Saving again without a change therefore leaves the criteria as they were. Every list of small variants (the table and the cards, the report, the NIPT candidates, the mtDNA analysis) delivers the review with the same ACMG record as reading that single review (_fetch_review_rows_for_variants in small_variant_review_repository.py).

What the evaluator pre-assesses

The evaluator reads the variant and, where available, the gene profile (ClinGen dosage, mode of inheritance from GenCC, the gene's phenotypes), the proband's HPO terms, the genotypes in the family and the relatedness checks of the Sample QC. It only proposes and changes nothing. The main rules:

Criterion Source Rule (summarised)
PVS1 consequence, LOFTEE, ClinGen dosage Predicted loss of function (stop codon, frameshift, canonical splicing, …). Very strong if LOFTEE says HC and the loss-of-function mechanism is proven; otherwise strong, or consider if the mechanism is not confirmed. With a LOFTEE flag (e.g. SINGLE_EXON, NAGNAG_SITE) or a variant that, according to VEP's NMD plugin, escapes nonsense-mediated decay: consider (strong), with the reason in the evidence
PM2, BA1, BS1, BS2 gnomAD Very rare → PM2 (supporting); without a gnomAD frequency, see Absent from gnomAD below. BA1 and BS1 read gnomAD's filtering allele frequency (FAF95, the highest across the genetic ancestry groups) where the annotation has it, as ClinGen SVI recommends, otherwise the allele frequency. Very frequent → BA1, which makes the variant benign on its own. Frequent → BS1. Homozygotes present → BS2: strong for a gene with a recessive mode of inheritance, otherwise consider at supporting. Without a homozygote count in the annotation, BS2 stays unmarked: check gnomAD yourself
PP2 gnomAD missense Z: from the gene profile, otherwise the VCF's own MISSENSE_Z Missense in a gene with a missense Z of 3.09 or more (the threshold the ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation working group discusses for PP2) → consider (supporting), never applied: the analyst judges whether missense in that gene is a common disease mechanism. The evidence says which missense Z PP2 read. A gene profile below 3.09 decides, even if the VCF has a higher value (the owner's decision of 2026-10-28)
PP3 / BP4 REVEL, SpliceAI, AlphaMissense REVEL decides first, then SpliceAI, then AlphaMissense; whichever decides also sets the strength. Only a verdict on REVEL marks the other criterion as an argument against. BP4 requires that SpliceAI predicts no splice impact: without a SpliceAI score BP4 becomes consider. Without any prediction neither applies. A REVEL between the thresholds or an ambiguous AlphaMissense class leaves both open
BP7 consequence and SpliceAI Synonymous without predicted splice impact (SpliceAI below 0.1). Without a SpliceAI score consider: check the splice impact yourself
PP5 / BP6 ClinVar ClinVar says pathogenic → PP5; benign → BP6, both consider, never applied: ClinGen SVI advises against counting another laboratory's classification as evidence. The evidence names ClinVar's review status, the stars and the condition(s). Conflicting classifications of pathogenicity gives neither. ClinVar is the ClinVar file the pipeline annotated; the older classification from the VEP cache counts only if no ClinVar file was annotated
PP4 Monarch phenotype score or HPO overlap How specifically the phenotype fits the gene. The score comes from the phenotype ranking; if the variant is not ranked, the dialog asks the server for the gene's score in the family (GET /families/{id}/gene-phenotype-score), the same number
PS2, PM6, PP1, BS4 genotypes in the family, Sample QC, phenotype score De novo (absent in both parents) → PS2 or PM6, at a strength from the ClinGen SVI de novo points (see De novo: PS2 or PM6 below). Several affected carriers → PP1 (consider); an affected family member without the variant → BS4 (consider). Two samples of one person count as one family member

The REVEL thresholds follow the 2022 ClinGen calibration; all thresholds are named constants in the evaluator. If the gene profile or the HPO list could not be loaded, the evidence says that the criterion was not assessed, not that it does not apply. The evaluator never proposes as applying the criteria that need a human judgement CoGA cannot derive from the annotation (among others PS1, PS3, PS4, PM1, PM3, PM5 and BP2).

Absent from gnomAD (PM2). A variant without a gnomAD frequency counts as absent from gnomAD if all three hold (the owner's decision of 2026-11-13):

  • its callset was annotated with gnomAD genomes or the joint set, from the VEP cache or from a gnomAD file (gnomad_annotated);
  • it lies on chromosome 1–22, X or Y;
  • the annotation has no gnomAD FAF95 or popmax.

Then PM2 is applied and BA1 and BS1 drop out. Otherwise (gnomAD not annotated, only gnomAD exomes, a chrM variant, a contig gnomAD does not have) PM2 becomes consider and BA1 and BS1 stay open: check gnomAD yourself. CoGA does not read gnomAD's coverage at the position (gnomadAbsence in evaluate.ts).

De novo: PS2 or PM6.

  • The parents are the father and mother the pedigree links to the proband, not the members with that role: a grandparent also has the role father or mother. For a son, on X or Y outside the pseudoautosomal regions, only the parent who passes on that chromosome decides.
  • PS2 or PM6. If the Sample QC confirms the parents (KING kinship and IBS0 as parent and child, and no Mendel check of the proband that warns or fails), then PS2; otherwise PM6, with the reason. If a parent's check fails (the genotypes are not those of parent and child), the data argue against both.
  • Consider instead of applied: a parent with fewer than 8 reads, a homozygous proband (outside a son's X or Y), a proband not registered as affected, a parent registered as affected, no phenotype score, or less than 0.5 point.

The strength follows the ClinGen SVI de novo points, depending on how well the phenotype fits the gene (the phenotype score, chapter 12):

The phenotype Phenotype score Confirmed (PS2) Assumed (PM6)
highly specific for the gene 0.6 or more 2 1
fits, but not highly specific 0.3 or more 1 0.5
fits only in general terms above 0 0.5 0.25

0.5 point is supporting, 1 moderate, 2 strong. One proband reaches strong at most; the analyst adds extra de novo cases from the literature themselves.

The coloured dots by the predictors on the card. In the In silico column of a variant card there is a coloured dot for each prediction, in seqr's six steps: green and olive benign, grey undecided, yellow, red and dark red pathogenic (supporting, moderate, strong).

  • CADD, REVEL, AlphaMissense, SIFT and PolyPhen are coloured on seqr's boundaries, which rest on ClinGen's calibration for PP3/BP4; a value on a boundary belongs to the step above. Those of REVEL coincide, to three decimals, with the evaluator's REVEL thresholds. AlphaMissense without a score is coloured by its class, as the evaluator reads it.
  • SpliceAI is coloured according to the evaluator's constants (below 0.1 benign, from 0.2 supporting, from 0.5 moderate), so that the dot and the proposed PP3/BP4/BP7 never contradict each other; seqr reads 0.5 and 0.8.
  • pLI and missense Z describe the gene and get no dot.

The dot is a display: the evaluator does not compute with it. The ACMG classify dialog shows the same dots by the in-silico scores on its evidence card. Code: frontend/src/pages/families/inSilicoTones.ts and PredictorMark.tsx.

Criteria that never apply together. Some criteria, taken together, would count one piece of evidence twice or read it in two directions. If the analyst ticks one, the dialog switches the other off; the server refuses a classification that applies both. The pairs, with their reason in the tooltip:

  • PS2/PM6: one de novo observation is either confirmed or assumed (ClinGen SVI);
  • PVS1/PP3: in-silico predictions add nothing to a predicted null allele;
  • PVS1/PM4: the length change of a null allele already counts in PVS1;
  • PS1/PM5, PS3/BS3, BA1/BS1, BA1/PM2, BS1/PM2, PM4/BP3, PP2/BP1, PP3/BP4 and PP5/BP6.

If the evaluator would tick both, it keeps the first-named, unless the other gives more points; a stored criterion takes precedence over a new proposal. PP1 and BS4 may go together (they can come from different family members), as may PP4 and a de novo criterion, even though the de novo points read the same phenotype.

PM1 and PP3 together count at most strong (4 points; ClinGen SVI, Pejaver et al. 2022), because a hotspot or critical domain and the in-silico predictors read overlapping evidence. Ticking one or making it stronger lowers the other to the strongest strength that still fits, or unticks it (⊘) if none fits: PM1 moderate brings PP3 strong down to moderate, PM1 strong leaves no room for PP3. Each on its own keeps its strength. The server refuses a save above the cap.

Code: EXCLUSIVE_CRITERIA and CAPPED_CRITERIA in frontend/src/lib/acmg/criteria.ts and backend/app/services/acmg_points.py.

Where in the code: frontend/src/lib/acmg/evaluate.ts (the evaluator, with the de novo points), pedigree.ts (the parents from the pedigree, their relatedness from the Sample QC) and criteria.ts (the catalogue of the 28 criteria and the pairs that never apply together); the ClinVar reading in frontend/src/lib/clinvar.ts; fetching the context in frontend/src/pages/families/AcmgClassificationModal.tsx.

The points scale and the five classes

CoGA uses the Bayesian points system of Tavtigian and ClinGen. Each accepted criterion counts points according to its strength; benign criteria count negatively.

Strength Pathogenic Benign
Supporting +1 −1
Moderate +2 −2
Strong +4 −4
Very strong +8 —

The total gives the class: ≥ 10 pathogenic (class 5), 6 to 9 likely pathogenic (4), 0 to 5 VUS (3), −1 to −6 likely benign (2), ≤ −7 benign (1). An accepted BA1 makes the variant benign, regardless of the rest. A VUS also gets a level according to its distance from the class 4 boundary: 4–5 hot, 2–3 warm, 0–1 cold.

The dialog shows the total on a bar following the Bayesian reading of the scale (prior probability 10%, odds of pathogenicity 350^(points/8)). Each VUS point has its own box, the ticks carry the posterior probability (0.1%, 10%, 18.8%, 32.5%, 50%, 67.5%, 81.2%, 90% and 99%), and the class boundaries are marked more strongly. The bar is only a display; the class follows from the thresholds above (frontend/src/pages/families/AcmgScaleBar.tsx).

The server always recalculates. The frontend sends its own total along, but the backend ignores it. It checks every criterion and refuses (400):

  • an unknown code or strength;
  • a criterion that occurs twice;
  • a strength the criterion does not allow;
  • two accepted criteria that never apply together (EXCLUSIVE_CRITERIA);
  • PM1 and PP3 together above 4 points (CAPPED_CRITERIA).

Each criterion therefore counts once, at a strength the dialog offers for it. Otherwise a PVS1 sent twice would count +16 (pathogenic), and BS1 at very strong −8. The backend then recalculates class, total and VUS level. A stored classification therefore never depends on the browser. Only the save is checked: a classification saved earlier is read as it was written. Frontend and backend use the same thresholds, and both sides are tested against those thresholds. The dialog also writes the class back as a tag (acmg_class_N, and for a VUS acmg_vus_<level>), so that cards and summaries show it.

Allowed strengths. The pathogenic criteria allow very strong to supporting, except PM2 (moderate or supporting). BA1 is stand-alone only, and stand-alone is only for BA1. BS1 to BS4 and BP4 allow strong to supporting, the other BP criteria moderate or supporting. The list exists twice: as allowedStrengths in frontend/src/lib/acmg/criteria.ts (the choices in the dialog) and as ALLOWED_STRENGTHS in acmg_points.py (the check on the server). backend/tests/test_acmg_frontend_parity.py reads criteria.ts and fails if the two differ.

Where in the code: frontend/src/lib/acmg/score.ts and backend/app/services/acmg_points.py; the check and the recalculation in backend/app/services/small_variant_review_acmg.py.

Mitochondrial variants

A variant from the mtDNA analysis goes to a separate evaluator following the ClinGen specifications for mtDNA (McCormick 2020). mtDNA is inherited through the mother and is haploid. Hence: no de novo rules, stricter frequency thresholds, PVS1 only in protein-coding loci, no in-silico predictors, and segregation through the maternal line and the heteroplasmy. With gnomAD-MT or HelixMTdb in the annotation, BA1 and BS1 read the highest homoplasmic population frequency; PM2 is applied only if the heteroplasmic one is also below 0.002%, otherwise consider. Where two mtDNA genes overlap (MT-ATP8/MT-ATP6, MT-ND4L/MT-ND4), the card shows the consequence per gene. The maternal line starts at the mother the pedigree links to the proband; PP1 requires that she carries the variant. The points scale and the classes are the same.

Where in the code: frontend/src/lib/acmg/evaluateMito.ts.

Part 3 — ACMG for CNVs

Copy-number variants are classified according to the 2019 ClinGen CNV standard (Riggs et al., 2020), a different points system:

  • The evidence sections and weights differ between loss (deletion) and gain (duplication): there are two catalogues.
  • Points are continuous (e.g. +0.90 or −0.60). Many criteria have an allowed range within which the reviewer picks a value.
  • The classes: ≥ 0.99 pathogenic, 0.90 to 0.98 likely pathogenic, −0.89 to 0.89 VUS, −0.98 to −0.90 likely benign, ≤ −0.99 benign.

The evaluator is cautious. It proposes only on the basis of what the SV reliably carries: overlapping genes, gene constraint, annotated inheritance and the number of genes. As with small variants, the server caps and recalculates: it keeps every value within the range of its criterion before adding up. A criterion that occurs twice is refused (400). Otherwise it would count twice, beyond its range: 2B at 0.90 twice would give 1.80, pathogenic instead of likely pathogenic. The catalogues are in the frontend and in cnv_acmg_points.py; test_acmg_frontend_parity.py fails if their codes, sections or ranges differ. Unlike for small variants, there is no analogue of BA1.

Separate proposals per kind. The dialog keeps a separate form for loss and for gain. Each gets the proposals the evaluator computes for that kind: the section 3 ladder according to that kind's thresholds, and 2H (from the pLI) only for loss. Switching kind therefore never brings in the criteria, points or notes of the other kind. A manual change stays with the kind in which it was made, and is still there after switching back. Only the kind shown is saved.

Where in the code: frontend/src/lib/cnvAcmg/ (catalogues, evaluator, score) and frontend/src/pages/families/CnvAcmgClassificationModal.tsx; backend/app/services/cnv_acmg_points.py and structural_variant_review_pg.py.

Part 4 — Storage and the frozen evidence

The full assessment per criterion is stored as JSON. The recalculated total and the class are stored next to it, for filters and summaries: acmg, acmg_point_total and acmg_class on small_variant_reviews, and cnv_acmg, cnv_point_total and cnv_class on structural_variant_reviews. That makes it possible to see afterwards which criteria were applied with which strength and which evidence.

The evidence snapshot. When a small variant is classified, CoGA freezes the evidence in acmg_evidence_snapshot: the annotation version, the hash of the annotation set (which changes as soon as any annotation changes), the ClinVar value and the time. In addition, the consequence, population frequencies and in-silico scores the classification rests on, as the ACMG dialog reads them: from the variant's primary transcript (MANE Select, then canonical, then the most severe impact; its id is in transcript_id), through the same helper functions as the variant list (small_variant_evidence). Per group:

  • consequence: the consequence term(s) (effect) that the criteria read for a null, missense, synonymous or length-changing variant (PVS1, PM4, PP2, BP7 and the criteria a consequence excludes); the impact; LOFTEE's loss-of-function call (lof), on which the strength of PVS1 depends, with LOFTEE's flags (lof_flags) and VEP's NMD prediction (nmd), which make PVS1 consider. Only for a multiallelic record (ALT G,T) also the ALT allele these values belong to (alt_allele).
  • frequencies: the gnomAD allele frequency the frequency criteria read; the gnomAD datasets the callset was annotated with (gnomad_annotated), which say whether a variant without a frequency is absent from gnomAD (PM2); the exome, genome, gnomAD popmax, VEP MAX_AF (max_af) and TOPMed frequencies and the gnomAD counts (alleles, homozygotes, hemizygotes) the filters read; gnomAD's FAF95 (gnomad_faf95_af), which BA1 and BS1 read; only for a chrM variant the homoplasmic and heteroplasmic frequencies of gnomAD-MT and HelixMTdb. Next to the ClinVar classification, also the review status of that ClinVar record (clinvar_review_status).
  • in_silico: CADD, REVEL, SpliceAI, SIFT, PolyPhen and the AlphaMissense class and score.
  • gene_constraint, only for a missense variant: the gene's gnomAD missense Z (gene_missense_z) that PP2 reads, and where it came from (gene_missense_z_source).

A missense variant has missense_variant in its consequence; that is how the dialog recognises one for PP2 (reads_gene_missense_z). For every other variant PP2 reads no missense Z: the group is absent and the gene profile is not read (the owner's decision, 2026-10-20). The missense Z comes from:

  1. The gene profile (gene_info), not the variant's annotation. PP2 reads this first, with the variant list's lookup (fetch_gene_constraint_metrics): in the gene profiles of the family's assembly, for the gene the variant is shown with. That is the gene id of the primary transcript, otherwise its symbol (in upper or lower case), otherwise the variant's first gene.
  2. The VCF, if the gene profile has no missense Z: the VCF's own MISSENSE_Z (pp2_gene_missense_z, the owner's decision of 2026-10-28). The import stores it as gene_missense_z in the annotation of the primary transcript. The variant card shows it under Other scores & annotations as Missense Z (gnomAD, from the VCF).

The source is gene_profile or vcf. If neither has a value, the source and the value are null.

Every field is frozen, even without a value (null), so that a value that appears later counts as a change. A value JSONB cannot hold (NaN, infinity) becomes null.

Every change to a review, of a small variant, an SV or a CNV, writes a before-and-after row, in the same transaction, to the append-only, hash-chained clinical audit trail (chapter 11): who, when and what changed (class, criteria, tags, note). The row for the class holds the whole stored record: per criterion the strength (for a CNV the points), whether it is accepted, the evidence and whether it was an automatic suggestion, with the points total (and for a CNV the kind). Every change to it goes into the trail, even if the class stays the same; an unchanged re-save writes nothing. Clearing or deleting a review is also recorded, and the review of a compound heterozygous pair gets a row of its own (action compound_het_pair, chapter 11).

The evidence snapshot of a CNV. An SV has no annotation-set hash in ClickHouse. When a CNV classification is saved, CoGA therefore freezes in cnv_evidence_snapshot (on structural_variant_reviews):

  • the values the CNV evaluator reads: the type, the overlapping genes and their number, the pLI and the annotated inheritance;
  • the event itself: the caller, the chromosome, the start, the end, the length and the breakpoint partner;
  • a hash of the SV's full annotation, and the time;
  • the versions the evidence comes from: that of the SV callset in the annotation manifest of the analysis whose call it is, the reference assembly and the gene loci.

The evaluator does not read clinical CNVs, dosage scores or DGV; the analyst scores those criteria themselves. The genotypes are not in the snapshot. The drift key is evidence_hash, a SHA-256 over the evidence; the versions are recorded, not compared. The server refuses a CNV classification of an SV that is not in the family's data (404). If the family has no assembly, there is no SV store to read, and the classification is stored without a snapshot.

Which row is frozen. Several callers can call the same event under one SV id (the id of an uploaded SV names no caller, and that of a NeedlR SV has the same form). They then share one review, but each caller has its own row on the SV page, with its own genes, pLI and inheritance. The snapshot therefore comes from the row of the caller on which the classification was made: the CNV dialog sends that caller along in source.

  • If the save names no caller, CoGA takes the SV's only row.
  • If several callers then call the SV, it cannot be told on which row the classification was made. The server then refuses (422) instead of freezing another caller's evidence. (On this route 409 already means that someone else saved the review in the meantime.)
  • A caller that does not call the SV gives 404.

The snapshot names the caller it comes from (evidence.source) and holds that caller's genes, pLI and inheritance; the drift check compares it with that caller's row.

Where in the code: build_evidence_snapshot in backend/app/services/small_variant_review_acmg.py; build_structural_evidence_snapshot and fetch_structural_variant_records in backend/app/services/structural_variant_evidence.py, the frozen row in _classified_row (structural_variant_review_pg.py); the audit trail in backend/app/services/clinical_audit_service.py (record_review_changes for small variants, record_structural_review_changes for SVs and CNVs, record_compound_het_pair_changes for a pair).

Part 5 — Classification drift

Annotations change: a new ClinVar or gnomAD release can shift the evidence under a classification, a re-import the genes under a CNV. That is why CoGA compares, for each classified small variant and for each SV or CNV with a CNV classification, the frozen snapshot with the current data, using the same function that built the snapshot:

Status Meaning
current Unchanged (the hashes and every frozen value are equal)
drifted The evidence changed since the classification
variant_missing The variant is no longer in the data
unknown Nothing has visibly shifted, but one of the two hashes is missing, or the frozen evidence cannot be read; the link cannot be checked

If a hash is missing, the check does not report current but unknown; at sign-out unknown counts as drift. A stored snapshot that is not a JSON object (the writer never stores one) is compared as a snapshot that froze nothing. It therefore also reports unknown (or variant_missing). A drift must be re-reviewed, or acknowledged with a reason, before a report can be signed out (chapter 11). Whoever saves the classification again freezes the evidence as it currently is.

For a small variant, drifted also says what shifted (changed):

  • the ClinVar value (clinvar);
  • the primary transcript (transcript_id);
  • every frozen consequence, frequency or in-silico score, by its name (effect, impact, lof, gnomad_af, revel, …);
  • the gene's missense Z (gene_missense_z);
  • its source (gene_missense_z_source), if PP2 now reads the missense Z from the other source because the gene profile gained or lost one (gnomAD missense Z 4.20 (VCF) → 3.52 (gene profile));
  • annotations, if the hash changed.

evidence_from and evidence_to give the transcript, the consequence, the frequencies, the scores and the missense Z with its source, as frozen and as they currently are. Rules:

  • A frozen value that shifted is drift, even under the same hash.
  • The missense Z of a missense variant does not fall under that hash: a refresh of the gene profiles can shift it while the hash stays the same. A classification of another variant (e.g. a stop codon) froze none, and as a result never shifts.
  • The check compares every value the snapshot froze, and numbers by their value (JSONB stores the digits of a number, not whether it was an integer).
  • The current values are read as a classification saved at that moment would freeze them. A variant that was classified as a missense variant and no longer is one names its consequence and its missense Z as gone (gnomAD missense Z 2.95 → n/a).
  • The missense Z of the family's missense variants is read in one query.

For an SV or CNV, the check compares the snapshot with the row of the caller from which it was frozen (evidence.source): the evidence as a whole, by its hash. Another caller's call is different evidence, not a change to this evidence.

  • drifted also says what shifted (changed): the genes, the pLI, the inheritance, the type, the position or the remaining annotation, with the value before and after.
  • variant_missing means that that caller's call is no longer in the data, even if another caller still calls the SV. The drift banner and the signed version name that caller (its needlr call is no longer present).
  • Frozen evidence that names no caller counts as unknown.

The check compares only the fields the snapshot froze, and reads the SV as the SV page reads it. The header of the CNV dialog names the caller of the row on which it was opened; the SV table shows the Source column by default.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/classification_drift_service.py (the status logic in _diff; for SVs and CNVs evaluate_structural_classification_drift, with fetch_structural_variant_records, frozen_evidence_source and diff_structural_evidence from structural_variant_evidence.py).

Key files

File Role

frontend/src/lib/acmg/ Catalogue, evaluator (mtDNA included) and points scale
frontend/src/lib/cnvAcmg/ CNV catalogues, evaluator and points scale
frontend/src/pages/families/AcmgClassificationModal.tsx · CnvAcmgClassificationModal.tsx The classification dialogs

backend/app/services/small_variant_review_pg.py · small_variant_review_acmg.py Saving reviews, checking ACMG, the evidence snapshot
backend/app/services/structural_variant_review_pg.py CNV/SV reviews and CNV ACMG

11. Report & full traceability

This chapter brings everything together. A case is signed out into a frozen, versioned and hashed snapshot of the report, bound to the software, annotation and reference versions that made it. That is the analytical sign-out, by a user with the role supervisor or higher: it closes the analysis and freezes it. The medical sign-off does not happen in CoGA: the clinical report is drafted and medically signed in the EPD (the hospital's electronic patient record) and refers 1:1 to the frozen analysis.

It covers the gates that must be met first, the append-only, hash-chained audit trail and the external integrity anchors. The common thread is the full chain: from the raw file with its hash, via the annotation manifest and the variant, to the signed analysis that the clinical report in the EPD refers to.

What the user sees on the report page (the colours of the sign-out record, the messages when a request fails) is in the app: Docs → Report traceability & sign-out (frontend/src/content/docs/clinical-traceability.md). The design is in docs/clinical-traceability.md, the risks and requirements in the technical file (TF-06, TF-09b).

A few terms:

  • Snapshot: a frozen JSON object that records what applied at that moment.
  • Hash: a short, fixed fingerprint (SHA-256) of data. If one character changes, the hash changes completely; that is how tampering becomes visible.
  • Append-only: only add, never change or delete. The database enforces this with a trigger (database code that runs before every change and can refuse it).

The report

There are two report pages:

  • FamilyReportPage.tsx — the family report. The live report shows the variants with the review tag report (small and structural variants), with for each reported gene the gene profile and the family's HPO terms. Repeat loci and Paraphase regions with report are in the section Reported repeat expansions and Paraphase findings (ReportedFindings.tsx, from the tables of the repeat and Paraphase page). The report requests up to 10,000 reported variants per kind, the API's maximum. If a list is incomplete (more reported variants than that page holds, or a capped search), it says so on screen and on the printout (reportedListCompleteness.ts). The signed snapshot reads the reported reviews directly from Postgres and has no such limit. The report's sentences are built by reportNarrative.ts, tested separately. SignedFamilyReport.tsx renders a signed version from the frozen snapshot (see below).
  • FamilyNiptReportPage.tsx — the report for the monogenic NIPT of one pregnancy: the fetal fraction, the quality checks (fetal sex, paternity, the plasma sample), the coverage, the candidate variants and, for a multiple pregnancy, the note about it (chapter 8).

The family is signed out, a PGT family with its embryo calls and a NIPT family with its NIPT results (the owner's decisions of 2026-10-14). For a PGT family, signing out the family report freezes the embryo calls (pgt_analysis): the same object that the backend derives from the stored haplotype blocks and the family page shows (chapter 8; see The embryo calls below).

A monogenic NIPT family uses the same sign-out:

  • It is signed out from the NIPT report (Sign out NIPT analysis) or the family report, not from the NIPT page itself; if the family holds other analyses too, only from the NIPT report, which signs out its pregnancy's monogenic NIPT (see One sign-out per analysis). There is one signed record per analysis, with the same gates, version and report code.
  • Its record also contains the section nipt (signed_record_nipt.py, see below): its pregnancy's NIPT analysis as the NIPT page showed it, computed by the backend.
  • The sample-QC checks stay in sample_qc: paternity, the fetal sex from the father's X alleles, the category pattern of the cfDNA and the sex of the parents.
  • A reported NIPT variant is in reported_variants and variant_descriptions, like every reported small variant, and in nipt with its category, reads and probabilities.
  • The NIPT report names the latest signed version with its report code, and says whether the data still match it.
  • It shares the button, the gate dialogs (reportSignOut.tsx) and the rule that says when the button is not offered (signOutRefusal) with the family report. Anyone who may not sign out sees the button disabled on both pages, with the reason (see Who may sign out).

A family with ccnv output (conventional NIPT) uses the same sign-out:

  • It is signed out from the family report, which shows the live cNIPT result above the reported findings (Conventional NIPT result).
  • Its record also contains the section cnipt (signed_record_cnipt.py): the result per maternal plasma as the cNIPT page shows it (for each target whether the validated claim covers it, claimed), with the bounds it applied and the inputs it read.

What each variant section contains is described in docs/report-template.md. Exporting is done with the browser's print function.

Both pages carry a disclaimer: the report is decision support that a qualified clinical scientist must confirm. The NIPT report also asks for confirmation with an invasive diagnostic test.

Both pages carry the warnings of every family page in their header, on the printout too:

  • Not validated for clinical use for a family outside the validated scope (gate 0);
  • Import incomplete as long as an import or a single-file upload left the family partly loaded or did not finish (gate 3);
  • Package folder changed after import (or Package folder gone), one per analysis, as long as the package folder that analysis's data were imported from has changed since the import or is gone (gate 3b); Source files archived if a superuser confirmed that missing folder as deliberately archived.

The NIPT report is a live report that is printed without a gate; with incomplete data the printout says so itself. Like the live family report, it says that it is not the signed version: on screen next to the latest signed version, and at the top of every printout (Draft …, Not the signed report …, Not verified …; liveReportSignedState and liveReportSignedNotice in signedReportRecord.ts, for both pages).

Both pages end with a footer: when the report was made and with which build (Software: CoGA x.y.z (commit), from GET /api/version). A build that is not a release gets dev added to its version, e.g. CoGA 0.1.0-dev (commit). Then follows the label: in-house IVD under IVDR Article 5(5), not CE-marked, for internal use at CMGG only, and the manufacturer.

  • The report requests the build every time it opens and shows no stored value: after an update the footer never names the previous build.
  • If the request fails, the footer says so, and a printout starts with the message that it is incomplete.
  • A signed version names two builds: Signed with, the build that froze it, and Rendered by, the build that drew the page from the record.
  • The same version and the same label are in the footer of every page of the app.

Where in the code: useReportBuild in frontend/src/lib/appVersion.ts, frontend/src/pages/families/ReportSoftwareIdentity.tsx, and the text of the label in frontend/src/lib/deviceLabel.ts.

Besides the variants, the family report shows three provenance elements, each with its own endpoint in backend/app/routers/families_reports.py:

Element Shows Endpoint
