12. HPO, Monarch & variant prioritisation

This chapter describes how CoGA turns a patient's phenotype (the observed clinical features) into help for the analyst: a list of candidate genes and a ranking of the variants. The chain runs from the HPO terminology, through the knowledge base of the Monarch Initiative and semantic similarity, to variant prioritisation. The ranking cache keeps that fast and reproducible. An explanation for users is in the app (Docs → Phenotype matching with Monarch, frontend/src/content/docs/monarch-integration.md); the design is in docs/monarch-integration.md and docs/variant-ranking-cache.md.

A few terms:

  • HPO (Human Phenotype Ontology): a standardised, hierarchical list of clinical features. Each feature has a fixed code, such as HP:0001250 (seizure). The terms are related as parent and child: a specific term is a subtype of a more general one.
  • CURIE: a short identifier with a prefix, e.g. HP:0001250 (phenotype), MONDO:0007739 (disease), HGNC:1100 (gene). CoGA uses the same identifiers as the sources.
  • Phenotype score: a number between 0 and 1: how well does a gene's phenotype profile fit the patient's features?

HPO: the dictionary of phenotypes

The ontology is in four Postgres tables:

  • hpo_term: one row per term, with the release;
  • hpo_synonym: synonyms, for searching on free text;
  • hpo_edge: the parent-child relations;
  • hpo_closure: per term all its ancestors with their distance. That way "does the patient have this term or a more specific subtype?" is one fast query.

The table individual_hpo links phenotypes to a family member, with the status present, absent or unknown. Only present counts for the prioritisation.

Loading and versions. With an empty database the backend downloads the newest HPO release from the release's own fixed PURL and loads it, if the file states that release. If that fails, it loads the fallback: the file fixed in the repository (data/ref-data/hpo/hp.obo), only with that file's SHA-256; it refuses any other. The sources and the SHA-256 of the fallback are fixed in the code, not in a setting (chapter 4). The release is read from the file itself and stored with each term. That way an analysis can later be traced back to the ontology version that applied.

Search and administration. Analysts search for terms through GET /api/hpo/search: first exact match, then start of the label, then label and synonym. The administration page (HpoTerminologyAdminPage.tsx) shows the number of terms and the loaded release, and reports a newer HPO release (GET /api/admin/hpo/release-check, from HPO's latest GitHub release). A new release comes from a file on the server or from the release's own fixed PURL (https://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/hp/releases/<date>/hp.obo); a downloaded file must state that release. Nothing is read in without an administrator, because a new release changes the phenotype matching. The administrator first looks at a preview (how many terms are new, changed or gone) and only then applies it. Only the page enforces that order: it allows applying only after a successful preview of exactly the same file and sends along the SHA-256 from that preview, so that the backend reads in only those bytes. The endpoint POST /api/admin/hpo/sync itself also accepts an immediate application (preview_only: false).

The release is the one that the file itself states (its data-version). The terms keep the SHA-256 of the bytes read in (metadata.release_sha256); the administration page, the loaded release and every signed record name it. Expected release and Expected release date are what the administrator expects. If the file states a different release, or none, the sync refuses (400) and nothing is read in.

Security.

  • Searching and reading require a login; importing and synchronising require an administrator.
  • Adding, changing and deleting a family's phenotypes is allowed for an analyst of the family's project with the role analyst or higher, a superuser or an administrator; not for a reader and not for a viewer (chapter 2).
  • Every change goes into the clinical audit trail (chapter 11). So does a change made by a package import: per member, in the name of whoever started the import.
  • The file path in a sync request must lie within a permitted folder. That way a request cannot have an arbitrary file on the server read in.
  • A phenotype cannot point to an unknown term (the reference to hpo_term is enforced). An import skips unknown terms and reports them.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/hpo_service.py; backend/app/routers/hpo.py and the HPO endpoints in backend/app/routers/admin.py; the tables in 02_reference.sql and 03_assay.sql.

Monarch: connecting genes, diseases and phenotypes

The Monarch Initiative brings dozens of sources (OMIM, Orphanet, ClinGen, HPO annotations, …) together in one knowledge graph with fixed identifiers. CoGA uses two kinds of links, each in a table of its own:

  • gene → disease (monarch_gene_disease: HGNC → MONDO, with the relations, the sources and whether there is a causal relation);
  • disease → phenotype (monarch_disease_phenotype: MONDO → HPO, with a mark for a phenotype that explicitly does not occur with the disease).

Through the shared disease, gene → phenotype follows from these.

Loading. CoGA downloads small, pre-split files from Monarch, not the whole knowledge graph. It replaces both tables in one transaction, so that they are never on different releases. If the release cannot be determined, CoGA refuses to load: the provenance of the data behind a signed report must never be empty. A start on a database without Monarch data loads the newest release (ensure_monarch_on_startup, REFERENCE_BOOTSTRAP_MONARCH; decision of the owner, 2026-11-05). If that fails, the backend logs a warning and the start continues; the next start or the administration page tries again. The start does not build the Mendeliome panel, because a panel is created by an account: that happens on the Gene panels page. The administration page (MonarchDataAdminPage.tsx) shows the loaded release and the table sizes, refreshes the data and searches by disease or phenotype. All Monarch administration is for administrators only. After a new release the Mendeliome panel is also rebuilt (chapter 15).

Where in the code: backend/app/services/monarch_ingest.py; the endpoints /api/admin/monarch/... in backend/app/routers/admin.py.

Semantic similarity

A patient rarely has exactly the terms from the textbook. Semantic similarity therefore measures how closely a gene's phenotype profile resembles what we see in the patient. A specific shared feature weighs more than a general one. That weight is the information content of a term: the more rarely the term (or a subtype of it) occurs with diseases, the higher it is. "Intellectual disability" occurs with very many diseases and says little. "Congenital hypothyroidism" is rare and makes a gene that explains it stand out. One broad term therefore gives a flat, almost arbitrary ranking.

CoGA computes similarity in two ways:

  1. Live through Monarch (monarch_semsim.py), for the panel of candidate genes on the family page. CoGA sends only the HPO terms (no identity) to Monarch's public API and gets the best-matching genes back. The result is cached briefly; if Monarch cannot be reached, the UI says so.
  2. Locally (monarch_phenotype_score.py), for variant prioritisation. There every gene with a candidate variant must get a score, not only the best ones. The method (Resnik, best-match average) computes the information content from the local Monarch tables. The selection of terms does not depend on their order: the same input always gives the same score.

Variant prioritisation

The scoring is in backend/app/services/variant_prioritization.py: a pure function, without database or network. That makes testing and repeating simple. It follows the Exomiser model and combines four partial scores:

Partial score Measures
Pathogenicity Predicted harmfulness: impact and loss of function, ClinVar, the predictors (CADD, REVEL, SpliceAI, AlphaMissense) and gene constraint. A structural variant does not have those predictors: it scores on the kind of event, the number of genes hit and the gene constraint. A copy loss scores as a deletion, in a gene with a pLI of 0.9 or more as haploinsufficient: a DEL, including DEL:ME, or a CNV whose stored copy number shows a loss (the same rule as for the second hit, chapter 8, in sv_copy_change.py). A copy gain scores as a duplication: a DUP, including DUP:TANDEM, or a CNV that shows a gain
Frequency Rarity in gnomAD: the rarer, the higher
Segregation The inheritance pattern in the pedigree (de novo, homozygous recessive, compound heterozygous, X-linked, dominant). For a son, on X or Y outside the pseudo-autosomal regions, the de novo weight follows the parent who passes on that chromosome (chapter 8). A structural variant carries NeedlR's Inheritance annotation for the query sample. De novo counts as de novo. An inherited SV counts as dominant only if the child and the parent it comes from (maternal: the mother, paternal: the father) are affected; otherwise it does not count
Phenotype How well the gene fits the clinical picture

The first three together form the variant score. The final score is a weighted combination of the variant score and the phenotype score. Two choices safeguard clinical reliability:

  • ClinVar comes first. Only a pathogenic ClinVar assertion gives the full pathogenicity score; evidence from predictors alone stays below it. "Conflicting interpretations of pathogenicity" does not count as pathogenic.
  • New candidate genes do not disappear. A gene without Monarch data scores 0 on phenotype, but the variant score stays visible separately in the breakdown of the score (Variant). By default the ranking follows the combined score, with the variant score as second key. With rank_by=variant_score (in the UI: Rank by → Variant score in the filters under Phenotype) it follows the variant score, with the combined score as second key: a strong variant in a gene without phenotype data then comes to the top. The scores stay the same; only the order and the rank change, across the whole ranking and not only the page shown. The cache keeps the combined order; the other order is applied to the ranking when it is served. The response names its order in ranked_by, and the CSV export of a ranked search writes both scores and the rank.

Prioritisation runs at GET /api/families/{family_id}/small-variants?prioritize=true. The page turns this on by default; in the API itself it is off by default. The service fetches the filtered candidates, determines the segregation and the phenotype scores, ranks, and returns a score block per variant. The candidate set is bounded. If it overflows, the response reports the real count, and the UI says that the ranking is incomplete and that the filters must be refined. The scores rank within one family; they are not calibrated probabilities.

Prioritisation changes the order, not what a search finds. That holds for an inheritance model that pairs variants (compound het, recessive) and for carrier screening. A ranked search then keeps exactly what the same search without prioritisation keeps: the same rules on the same candidates (the pairs, with their phase; the homozygous and X-linked variants, as a flag from the SQL; the couple's gene rule, chapter 8). Only those variants are ranked, with the segregation they have among themselves.

  • A pair stays a pair and stands at the place of its best-ranked variant. If it shares that variant with another item, the next variant decides.
  • Each variant shows its own rank.
  • Such a search reads one window of 5,000 candidates, the largest that the search without prioritisation reads. If it overflows, the ranking and the candidates are both bounded (ranking_truncated and candidates_capped). The count is then what was found within the window: a lower bound.

Where in the code: variant_prioritization.py; the prioritisation in clickhouse_family_variants.py; the score breakdown in the review dialog.

The ranking cache

Prioritising takes a few seconds, mainly because of the per-gene scoring. The outcome is deterministic: the same input gives the same outcome. That is why CoGA keeps the ranked order in the Postgres table family_variant_ranking_cache: only the order and the score per variant, never the annotation or the review state. Those are fetched fresh at every view. That way a cached ranking never shows an outdated annotation or review status.

Each cache row is tied to a SHA-256 over everything that can change the ranking:

Input Changes when …
The filters (without pagination), including the inheritance model and the carrier screening the analyst changes a filter
The gene panel and its version the panel is updated
The genes and regions that the panel filter applied (a digest; the regions contain the loci of each gene from the gene reference) the panel gets other genes or regions, or a reloaded gene reference moves one of its genes
The regions to which the search was restricted or which it excluded (the intervals and the loci of the excluded genes), and the excluded genes the analyst changes those filters, or a reloaded gene reference moves one of those genes
The HPO terms of the affected members a phenotype is added or removed
The pedigree, the affected status and the sex of each member (including the couple of a carrier screening) the family structure changes
The version of the family's variant data something changes in the variants: import, upload, deletion by an administrator or restore
The review selections in the filters a tag or review that the filter touches changes
The Monarch release, the HPO release and the time of the last gene constraint update the reference data is refreshed
The assembly and the version of the algorithm the scoring code changes, or which variants a filter keeps

If one input changes, the hash changes: the cache misses and the ranking is recomputed. An exact hit is therefore never a ranking on different input. The loci of a gene come from the gene reference at every search, not from a version. That is why what the search applied counts, and not only the version of the panel.

A narrower panel can be served from a broader ranking of the same family (the Mendeliome covers its sub-panels), but only if:

  • that ranking is complete;
  • its panel still contains exactly the genes and regions on which it was computed. Each cache row records them (provenance.panel_members). After all, the narrower panel can only leave out variants from the broader ranking, never add them. A ranking from before a gene was added to its panel misses the variants of that gene and therefore serves no panel. A row whose panel has been deleted is not used either;
  • it contains every variant that the narrower panel reaches, with the segregation that variant has within that panel. CoGA therefore fetches those variants first.

Each panel is compared by gene and by position, the Mendeliome included (the owner's decision of 14 October 2026). The Mendeliome ranking therefore also contains a variant that the smaller panel reaches through a gene's locus, e.g. because the annotation names the gene differently from the gene reference. Two cases can make the last condition fail; the narrower panel is then computed directly:

  • It reaches a variant only through a region of its own that the broader panel does not have: coordinates that PanelApp gave for a gene, or a locus that was stored when the panel was created. The broader ranking can miss that variant.
  • It leaves out the partner of a compound heterozygous pair. Within that panel it is then not a pair: the variant loses that mode of inheritance, and with it part of its segregation weight and score, unless another mode weighs as much.

A panel that comes from a broader ranking gets its own rank numbers, starting from 1. That way it always shows what a direct computation of that panel gives.

A search with pairs or carrier screening first fetches its candidates and determines its pairs within its own scope, even on an exact hit. The cache keeps the order of the variants, not the pairs. That order is only used if it contains every variant found, with the same segregation.

After a change to phenotypes or pedigree, the backend recomputes the last ranking in advance, so that the next opening is fast. In doing so it does not apply that search's intervals and its excluded genes and intervals: a search with such filters is recomputed at the next opening. The UI reports whether the ranking comes from the cache or was computed.

Looking up a panel. CoGA does not read again at every search what a panel filter applies: the panel's genes, its stored regions for the family's assembly, and the loci of its genes in that assembly's gene reference. Each process keeps that, with its digest, per panel and assembly. It uses it only as long as its fingerprint is unchanged. CoGA reads that fingerprint at every use: the panel's version, a SHA-256 of its gene rows and of its region rows for the assembly, and the imports of the gene reference for the assembly. The panel is therefore read again after every change to the panel, by whatever route, and after every new load of the gene reference (each import registers itself in the transaction that writes its rows). A lookup is kept only if the fingerprint after reading is still the same as before.

Why: for the Mendeliome (5,300 genes and, with one row per transcript, some 40,000 loci) the lookup at every search would cost more than computing a small sub-panel, even on an exact hit of the default view and on the check that serves a sub-panel from the Mendeliome ranking. This way such a sub-panel costs about what its own computation costs. A row of genes that is written into the database outside the import is seen by a kept lookup only after the next import of the gene reference or a restart.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/variant_ranking_cache.py; the lookup of a panel in backend/app/services/clickhouse_family_variants.py (_fetch_panel_constraints); the design note docs/variant-ranking-cache.md.

Candidate genes on the family page

The panel MonarchPhenotypeMatchPanel.tsx calls Monarch only after a click on Find candidate genes (GET /api/families/{family_id}/phenotype-match). That way the external service is not called at every page load. Every click, including one on Re-run match, asks the question again, with the terms of that moment. The backend reuses Monarch's response for the same terms for one hour (monarch_semsim.py). During a query the panel shows no previous result; a failed query appears as an error with the reason.

The endpoint collects the present terms of the family (or of one member) and enriches each gene found:

  • Does the gene exist in CoGA? Then the UI links to the gene profile (chapter 13).
  • Which of the gene's phenotypes does the family have, and which not? The ontology counts: a general gene phenotype also counts if the patient has a more specific subtype.

The score of one gene. For a variant that no ranking scored, the ACMG dialog reads the phenotype score of its gene at GET /api/families/{family_id}/gene-phenotype-score?symbol= (family_gene_phenotype_score in clickhouse_family_variants.py). That is the score the ranking gives the gene: the same present terms of the affected members, the same local scoring. If the family has no terms or the gene has no Monarch phenotypes, the score is empty ("not assessed"), never 0. PP4 and the phenotype step of the de novo criteria (PS2, PM6) read that score (chapter 10).

Safety and traceability

  • Deterministic. The same input always gives the same ranking: a precondition for an auditable, repeatable result.
  • Bound to versions. The cache key contains the Monarch, HPO and panel versions and the genes and regions that the search applied. HPO terms carry their release. Monarch refuses to load without a known version.
  • Recompute rather than trust. Every relevant change changes the hash, and when in doubt the code recomputes.
  • Access. Phenotype matching requires a login; loading and refreshing HPO and Monarch data require an administrator.

13. Gene Explorer & version control

This chapter describes the gene profile: from a gene symbol (e.g. BRCA1) to a page with transcripts, constraint metrics (measures of how sensitive a gene is to mutations), disease and phenotype associations and external links. Further: the sources, why CoGA stores them in Postgres instead of querying them live each time, the refresh as a background job, and how each import of reference data is recorded with source, time and the person who ran it. Reference for gene synchronisation: docs/data-import.md.

A cache is a local copy that you do not have to fetch again each time; a worker is a background process that does long-running work, separate from the web request.

The Gene Explorer

The Gene Explorer is the page /genes (frontend/src/pages/genes/GeneInfoPage.tsx). The user types a symbol, chooses a suggestion and sees one merged profile. The page uses two endpoints, both behind a login:

Endpoint Supplies
GET /api/genes/search?q= Suggestions: symbols that start with the input (at least two characters)
GET /api/genes/profile?symbol=… The full gene profile

The profile shows, among other things:

  • the gene's location on GRCh38 and, where available, on T2T-CHM13 and GRCh37;
  • the transcripts with their badges (MANE, Canonical, CCDS, …);
  • constraint metrics (gnomAD pLI and LOEUF, pHaplo/pTriplo, missense Z);
  • disease and phenotype associations (OMIM, GenCC, ClinGen, Orphanet, ClinVar, and Monarch with the phenotypes the family shares);
  • whether the gene is on the ACMG list of secondary findings (below);
  • the panels the gene is in;
  • external links (Ensembl, NCBI, OMIM, ClinGen, gnomAD, …);
  • for each source a status with the time of the last refresh. This makes the provenance visible on the page itself.

ACMG secondary findings. The row ACMG secondary finding says whether the gene is on the ACMG SF list: the genes that the ACMG recommends reporting as a secondary finding in exome and genome sequencing. CoGA ships that list (ACMG SF v3.3, below).

  • If the gene is on it, the row shows the version (with a link to the publication), the phenotype, the category, the inheritance, the variants to report and the list's footnotes for the gene (e.g. for TTN: only truncating variants).
  • Otherwise it says Not on ACMG SF v3.3.
  • Not checked means that the list was not read for this gene: the gene information has no status for the list, or the list could not be read.

ClinGen dosage. Under ClinGen dosage assertions there are two kinds of items. ClinGen dosage curation comes from ClinGen's own dosage file: the haploinsufficiency and the triplosensitivity in words, the date of the curation and a link to ClinGen's report. The item with an HI score is the same haploinsufficiency score as dbNSFP supplies it.

The profile combines two Postgres tables: genes (reference genes per assembly, with chromosome, position, exons and transcript) and gene_info (the stored enrichment: name, summary, aliases, IDs, constraint, disease associations). If a gene is on both an ordinary chromosome and an alternative sequence, the ordinary chromosome wins. If the chosen assembly has no enrichment yet, the profile takes the most recent enrichment of the same symbol on another human assembly.

Access. If a family or project is passed (for phenotype matching), the backend first checks access. A family or project outside the user's projects gets the same answer as an ID that does not exist (404 Family not found or 404 Project not found). This way the profile leaks no family context, nor which families or projects exist.

Where in the code: backend/app/routers/genes.py and build_gene_profile in backend/app/services/gene_metadata_service.py.

Diseases on the variant cards. The cards of the small variants and of the monogenic NIPT fetch the disease links of all genes on the page in one request: GET /api/genes/disease-links?symbol=…&symbol=… (at most 200 genes, behind a login). For each gene come the links from Monarch (causal first, then by name, as in the profile) and the OMIM diseases from gene_info of the first human assembly that has the gene (GRCh38 first). Under the card's header there are up to three diseases: Monarch's causal links, otherwise the OMIM diseases, otherwise Monarch's associations, marked as not causal. Each name links to the disease in Monarch, or in OMIM for an OMIM disease (which has no MONDO ID). More annotations & detail shows all links, from the same response. If the request fails, the card says so, so that a gene does not appear to have no disease.

Inheritance, dosage sensitivity and ACMG SF on the card. The same response gives three more things per gene, from the same gene_info. The card shows them in a line under the diseases.

  • Modes of inheritance (inheritance). A mode counts if a curation from GenCC (gencc_assertions, moi_title) or from ClinGen gene–disease validity (clingen_validity_assertions, moi) names it with the classification Definitive, Strong, Moderate or Supportive. Limited, Disputed, Refuted, No known disease relationship, Animal model only or no classification do not count, nor does an unknown or other mode. The modes are AD, AR, SD, XLD, XLR, XL, MT and YL, each with the curations that name it (e.g. GenCC Definitive), the strongest first. Dominant and recessive each have their own colour. If the gene has a disease but no counted curation, it says None curated in GenCC or ClinGen.
  • ClinGen's dosage curation (dosage): from ClinGen's own file (both scores, the curation's page), otherwise from the copy of the HI score in dbNSFP. The scores are ClinGen's: 3 sufficient, 2 emerging, 1 little, 0 no evidence, 30 autosomal recessive phenotype, 40 dosage sensitivity unlikely. The card shows them only if there is a curation.
  • The ACMG SF list (acmg_secondary_finding). If the gene is on it, the line shows a chip such as ACMG SF v3.3, with the list's phenotype, category, inheritance and variants to report on hover. The status follows source_status.acmg_sf: listed, not_listed (the list was read and does not name the gene), unread (the list could not be read) or not_consulted. With unread the card says The ACMG SF list could not be read, so that a missing chip does not read as "not on the list"; with the other two it shows nothing.

Where in the code: list_gene_disease_links, _inheritance_entries, _dosage_entry and _acmg_secondary_finding_entry in backend/app/services/gene_metadata_service.py; frontend/src/pages/families/geneDiseaseLinks.ts and VariantGeneDiseases.tsx.

Transcript badges

Not every transcript is clinically equivalent. MANE Select is the recommended reference transcript, MANE Plus Clinical a clinically important additional transcript; Ensembl Canonical and CCDS are supplementary references. The badges come first from the per-transcript tags in the gene annotation: GENCODE labels MANE and Canonical, and gives the CCDS ID. Only if those are missing does the page compare the transcript ID with the reference transcripts in the profile, without the version number (NM_007294.4 = NM_007294). Annotated transcripts are at the top, MANE first.

In a genome window the backend chooses the best transcript per gene in the same way: MANE Select, then Ensembl Canonical, then the rest.

Where in the code: GeneInfoPage.tsx; the choice per gene in backend/app/services/reference_metadata_service.py.

Where the data come from

Reference genes. For GRCh38 the genes come from the GENCODE annotation, for T2T-CHM13 from UCSC's RefSeq-derived annotation. If that fails, CoGA falls back on a UCSC gene table and records that (chapter 4).

The enrichment comes from two kinds of sources:

  • Bulk files, read once per job and looked up per symbol: the HGNC complete set (the register of which genes exist, with previous symbols, aliases and IDs), the local dbNSFP gene file (the richest source: constraint, OMIM and Orphanet associations, GO terms, pathways, HPO terms, expression, orthologues), ClinGen gene validity and dosage, GenCC, ClinVar gene-condition and the ACMG SF list. Each bulk source is consulted for every gene.
  • The ACMG SF list ships with CoGA in data/ref-data/acmg-sf/: ACMG SF v3.3 (Genetics in Medicine, 2025), 84 genes. The README there names the publication, how the list was transcribed and checked, and how to update it (a controlled change). CoGA looks up a gene on the list by its HGNC ID. This way a gene that HGNC renamed after the publication is still on it.
  • One live source per gene: NCBI Gene, for a summary of genes that dbNSFP does not cover. Only during a refresh, never when a page is opened. Across the whole process one request goes to NCBI every 0.4 seconds, under the limit of three per second that NCBI applies without an API key. If the HGNC complete set gives the NCBI Gene ID, one request suffices instead of two.

HGNC, not the annotation, determines which genes exist. A locus with a symbol that HGNC does not know is not a gene and gets no enrichment. A renamed symbol is folded into the current one via the previous symbols and aliases. An old symbol that two genes lay claim to is left out rather than guessed. If the HGNC complete set could not be loaded, HGNC is error for every gene, and the refresh takes the annotation's symbols as they are, without folding renamed symbols.

Provenance per source. Each source gets a status per gene:

  • success: the source had a record;
  • missing: queried, but nothing for this gene;
  • not_consulted: never queried, so no statement about coverage;
  • error: downloading or reading failed.

If the local dbNSFP file is missing, dbNSFP is missing for every gene, without a release and with the message that the file was not found. A new installation synchronises its genes even without the file; the first start that finds the file while no gene has been synchronised with it queues a synchronisation that adds it (chapter 4). For the ACMG SF list, missing means "not on the list". That is why CoGA refuses, as a whole, a list that is missing, unreadable or incomplete. Incomplete means: no version, a gene without a symbol, HGNC ID, phenotype or category, a gene that appears twice, or a number of genes other than the list itself states. Each gene then gets error, and the gene page says that the list could not be read, never that the gene is not on it.

Each status comes with the time, the URL and, if the source states it, the release that the response gave, with the SHA-256 of the bytes read. A source that states no release (ClinVar) deliberately gets none, instead of an invented version. The URLs of the bulk sources and the path to dbNSFP are settings (.env.example).

Gene panels from PanelApp are not used for the enrichment, but are imported as panels (chapter 15).

Where in the code: backend/app/services/gene_info_bulk_sources.py (the bulk sources) and gene_info_external.py (NCBI and the merging).

Why and how CoGA stores this

The external sources are not queried at every page visit. That would be slow, fragile and not reproducible: two reviewers could see different data. The enrichment is therefore in the Postgres table gene_info, one row per assembly and symbol, with the source status and the time of the last refresh. The page reads only from that table.

Refreshing as a background job. A full refresh covers thousands of genes and therefore runs as a job in gene_info_refresh_jobs, for one gene or all human genes.

  • There can be only one active job at a time. The database enforces that; a second request gets 409.
  • Each job stores who requested it: the administrator's account (requested_by_id) and the e-mail address under which it was requested (requested_by). The first job at installation belongs to no account and gets startup-bootstrap.
  • A worker runs the job only while that account is an active administrator. If the account has been deactivated, is no longer an administrator or no longer exists, the job ends failed with the reason, without writing a gene record. The slot then becomes free for the next refresh.
  • A worker takes the job, processes the genes and regularly writes the progress. A job whose worker stopped is picked up again after a while.

Administration. On the Gene reference sync page (GeneReferenceAdminPage.tsx) an administrator can have one gene or all genes refreshed, follow the active job, view the coverage per source (with the columns Release, No record and Not consulted) and see the recent jobs. All endpoints for this (/api/admin/gene-reference/...) are for administrators only.

Where in the code: backend/app/services/gene_info_jobs_pg.py; the worker starts and stops in the lifespan of backend/app/main.py.

Version control of reference data

For reproducibility under the IVDR, every import of reference data is recorded. That applies to genes, cytobands, blacklist, clinical CNVs, segmental duplications and DGV, via an upload, the automatic import, a rebuild of the CNV knowledge base, a DGV load or the DGV import script (scripts/import_dgv.py). Every import writes a row in reference_dataset_imports: the assembly, the kind of dataset, the number of rows, whether existing data were replaced, the source and its URL, the release that the source states about itself, who did the import and when.

Only GENCODE states a release: the import takes the version and the date from the GTF header. A rebuild of the CNV knowledge base records as its release the files it was built from, without a date (chapter 15). A DGV load records the pinned release, the file and its SHA-256, with the date of the release. For the other sources (the UCSC tables and UCSC's T2T GTF, uploads, the built-in reference files and the DGV script) it says not stated, without a date. The Organisms and assemblies page (/reference-data) shows that history (Recent reference activity) and the status per assembly and dataset.

Gene panels get a new version whenever their genes or regions change, also through a new import from PanelApp (a local panel also on a new description). Each version is kept with the full gene list; deleting a panel also deletes its versions (chapter 15).

Together, reference_dataset_imports (which reference data were active, and since when), the panel versions (which gene set a panel had) and the source status in gene_info (which sources and releases supplied the enrichment) thus answer an auditor's question: which reference data lay under this result? In addition, the signed report freezes the source of the gene loci and the Monarch release (chapter 11).

Where in the code: backend/app/services/reference_metadata_service.py (the imports and their registration) and reference_source_service.py (the automatic import); the page frontend/src/pages/reference/ReferenceCatalogPage.tsx.

backend/app/services/gene_info_bulk_sources.py · gene_info_external.py The bulk sources, the ACMG SF list included; NCBI and the merging
data/ref-data/acmg-sf/ The ACMG SF list shipped with CoGA (v3.3) and its README

14. Variant Explorer

This chapter describes the Global Small Variant Explorer: a search function that summarises small variants (SNVs and indels) across all projects a user has access to, not within one family. Results never leak outside the user's projects (see Isolation between projects). An explanation for users is in the in-app user guide (section explorers).

A few terms:

  • Carrier: a sample that carries the alternative allele, heterozygous or homozygous.
  • Aggregation: counting, per unique variant, how many samples and families carry it.
  • Assembly: the version of the reference genome (e.g. GRCh38); variants of different assemblies are never counted together.
  • Keyset pagination: paging through a large result page by page without costly jumps (OFFSET), by remembering where the previous page ended.

Purpose and screen

A family's filter page (chapter 8) answers "which variants are in this family?". The Variant Explorer turns the question around: "in how many samples and families of my accessible cohort does this variant occur?". Each row is one unique variant, with the counters Total samples, Het, Hom and Families.

The screen (/variant-explorer) has a drop-down list for the assembly, a filter on genotype per sample, the usual annotation filter form and the results, with tabs for four views of the same filtered variants: by variant, by gene, by transcript and by cohort frequency (see The views by gene, transcript and cohort frequency). A click on a counter opens a window with the carriers, grouped by family, with a link to each family. The form is that of the family page, without the fields for family and samples. Filters the Explorer does not apply are not shown, and their parameters are not sent: an interval list, transcript, callset, genes and intervals to exclude, tags to exclude, "has notes" and Pass variants only. That last one remains a filter of the family page, which reads only the family members shown (the owner's decision of 6 November 2026).

Where in the code: frontend/src/pages/variant-explorer/ (GlobalSmallVariantExplorerPage.tsx, globalSmallVariantSearch.ts, GlobalSmallVariantTable.tsx, ExplorerViews.tsx, VariantCarrierModal.tsx).

Endpoints

All endpoints are under /api/variant-explorer and require a login.

Endpoint Purpose
GET /variant-explorer/assemblies The accessible assemblies, with the number of projects per assembly
GET /variant-explorer/samples The samples the user's families show, their active members (for the genotype filter)
GET /variant-explorer/small-variants The paginated, aggregated variant list
GET /variant-explorer/small-variants/export The same results as CSV, up to 50,000 rows; a file that does not hold every hit says so (see The CSV export)
GET /variant-explorer/small-variants/genes The view by gene: per gene the variants and the summed carriers
GET /variant-explorer/small-variants/transcripts The view by transcript: per transcript the variants per consequence class and the summed carriers
GET /variant-explorer/small-variants/frequency The view by cohort frequency: the variants per class of carriers and of gnomAD frequency
GET /variant-explorer/small-variants/{variant_key}/carriers The carriers of one variant, per family
GET /variant-explorer/small-variant-tags The tag definitions of the accessible projects

The filters are parsed in one place. That guarantees that the list, the CSV export and the three views use the same filters.

Where in the code: backend/app/routers/variant_explorer.py; the logic in backend/app/services/variant_explorer_service.py and variant_explorer_views.py.

How the carriers are counted

The Explorer counts from the carrier summary (SNV_INDEL/carriers, backend/app/services/variant_carrier_summary.py), which CoGA maintains while the families' variants are written. Counting directly from entries would read every row of every family for each page: from three or four whole genomes on, that goes over the limit of 110 s (docs/clickhouse-scale-benchmark.md). The summary is derived data: every row can be recomputed from entries and the families' members and projects in Postgres.

What a family contributes. A family's contribution reads its rows of entries under one project it is linked to (every write writes the rows under every project of the family, so every copy holds the same rows), with FINAL. Per variant it counts the carriers among the samples the family shows, and keeps the rows apart per class: annotation set, rsID, gene symbols and whether the callset is imputed, the columns the filters read per row.

  • A variant whose rows in the family all fall in one class, and that is carried by no sample another family also shows, gives one sum row: one family, its carriers, heterozygous and homozygous carriers, deduplicated across its callsets. Sum rows of the same variant, the same projects and the same class are added up across the families.
  • Otherwise the variant gives one carrier row per class and carrier, with family and person: two callsets with a different annotation, an ordinary and an imputed callset, or a person two families show. That way the Explorer counts each person once across the classes and families its filters keep. Two samples linked as the same individual (a person sampled twice) are one carrier under the first of their sample IDs, over the links of every family of the assembly. A carrier counts as homozygous when any of the person's calls of the variant is homozygous, and as heterozygous otherwise: the heterozygous and homozygous carriers add up to the carriers, in a sum row too.
  • A marker per family (xpos = key = 0) says which generation of its contribution the table holds. Contribution and marker arrive together in one part of the table (ATTACH PARTITION … FROM from a staging table, merged into one part): the table holds both or neither. A contribution disappears by writing the same rows negatively; the sums then cancel out, even before the parts are merged.

Who maintains the summary. Every function that writes a family's rows of entries first removes its contribution (detach_family_variant_carriers), under the family's write lock (chapter 3). It recomputes that contribution from the rows it was computed from; the data version proves that those have not changed. The variant-carrier worker (reconcile_variant_carriers) adds, every 5 s, the contribution of each family whose rows, shown members, their same-individual links or projects differ from what the table holds. It too works under the write lock, but only tries to take it: a family an import is holding comes up in the next round. If a contribution cannot be removed exactly, the summary is emptied and rebuilt. A family that the table does not hold as it currently is, is called pending: the page says how many families of the scope are pending, and counts them as the table holds them (during an import not at all; after a change of members or projects, for a few seconds as before the change).

Per variant:

  • only real carriers count. Het, Hom and carrier follow the genotype classes of backend/app/services/genotypes.py (chapter 8), so that e.g. a haploid 1 counts as homozygous;
  • each sample and each family counts once, even if it occurs under several accessible projects or in two callsets;
  • imputed and phased calls (source glimpse2 or shapeit) do not count, unless the user ticks Include imputed variants (GLIMPSE2 / SHAPEIT). That applies to the counters, the per-sample conditions and the carrier window;
  • only the calls of the samples their family shows count (below).

Only the samples their family shows. A row of entries holds a call of every sample of the VCF it was imported from. If a member is removed from the family (remove_members on a change of the family structure, without erasing the data), their calls stay in those rows. The family page no longer shows the member: it reads only the calls of the active members (_visible_clickhouse_sample_ids). The Explorer reads every row the same way (the owner's decision of 6 November 2026):

  • A family's contribution to the summary counts only the calls of its active members; if the list changes, the worker recomputes the contribution.
  • The carrier window and the per-sample genotype filter read in Postgres the active members of each family of the accessible projects (_shown_members in variant_explorer_service.py). From those they make the pairs (family, sample), each sample under its name and its UUID (_shown_calls): a call counts only if its pair is among them.

This therefore applies to the count, the counters, the CSV export, the carrier window and the per-sample genotype filter. A variant that only such a removed member carries does not appear. A sample that is a member of another family does count in that family's rows, not in those of the old one.

The carriers per family. The carrier window fetches the carriers of one variant (capped, with a notice if there are more), only the members their family shows. It keeps one record per family and sample (homozygous takes precedence) and links it to the names of family and project from Postgres, and to the name, role and phenotype of the member in that family. A family the user may not see is missing from that link; its carrier is then skipped. The link is therefore also a second access check.

Where tested: backend/tests/integration/test_variant_explorer_visible_members_clickhouse.py (on real ClickHouse and Postgres: a family of four from which father and brother were removed, the father as a member of a family of his own; the count, the counters, the export, the carrier window, the genotype filter and the drop-down list of samples); backend/tests/integration/test_variant_carrier_summary_clickhouse.py (on real ClickHouse and Postgres: the list and the export from the summary count the same variants and carriers as the count over entries, under five filters and three scopes, with a family under two projects, two callsets with a different annotation, an imputed callset, a removed member and a sample two families show; and again after a change of members, a deletion and a new write, which are pending until the next round; a broad filter, read window by window, gives the same list, export and count as one query, in four sort orders, also for a variant on a contig outside the chromosomes); backend/tests/test_variant_carrier_summary.py.

Filters

On top of the family page's filters (location, type, gene, rsID, panel, impact, ClinVar, gnomAD, CADD, REVEL, SpliceAI, …) the Explorer knows two kinds of filters:

  1. Tags and classifications. These are stored per family in Postgres. If the user filters on them, the Explorer first looks up in Postgres the matching variant ids within the accessible projects, and passes that list to the ClickHouse query. An empty list gives an empty result straight away. The list is written literally into the query and therefore holds at most 200,000 ids: the first in variant id order, so that the same filter always gives the same list. Postgres reads one more, to know whether more matched; in that case the search can miss hits. The CSV export reports that, the list on screen does not.
  2. Genotype per sample. The user adds rules of the form sample with Het, Hom or Het + Hom. Each rule is a separate condition; a variant must satisfy all rules. The Explorer reads the sample's call with the sample filter of the family page (_small_sample_call_condition in clickhouse_variant_queries.py), so with the same genotype classes: a haploid 1 is homozygous, a 1/2 heterozygous. It does read per variant, though, not per row: it keeps a variant that the sample carries with that genotype in one of its rows, and then counts all carriers of the cohort. Reading per row would count only the carriers of that sample's family; the family page keeps only the rows of its own family. This is the only documented difference between the two (the owner's decision of 6 November 2026). It reads the sample's call only in the rows of a family that shows it, under its name or its UUID. A sample no family shows, such as a member removed from their family, keeps no variant, and the drop-down list does not offer it.

One definition: the building blocks of the family search. Every filter the Explorer shares with the family page, it builds with the function of the family search in clickhouse_variant_queries.py (_carriers_where in variant_explorer_service.py calls them, on the rows of the summary, which have the same columns):

  • _small_row_filter_clauses: the variant type, the location and the rsID (it reads the imputed callsets from the summary's own column imputed);
  • _small_annotation_filter_clauses: the gene, the annotation filters per transcript and the ClinVar statuses to exclude;
  • _small_panel_filter_condition: the panel (below).

It reads each row of the summary the way the family page reads the rows of that class, with their own annotation: the variant key and the annotation set (chapter 8). A row is therefore kept exactly when the family page of its family shows the variant, and a row of the Explorer adds up the families and carriers of those family pages. This only makes a difference if the same variant was imported in two families with a different annotation (two VEP runs). An example: family A says stop gained (HIGH), family B missense (MODERATE). With impact HIGH, A's family page shows the variant, B's does not; the Explorer shows it with only A's carriers (the owner's decision of 6 November 2026).

  • The location. The chromosome applies with or without chr, and the mitochondrion as chrM, M or MT (_chromosome_options). A variant falls within the location if it starts there (its position on or after the start, on or before the end).
  • The gene. In the row's gene symbols, or in the gene index of its annotation (gene symbols and Ensembl gene ids), however it is written.
  • The rsID. In the row's rsID or in that of its annotation, as typed but without surrounding spaces.
  • The ClinVar statuses to exclude. No transcript of the row's annotation has that status.
  • The annotation filters per transcript must hold together for one transcript (one row of the table annotations), with the condition _small_annotation_filter_condition: impact and consequence, HGVS, the ClinVar status, the frequency limits, the predictors, and Canonical only, MANE only and LoF only. The family page reads that condition on its rows' own transcripts (_small_own_transcripts_condition), except with a transcript or HGVS text. The rows of the summary have no transcripts: the Explorer reads the condition on the shared table annotations (_small_annotation_row_membership_condition). Both keep the same rows. The frequency limits have the exception "a (likely) pathogenic ClinVar variant passes the frequency filter", on the same ClinVar terms. With MANE only and impact HIGH, a variant whose HIGH transcript is not the MANE transcript thus drops out. Of the predictors (CADD, REVEL, SpliceAI, SIFT, PolyPhen), one is enough. A SpliceAI score at or above the threshold also counts as a hit for impact and consequence.

Where tested: backend/tests/integration/test_variant_explorer_filter_rule_clickhouse.py (on real ClickHouse: two families, one variant under two annotations, the mitochondrion as M and as MT; for each filter, each family page keeps what the rule keeps, and each row of the Explorer adds up the families and carriers of those pages); backend/tests/test_variant_explorer_service.py (each clause of the Explorer is that of the family search, with the same parameters, the per-transcript conditions read on the shared table).

The gene panel, as on the family page. The Explorer reads a panel the way the family page reads it (_fetch_panel_constraints in clickhouse_family_variants.py), for the search's assembly:

  • the panel's genes and the names of its stored regions;
  • the regions stored for that assembly (PanelApp's coordinates);
  • the locus of each gene in that assembly's gene reference.

It applies it with the family page's condition (_small_panel_filter_condition in clickhouse_variant_queries.py): a variant in one of the regions, or with one of the genes in its row's gene symbols or in the gene index, however large the panel. A gene panel with more than 1000 regions, such as the Mendeliome, it also compares by position (as the family page does) (the owner's decision of 14 October 2026). A panel without genes and without regions for the assembly keeps nothing. A panel that does not exist gives 404, an id that is not a UUID 400, as on the family page.

Only the regions does the Explorer look up differently, with the same answer. Testing every row against every region (arrayExists, the rule of _small_region_filter_condition) would take minutes across all families of the cohort for a panel of a thousand genes. The Explorer (_region_key_condition in variant_explorer_service.py) therefore makes a join on windows of 64 kb:

  • each region goes under every 64 kb window it touches;
  • each variant goes, at its position in the annotation index, under every window its REF touches;
  • a pair that shares a window is kept if the two overlap according to the family page's rule: the same chromosome (chr1 and 1, M and MT count as the same), the first base of the REF on or before the end of the region, and the last on or after its start.

Two that overlap share the window of a base they have in common; none therefore drops out. It reads the regions as the family page reads them (_small_region_bounds). The family page makes the same join, over the family's own rows (_small_family_region_condition in clickhouse_variant_queries.py). Testing every row against every region costs 1.3 s there for 500 regions and 2.1 s for 1000, for a family of about 190,000 rows.

MANE only also follows the family page: a transcript counts if it is MANE Select or MANE Plus Clinical. Both read those flags from one list, MANE_ONLY_TRANSCRIPT_FLAGS in backend/app/services/clickhouse_variant_records.py. VEP sets those flags only on GRCh38: on GRCh37 and T2T, MANE only keeps nothing on either page.

Every value the user supplies goes as a named parameter (%(naam)s) to the ClickHouse client, which puts it escaped into the query. CoGA's code never pastes it into the text itself (chapter 7).

The views by gene, transcript and cohort frequency

Besides the list by variant, the Explorer shows the same filtered variants in three other ways (the owner's choices of 12 November 2026). Each view reads the same rows of the summary with the same filters (_carriers_where), linked to their own annotation (variant key and annotation set), per genome window of 50 Mb, the same windows as those of the list for a broad filter (see Speed): that way the query of a window holds only the variants of that window, however large the cohort. The windows are then added up. Each variant lies in exactly one window, including a variant on a contig outside the chromosomes (chrUn_… and the like, to which xpos jointly gives rank 99).

  • By gene. One row per gene that the annotation of a filtered variant names (VEP's gene symbol): the number of variants, also per most severe impact on that gene, and the carriers summed across those variants: a sample with two variants in the gene counts twice. A variant counts for a gene over the rows whose annotation names that gene, as the list with that gene filter counts it; a gene's row is therefore the sum of that list. A click on the gene opens that list.
  • By transcript. One row per transcript that the annotation of a filtered variant names, all transcripts or only the MANE (Select or Plus Clinical) or canonical transcripts, with the gene, the variants per most severe consequence class on that transcript (loss of function, missense or in-frame, splice region, synonymous, other) and the summed carriers.
  • By cohort frequency. A cross table of the filtered variants: their number of carriers in the user's projects (1, 2–5, 6–20, 21–100, more than 100) against the class of the gnomAD allele frequency of their own annotation (not in gnomAD, below 0.1 %, 0.1–1 %, 1–5 %, 5 % and more). What is frequent here and rare in gnomAD can be an artefact or a founder variant. A click on a cell opens the list with two filters only the Explorer knows: the number of carriers (min_total_samples, max_total_samples, after the count) and the gnomAD class (gnomad_af_class, on each row's annotation).

Where tested: backend/tests/integration/test_variant_carrier_summary_clickhouse.py (the row of a gene and of a transcript is the sum of the list with that gene filter; the cells count each variant once); frontend/src/pages/variant-explorer/__tests__/ExplorerViews.test.tsx.

The CSV export

The export uses the same filters and sort order as the list, without pagination, and writes at most 50,000 rows. It asks ClickHouse for one row more: if that row comes back, more variants matched than the file holds. Such a file reports that, just like the exports of the family page:

  • the file name says TRUNCATED: variant-explorer-…-TRUNCATED-first-50000.csv;
  • the headers say how many rows were written (X-CoGA-Export-Rows), that more matched (X-CoGA-Export-Truncated), the limit (X-CoGA-Export-Limit) and why (X-CoGA-Export-Truncated-Reason: row-limit);
  • the screen shows a warning asking to refine the filters.

If the list of the tag or classification filter was cut off (see Filters), a hit can be missing anywhere in the file, however few rows it has. The reason is then review-filter-limit, the name …-TRUNCATED-partial-search.csv, and the warning asks to filter on fewer tags or classifications. That reason takes precedence over row-limit.

The column Classification holds the most severe class the variant's reviews show (see Traceability), Classification text next to it the classification text of the review that shows that class, as stored: its own text or that of the compound-het pair, empty for a review with only a class tag (classification_text in GlobalVariantRowOut). The tags come from all reviews.

The export looks up the rows' reviews (tags, classification, last review) in Postgres, with the variant ids as one array parameter. With one parameter per id, every export of more than 32,767 rows would fail: asyncpg refuses a query with more parameters.

Where in the code: export_global_small_variants and _review_filter_variant_ids in backend/app/services/variant_explorer_service.py; export_response_headers in backend/app/core/csv_export.py; describeCsvExport and truncatedExportMessage in frontend/src/lib/csvExport.ts.

Isolation between projects

For an auditor this is the most important part. Every query is strictly limited to the user's projects:

  • The scope is determined in one place. A superuser and an administrator (superuser, admin; has_superuser_rights) see all projects, other users only their own projects. Without projects the result is guaranteed to be empty.
  • Every query is given those projects as a mandatory argument: the list query, the capped count and the views read only the summary rows of families linked to one of those projects (hasAny(projects, …)); the per-sample conditions and the carrier query only the rows of entries of those projects (project_guid IN …). Postgres reads the list of members the families show only for the families of those projects. project_guid and the projects of a summary row are the project UUIDs in Postgres. Rows of other projects therefore drop out before anything is counted. The annotation filters and the panel read, per row (variant key and annotation set), the tables annotations, annotation_index and gene_index; the annotation of the visible page then comes from the annotation index. None of those tables holds project, family or sample data.
  • The frontend only shows a message when there is nothing ("… in your accessible projects"); the isolation lies entirely on the server.

The file backend/app/services/data_scope.py, despite its name, is not about this isolation but about chromosome names. The access scope is in variant_explorer_service.py (resolve_scope).

Traceability. Every carrier can be traced back to its family and project. The review (tags, classification, last review) comes from small_variant_reviews (chapter 10). If a variant was reviewed in several families or in several analyses of a family, the row shows the tags of all reviews and the most severe classification (_classification_rank); a shared review that every analysis of the family replaced with its own does not count (review_in_effect_sql). That ranking reads the class from the stored text, in any form: the label of the review window ("Pathogenic - class 5"), a class key (acmg_class_5, cnv_class_5) or the class word, however it is written. Text that names no class ranks lowest.

Each review counts with the class the family page shows for it (review_class_label in review_pg_utils.py, the same rule as normalizeReviewClassification in the frontend): a bare class word ("VUS") as its label, otherwise the review's most severe class tag (acmg_class_5 … acmg_class_1) as its label, otherwise the text as stored. So a review that has only a class tag, without classification text, also shows its class. The variant's own review takes precedence over that of the compound-het pair. Postgres reads the reviews in a fixed order (last saved first, then by family id), and the server also imposes that order itself: of two reviews with the same class, the row shows that of the last saved, at equal time that of the lowest family id. The classification filter, like that of the family page (list_matching_small_variant_review_ids), keeps a variant by the class the review or the pair's review shows, with the same rule in SQL (review_class_label_sql, chapter 10); that way it also finds a review with only a class tag. It keeps a variant for which one review shows that class, as the family page of that family does; the row can show the more severe class of another family.

Where in the code: resolve_scope in backend/app/services/variant_explorer_service.py; the role rules in backend/app/services/access_control.py.

Speed

The Explorer may query many projects and millions of genotypes. A few choices keep that workable:

  • The carrier summary. A page reads one row per variant, project set and class, not one per family: what it reads grows with the number of distinct variants, not with the number of genomes. The table is sorted on xpos, key and the Explorer groups in that order (optimize_aggregation_in_order), so that a query holds the sums of one variant at a time. On the synthetic cohort of 250 genomes (a quarter of the variants per genome, 150 million rows in entries) the unfiltered page directly from entries takes more than 110 s; the times from the summary are in docs/clickhouse-scale-benchmark.md. On a synthetic summary the size of 1000 genomes (61 million variants) it takes about 7 s.

  • A broad filter, window by window. A filter that reads a subquery (an annotation filter, the panel, the rsID, the per-sample genotype filter) collects the variants it keeps, from the whole cohort, in a set that the query holds in its entirety.

    • The Explorer first asks in a single query, in which each set may hold at most two million variants (max_rows_in_set). Above that, ClickHouse refuses the query, without ever cutting the set short (set_overflow_mode = 'throw').
    • Then the Explorer reads the summary per genome window of 50 Mb (ExplorerWindow in variant_explorer_service.py), four at a time. Each variant lies in exactly one window, under every name of its chromosome the summary holds (1 and chr1, every contig outside the chromosomes). The subqueries read only that window's annotation, via the sort key of the annotation tables.
    • The count adds up the windows until it passes the limit. A page sorted by position reads the windows in order from the cursor until it is full. A page sorted by a count takes the first rows of each window and keeps the first of those. That way it gives the same variants, numbers and order as one query.
    • The Explorer reads the columns of a page (ID, rsID, gene symbols) for its variants only: each subquery is given their keys (annotation_keys).

    On a cohort the size of 1000 genomes (61 million variants), rare only keeps 52 million variants. In one query that goes over the 4 GB a query may use; window by window the page took 25 to 35 s with 320 MiB (6 to 9 s sorted by position). The panel of 5300 genes held 1.2 GiB in one query, 150 MiB window by window, in about the same time (docs/clickhouse-scale-benchmark.md).

  • Capped count. Above a fixed limit the Explorer reports the number as "N+" (total_is_estimated), instead of counting everything exactly. Grouped in the order of the table, the count stops at that limit.

  • The pairs (family, sample). For the carrier window and the genotype filter, the pairs of the members the families show are written literally into the query: two per member (name and UUID), each about 60 bytes. Ten thousand members give about 1.2 MB, within the 16 MiB of CLICKHOUSE_MAX_QUERY_SIZE. The carrier window looks up the rows of its variant by position in each family's rows (the position from the annotation index), not by reading the whole of entries.
  • Keyset pagination. The cursor remembers the last row, the sort order and a fingerprint of the filters. A cursor of a different sort order or of different filters is ignored, so that nobody pages wrongly without noticing.
  • Annotation filters per transcript (see Filters). The table annotations has one row per transcript, the smaller annotation index one per variant. A locus (chromosome, start, end) also bounds the transcript rows read, the gene index and the rows of the per-sample conditions, as on the family page. The display fields come only for the visible page.
  • A row's annotation by key and set. Each annotation filter builds a set of (variant key, annotation set) over the whole cohort (or over one window, see above), without the annotation version. In a measurement with the version included, a search with a frequency, impact or CADD filter on 4 million rows of 2 million variants took 0.6 to 1.0 s, without it 0.23 to 0.47 s, with about 10 % less memory (chapter 8).
  • A panel's regions as a join (see Filters). On a synthetic cohort of 2 million variants and 7.6 million rows in 40 families, that join found the variants of a panel of 1000 regions in a twentieth of a second. The per-row test took almost three minutes over the same cohort. With the Mendeliome by position (about 42,000 loci, merged into roughly one region per gene), the capped count on a synthetic cohort of 1.19 million variants took 0.16 s, against 0.10 s on gene symbol alone (docs/variant-ranking-cache.md).
